title: Android, Java & Kotlin
subtitle: Java core, Kotlin, Compose, Spring Boot

modules.title: Java Fundamentals
modules.summary: Core Java for Android and backend: types, control flow, strings, classes, collections, generics, lambdas.

blocks.text: A variable is a named box. In Java every box has a fixed type, written before the name: int price = 120.
There are two kinds of boxes. A primitive box (int, long, double, boolean, char, byte, short, float) holds the value itself. A reference box holds the address of an object that lives somewhere else.
Copying a primitive copies the value. Copying a reference copies the address, so two names can point at the same object.
Why it matters

The compiler uses the type to catch mistakes before the app runs, and the runtime uses it to know how much memory to reserve. The primitive and reference split exists for speed: small numbers are stored directly, with no object overhead.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A primitive is cash in your hand. A reference is a locker key. Photocopying cash gives you separate money. Copying a key gives two people access to the same locker.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift

Swift splits types into value types (struct, enum) and reference types (class). Java has no user-defined value types: only the eight primitives are copied by value, and every class instance is a reference.
Swift
final int x is close to let x. A plain int x is like var x. Java has no type inference for fields; local variables can use var since Java 10.
Flutter
Dart treats everything as an object, including int. Java int is not an object; the object form is Integer, and converting between them is called boxing.

blocks.text: What the JVM does for int[] cart = {1, 2, 3}

items: Reserve heap space for an int array of length 3
Write 1, 2, 3 into it
Store the array address in the local slot named cart
Later, when no reference points at the array, the garbage collector may reclaim it

blocks.text: The Kotlin file is the matching first lesson on the Kotlin side: val, var and nullable types.
Walkthrough
Declares a 32-bit integer and stores 120 in it. The type never changes.
Reads 120 out of price and stores a separate 120 in copy.
Copies the address. There is still one array.
Follows the address and changes the shared array, so cart[0] is now 42 as well.
final stops reassignment of the variable. It does not make an object immutable.
int times double gives a double (126.0). Math.round turns it into a long.
What happens when it runs

items: The JVM loads the Variables class and calls main on the main thread.
Each statement runs top to bottom in the same frame.
When main returns, the frame is dropped and the array and strings become unreachable.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Primitives declared inside a method live in that method frame and vanish when it returns.
Objects live on the heap for as long as something references them. In Android, holding a reference to an Activity after it is destroyed is how leaks start.
Integer, Long and friends are heap objects. A List<Integer> boxes every number, which costs memory and allocation time in hot loops.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Set a breakpoint and read the Variables pane in Android Studio. Objects show an @id; two variables with the same @id are the same object.
Use Evaluate Expression (Alt+F8 or Option+F8) to test a == b against a.equals(b).
A NullPointerException stack trace names the line. Since Java 14 the message also names the variable that was null.

blocks.text: In production

items: Money in e-commerce apps is carried as long paise or cents, never double, because 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in binary floating point.
Android SDK callbacks hand you references to shared objects such as Bundle and Intent. Mutating them affects every holder.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Money and ids on a server follow the same rules: long for amounts in the smallest unit, never double. BigDecimal is used where exact decimal arithmetic is required.
A request object passed between layers is a reference: a method that mutates it changes it for every later step.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Comparing strings with ==, which compares addresses.
Use a.equals(b), or Objects.equals(a, b) when either may be null.
int total = price * qty overflowing silently past 2,147,483,647.
Use long for money and counters that can grow, and keep money in the smallest unit (paise).
Assuming final List<String> items cannot be modified.
final only fixes the reference. Use List.copyOf or Collections.unmodifiableList for a read-only list.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Predict the output, then check it: create String a = "hi", String b = new String("hi") and print a == b and a.equals(b).
blocks.text: Hint: One compares addresses, the other compares characters.

blocks.title: Write a method swapFirstTwo(int[] values) that swaps elements 0 and 1. Explain why the caller sees the change.
Change int to Integer for price and copy. Does the behaviour of copy = 99 change? Why not?

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
blocks.text: Always pass-by-value. For primitives the value is copied. For objects the reference is copied, so the method can mutate the object but cannot make the caller point at a different one.

blocks.title: What is the difference between == and equals()?
blocks.text: == compares primitive values or object addresses. equals() compares content as defined by the class. Strings, boxed numbers and data holders must be compared with equals().

blocks.title: What is autoboxing and why can it hurt on Android?
blocks.text: The compiler converts between int and Integer automatically. Each boxing can allocate an object, which adds garbage collection pressure in loops and collections. Android provides SparseIntArray and similar classes to avoid it.

quiz.q: After int[] a = {1}; int[] b = a; b[0] = 5; what is a[0]?
quiz.why: b holds the same address as a, so the write is visible through both names.

quiz.q: Which of these is a primitive type?
quiz.why: String, Integer and arrays are objects on the heap. boolean is one of the eight primitives.

quiz.q: What does final guarantee for final List<String> names?
options: names cannot be pointed at another list
The strings are immutable because of final
quiz.why: final fixes the reference only. The list contents can still be modified.

blocks.text: Operators combine values: + - * / for arithmetic, % for the remainder, == and < for comparison, && and || for "and" and "or".
if and switch choose which code runs. for and while repeat code. break leaves a loop, continue skips to its next turn.
A method is a named block of code that takes inputs (parameters) and may give back a result (return value).
Why it matters

A program that only runs top to bottom can do one thing. Decisions and repetition are what let twenty lines handle a thousand different inputs. Methods let you name a piece of logic once and use it everywhere.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A recipe. "If the dough is sticky, add flour" is a condition. "Knead ten times" is a loop. "Make the sauce (see page 12)" is a method call.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
Java needs parentheses around conditions and semicolons after statements. switch falls through to the next case unless you write break or return; Swift never falls through by default.
Swift
7 / 2 is 3 in both languages for integers. Java silently widens int to double in 7 / 2.0; Swift makes you convert explicitly.
Flutter
Dart syntax here is almost identical to Java: same if, for, while, switch and ternary operator.

blocks.text: A for loop: for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)

items: Run the initialiser once: i = 1
Check the condition: i <= n
True: run the body
Run the update: i++
Go back to the check. False: the loop ends

blocks.text: Both files compute the same things. Notice that Kotlin uses if and when as expressions that produce a value.
Walkthrough
Integer division drops the fraction. % gives what is left over.
&& stops at the first false, so the right side is not evaluated when the left is false.
The ternary operator: a compact if that produces a value.
Each case ends with return here. With plain statements you need break, or execution falls into the next case.
The for-each loop visits every element without an index.
Skips the rest of this turn for odd numbers.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output includes: 7 / 2 = 3, 7 % 2 = 1, 7 / 2.0 = 3.5; grades distinction, pass, fail; steps = 111 for the while loop starting at 27; evens: 0 2 4 6, because the loop breaks at 8.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Each method call gets a stack frame holding its parameters and locals. The frame is gone when the method returns.
A loop variable declared in the for header exists only inside that loop.
Deep recursion adds a frame per call and can overflow the stack. A loop uses one frame.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Step Over (F8) runs one line; Step Into (F7) enters a method. Watch the loop variable change in the Variables pane.
A conditional breakpoint (right-click the breakpoint, add i == 37) stops only on the turn you care about.
Print the value just before the if that surprises you. Most "wrong branch" bugs are a wrong value, not a wrong condition.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: view code branches on state constantly: if (items.isEmpty()) showEmptyView(); and onOptionsItemSelected is a switch over menu ids.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: A request handler is conditions over the request: method, path, auth, validation. Loops process rows from a database or lines from a file.
Business rules such as fee tables and eligibility checks are exactly the if and switch code in this lesson, kept in small named methods so they can be tested.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Forgetting break in a switch, so two cases run.
End every case with break or return, or use the arrow form (case X -> ...) on Java 14 and later.
Using = where == was meant, or == to compare strings.
= assigns. == compares primitives. Use equals for strings.
Off-by-one loops: i <= array.length.
Valid indexes run from 0 to length - 1, so use i < array.length.
A while loop whose condition never becomes false.
Make sure the body changes something the condition reads.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Write isLeapYear(int year) using only if and %.
Print the multiplication table for 7 with a for loop, then again with a while loop.
Rewrite deliveryFee with if and else. Which reads better and why?

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is short-circuit evaluation?
blocks.text: && does not evaluate its right side when the left is false, and || does not when the left is true. This makes checks such as list != null && !list.isEmpty() safe. & and | on booleans always evaluate both sides.

blocks.title: Difference between while and do-while?
blocks.text: while checks the condition before each turn, so the body may run zero times. do-while checks after, so the body runs at least once.

blocks.title: Can a switch use strings? What are its limits?
blocks.text: Yes, since Java 7, along with integral types, enums and their wrappers. Classic switch compares with equals for strings, throws NullPointerException on null, and cannot switch on long, float or arbitrary objects. Newer Java versions add arrow cases, switch expressions and pattern matching.

quiz.q: What is 7 / 2 in Java when both are int?
quiz.why: Integer division discards the fractional part.

quiz.q: What happens in a switch case with no break or return?
options: Execution continues into the next case
quiz.why: This is called fall-through.

quiz.q: What does continue do?
options: Skips to the next turn of the loop
quiz.why: break leaves the loop; continue only skips the rest of the current turn.

blocks.text: A String is text. Once created it never changes: every method that seems to change it returns a new String.
An array is a fixed-length row of values of one type. You reach each value by its position, starting at 0.
To build text piece by piece, use StringBuilder, which can change.
Why it matters
Nearly all data entering a program arrives as text: user input, JSON, file contents, URLs. Arrays are the simplest container and the thing every other collection is built on.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A String is a printed page: to change a word you print a new page. A StringBuilder is a whiteboard. An array is an egg carton: a fixed number of numbered slots.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
Swift String is a value type and == compares content. In Java, == on strings compares addresses, so you must call equals.
Swift
A Java array has a fixed length and no append. Swift Array grows; its Java counterpart is ArrayList.
Swift
Java has no string interpolation. You concatenate with + or use String.format. Kotlin and Swift both interpolate.

blocks.text: name.toUpperCase()

items: Read the characters of name
Create a new String holding the upper-case characters
Return the new String
name still refers to the original, unchanged

blocks.text: Walkthrough
Returns a new String. If you do not keep the result, nothing happened.
Compares addresses. False here even though both say milk.
%d is an integer, %02d pads to two digits with a zero.
One growing buffer. Using + in a loop would create a new String every turn.
Three slots, each starting at 0. The length can never change.
Sorts the array in place. Arrays.toString prints its contents.
Index 3 does not exist in an array of length 3, so Java throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output includes: == false, equals true; the sorted array [40, 75, 120]; and the message "Index 3 out of bounds for length 3".

blocks.text: Memory

items: String literals are shared from a pool, which is safe because strings cannot change.
Concatenating in a loop creates many short-lived strings. StringBuilder creates one buffer.
An array of objects holds references, not the objects. An int[] holds the numbers themselves in one block.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: The debugger shows a String's value and an object id. Two variables with different ids are different objects, even with the same text.
For "the strings look equal but equals is false", print the lengths and check for trailing spaces or different letter case.
The exception message for an array names the bad index and the length.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: user-visible text comes from string resources, not literals; TextView.setText takes a CharSequence; and Arrays appear in permission results and varargs.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Parsing and building text is daily work: paths, query strings, headers, CSV, log lines. String.split, substring and format do most of it.
Request and response bodies are bytes: text.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8) and new String(bytes, UTF_8). Always name the charset.
String concatenation into SQL is how SQL injection happens. Use PreparedStatement parameters.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: if (status == "ok")
Use "ok".equals(status), which also survives a null status.
Calling name.trim() and ignoring the result.
Assign it: name = name.trim().
Printing an array with System.out.println(array) and getting [I@1b6d3586.
Use Arrays.toString(array).
Storing a password in a String.
Strings stay in memory until collected and cannot be wiped. Use char[] and clear it.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Write a method that reverses a String using StringBuilder, and another that checks whether it is a palindrome.
Given int[] values, return the second largest without sorting.
Split "name=asha;city=pune" into a Map<String, String>.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Why are Strings immutable in Java?
blocks.text: So they can be shared safely between threads and pooled, so their hash code can be cached (making them good map keys), and for security, since a file path or class name cannot change after it was checked.

blocks.title: String, StringBuilder, StringBuffer?
blocks.text: String is immutable. StringBuilder is mutable and not synchronised: the normal choice. StringBuffer is the older, synchronised version, rarely needed.

blocks.title: How do arrays differ from ArrayList?
blocks.text: An array has a fixed length, can hold primitives directly and has no methods beyond length. ArrayList grows, holds only objects (so numbers are boxed) and offers add, remove, contains and so on. ArrayList is backed by an array that it replaces with a larger one when full.

quiz.q: After String s = "a"; s.concat("b"); what is s?
quiz.why: Strings are immutable. concat returned a new String that was not kept.

quiz.q: What is the last valid index of an array of length 5?
quiz.why: Indexes start at 0.

quiz.q: Why use StringBuilder in a loop?
options: It avoids creating a new String on every turn
quiz.why: It appends into one buffer.

blocks.text: A class is a blueprint. An object is one thing built from that blueprint with new.
Fields hold the data of an object. Methods are the actions it can perform. A constructor runs once to set up a new object.
Encapsulation means keeping fields private and exposing only the methods you want others to use, so the object can protect its own rules.
Why it matters
Without encapsulation any code could set a balance to a negative number. With it, the rule lives in one place (deposit) and every caller has to go through it.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A bank counter. You cannot reach into the vault. You hand a slip to the teller, and the teller checks it before changing your balance.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
Java has no struct. A Java class is always a reference type, like a Swift class. Java 16 added record for immutable data carriers.
Swift

Java access levels are private, package-private (no keyword), protected and public. Swift has private, fileprivate, internal, public and open. Java protected also grants access to the whole package, which surprises Swift developers.
Swift
static in Java matches static in Swift: it belongs to the type, not an instance.
Flutter
Dart marks private members with a leading underscore and privacy is per library. Java privacy is per class.

blocks.text: new BankAccount("Asha", 50_000)

items: Allocate space on the heap with fields at default values (null, 0)
Run the constructor body: assign owner and balancePaise
Increment the shared static counter
Return the address to the caller

blocks.text: The Kotlin side shows how much of this ceremony the language generates for you.
Walkthrough
private: only this class can read it. final: it must be assigned exactly once, in the constructor.
One counter shared by every BankAccount object.
this.owner is the field. owner alone is the constructor parameter, which shadows the field.
The object refuses bad input. This is an unchecked exception, so callers are not forced to catch it.
Static methods are called on the class name.
What happens when it runs

items: Two objects are created; the static counter reaches 2.
a.deposit(2_500) passes the check and changes only the balance of a.
b.deposit(-1) throws. Control jumps to the catch block and the balance of b stays 10000.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Each new allocates on the heap. The object is collectable once no reference reaches it.
A static field lives as long as its class is loaded, which on Android usually means as long as the process. Storing a Context or View in a static field keeps the whole screen in memory.
Non-static inner classes hold a hidden reference to the outer object. The static keyword on the nested class in this example avoids that.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Field watchpoints: right-click a field in Android Studio and choose Toggle Field Watchpoint to stop whenever it changes.
Override toString() so objects print usefully in logs and in the debugger.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android framework classes follow this exactly: View keeps its state private and exposes setText, setVisibility and similar methods that also trigger a redraw.
Domain models in a Clean Architecture app enforce rules in constructors and methods so an invalid Order can never exist.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Service, repository and controller classes are ordinary classes with private final fields set in the constructor, which is exactly what dependency injection frameworks expect.
Static mutable fields are shared by every request thread at once. On a server they are a concurrency bug waiting to happen.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Public mutable fields, so any code can break the invariants.
Keep fields private and expose intent-revealing methods such as deposit, not setBalance.
Forgetting this. in the constructor: owner = owner assigns the parameter to itself.
Write this.owner = owner. Android Studio flags the self-assignment.
Keeping an Activity in a static field for convenience.
Pass what you need as a parameter, or hold applicationContext when a long-lived Context is really required.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add withdraw(long paise) that rejects amounts larger than the balance. Decide what to throw and why.
Add a transfer(BankAccount to, long paise) method. Which object should own the rule that both balances change together?
Rewrite BankAccount as a Kotlin class with a private setter. Compare the line counts.
blocks.text: Hint: var balancePaise: Long = opening; private set
Interview questions

blocks.title: What is the difference between a static nested class and an inner class?
blocks.text: An inner (non-static) class holds an implicit reference to its enclosing instance and can use its fields. A static nested class does not. On Android, an inner class Handler, Runnable or AsyncTask that outlives its Activity leaks the Activity through that hidden reference.

blocks.title: What happens, in order, when you call new?
blocks.text: Memory is allocated and zeroed, field initialisers and instance initialiser blocks run in source order, then the constructor body runs. If there is a superclass, its constructor runs first.

blocks.title: Explain the four access levels in Java.
blocks.text: private: same class. No modifier (package-private): same package. protected: same package plus subclasses. public: everywhere. Prefer the narrowest level that works.

quiz.q: How many copies of a static field exist if you create 5 objects?
quiz.why: Static members belong to the class, so there is one copy regardless of the number of objects.

quiz.q: What does private final String owner allow?
options: Assigning owner once in the constructor
quiz.why: A final field must be assigned exactly once, in its declaration or in every constructor.

quiz.q: Which is the best reason to keep fields private?
options: The class can enforce its own rules
quiz.why: Encapsulation puts validation in one place so the object is always in a valid state.

blocks.text: An interface is a promise: any class that implements it provides these methods.
An abstract class is a half-finished class. It can hold fields and working methods, and it leaves some methods for subclasses to fill in.
Polymorphism means one call site, many behaviours. The loop calls p.amountPaise() and Java picks the right version at runtime based on the real object.
Why it matters
New payment types can be added without touching the loop that processes payments. Code depends on what something can do, not on what it is.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A wall socket. Any appliance with the right plug works. The socket does not know or care whether it powers a fan or a charger.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
A Java interface is a Swift protocol. Default methods are protocol extensions with one difference: Java default methods are always dynamically dispatched, so an override in the class always wins.
Swift
Swift has no abstract class. Java uses them where Swift would use a protocol plus a base class or a protocol extension.
Swift
Java allows single class inheritance and many interfaces, the same as Swift. Java classes are open by default; Swift and Kotlin classes are closed by default.
Flutter
Dart abstract class and implements map directly onto this lesson. Dart mixins have no Java equivalent; default methods cover part of that need.

blocks.text: How p.amountPaise() is resolved

items: Compile time: the compiler checks that Payable declares amountPaise()
Runtime: the JVM looks at the real class of the object p points to
It finds amountPaise() in Payment, which calls feePaise()
feePaise() is looked up again on the real class: UpiPayment or CardPayment

blocks.text: Walkthrough
A default method gives every implementer a working version that it may override.
No body. Any concrete subclass must provide one or it will not compile.
A subclass constructor must call a superclass constructor first.
Asks the compiler to verify this really overrides something. A typo in the name becomes a compile error instead of a silent new method.
The list is typed by the interface. It neither knows nor needs the concrete classes.
What happens when it runs

items: The list holds two objects of different classes behind the same Payable type.
For the UPI payment, label() comes from the interface default and prints the class name.
For the card payment, the overridden label() runs and feePaise() adds 200.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Every object stores a pointer to its class. Virtual calls use that to find the right method, at the cost of one indirect jump. ART inlines many of these.
A subclass object contains the fields of all its superclasses.
Anonymous classes and lambdas that capture this keep the outer object alive, a frequent source of Activity leaks in listener code.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Step Into (F7) at a polymorphic call lands in the implementation that actually runs.
Ctrl+H or Ctrl+Option+H on a method shows its type hierarchy and overrides in Android Studio.

blocks.text: In production

items: The whole Android SDK is built on this: you extend Activity and override onCreate, you implement View.OnClickListener, you implement RecyclerView.Adapter.
Repository interfaces with a real and a fake implementation are how Android codebases stay testable.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Backend code is written against interfaces: a PaymentGateway interface with one implementation per provider, chosen by configuration.
Spring injects whichever implementation is registered, so swapping a database or a provider does not touch the callers.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Deep inheritance chains such as BaseActivity → BaseNetworkActivity → BaseListActivity.
Prefer composition: give the class a helper object instead of another superclass.
Leaving out @Override.
Always add it. It turns signature mismatches into compile errors.
instanceof ladders that must be edited for every new type.
Move the varying behaviour into a method on the interface.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add WalletPayment with a flat fee of 500 paise. Confirm that main needs only one new list element.
Make label() abstract instead of default. Which classes stop compiling and why?
Add a method to the interface and see how default methods let you evolve an API without breaking implementers.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Abstract class or interface: how do you choose?
blocks.text: Use an interface for a capability that unrelated classes can share. Use an abstract class when subclasses share state or a partly implemented algorithm. Since Java 8 interfaces can carry default methods but still cannot hold instance state.

blocks.title: What is the difference between overloading and overriding?
blocks.text: Overloading: same name, different parameter list, chosen at compile time. Overriding: a subclass replaces an inherited method with the same signature, chosen at runtime.

blocks.title: Why is composition often preferred over inheritance?
blocks.text: Inheritance couples the subclass to the internals of its parent and fixes the relationship at compile time. Composition lets you swap collaborators, test them separately and avoid fragile base classes.

quiz.q: Which method runs for Payable p = new CardPayment(100); p.label()?
quiz.why: Instance methods are dispatched on the runtime class, which is CardPayment.

quiz.q: Can an abstract class have a constructor?
options: Yes, called by subclasses through super(...)
Only if it has no fields
quiz.why: It cannot be instantiated directly, but its constructor initialises the inherited part of every subclass object.

quiz.q: How many classes can a Java class extend?
quiz.why: Single class inheritance, multiple interface implementation.

blocks.text: An enum is a type with a fixed list of named values, such as the statuses of an order. Each value is an object, and the enum can have fields and methods.
An exception is how a method says "I could not do what you asked". It stops normal flow and travels up the call chain until some code catches it.
An annotation is a label you attach to code, starting with @. It does nothing by itself; a compiler, tool or framework reads it and acts.
Why it matters

Enums replace "magic" strings and numbers with names the compiler checks. Exceptions separate the normal path from the failure path so failures cannot be silently ignored. Annotations let frameworks be configured right where the code is.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: An enum is a form with tick boxes, not a free-text field. An exception is a fire alarm: work stops and someone responsible must respond. An annotation is a sticky note on a parcel that the sorting machine reads.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
A Java enum is a fixed set of singleton objects that all share the same fields. It cannot carry different data per case as Swift associated values do; Kotlin sealed classes cover that.
Swift
Java checked exceptions resemble Swift throws: the method declares it and callers must handle it. Java also has unchecked exceptions that no signature mentions, which Swift has no equivalent of.
Swift
try-with-resources closes things automatically, the job defer usually does in Swift. Annotations correspond to Swift attributes and, when they generate code, macros.

blocks.text: reserve("Ghee", 0) throws

items: new OutOfStockException is created, recording the stack trace
reserve stops immediately
The JVM looks for a matching catch in the caller
Found: the catch block runs
finally runs, whether or not anything was thrown
Execution continues after the try statement

blocks.text: Same behaviour in both. Kotlin has no checked exceptions and treats try as an expression.
Walkthrough
Each constant calls the enum constructor with its own data.
Enums are compared with ==, since each constant exists exactly once.
Extending Exception makes it checked. Extending RuntimeException would make it unchecked.
Part of the method signature. Callers must catch it or declare it too.
close() is called automatically when the block ends, in every case.
Decides how long the annotation survives: source only, class file, or available at runtime.
Reflection reads the annotation. This is what frameworks do with yours.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output: the status line with ordinal=1; "caught: Ghee is out of stock" (the line after it in the try never prints); "finally always runs"; open, send ping, close from try-with-resources; and "annotation says: checkout_tapped".

blocks.text: Memory

items: Enum constants are created once when the enum class loads and live as long as the class.
Creating an exception captures the whole stack trace, which is slow. Exceptions are for exceptional cases, not for normal control flow.
RUNTIME annotations are kept in the class and read by reflection, which has a cost at startup.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Read a stack trace from the top for what failed and scan down to the first line in your own package for where.
"Caused by:" sections show the original failure under a wrapping exception. The last one is usually the real cause.
An exception breakpoint in the IDE stops at the throw, before any catch hides it.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: enums model screen and order states; IOException from network and disk must be handled; and annotations drive Room, Retrofit, Hilt and lint checks such as @Nullable and @MainThread.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Server frameworks are built on annotations: Spring's @RestController, @GetMapping, @Autowired and @Transactional are read at startup to wire the application.
Domain errors become exceptions that a single handler maps to HTTP status codes: not found to 404, validation to 400, everything else to 500.
Database and file code relies on try-with-resources so connections return to the pool even when a query fails.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: catch (Exception e) { } with an empty body.
At least log it. A swallowed exception hides the cause of the next bug.
Saving enum.ordinal() to a database or sending it over an API.
Ordinals change when constants are reordered. Store name() or an explicit code.
Catching Throwable or Error.
You cannot recover from OutOfMemoryError. Catch the specific exceptions you can handle.
return inside finally.
It discards any exception in flight. Use finally only for cleanup.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add a method OrderStatus next() that returns the following status, and throws IllegalStateException from a terminal one.
Convert OutOfStockException to unchecked. What changes for callers, and what do you lose?
Write an annotation @Slow and a main method that lists every method in a class carrying it.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Checked versus unchecked exceptions: when do you use each?
blocks.text: Checked for conditions a correct program must expect and can recover from, such as a missing file or a failed network call. Unchecked for programming errors, such as a null argument or an illegal state. Many modern codebases prefer unchecked throughout to avoid signatures cluttered with throws, which is also what Kotlin chose.

blocks.title: What can a Java enum do beyond listing constants?
blocks.text: Hold fields and constructors, define methods, give each constant its own method body, implement interfaces, and be used in switch, EnumSet and EnumMap. Because each constant is a guaranteed single instance, an enum is also the simplest thread-safe singleton.

blocks.title: What are the annotation retention policies?
blocks.text: SOURCE: discarded by the compiler, used by lint and code generators (@Override). CLASS: kept in the class file but not visible to reflection, the default. RUNTIME: available through reflection while the program runs, used by frameworks.

quiz.q: Which must be caught or declared?
quiz.why: IOException is checked. The others extend RuntimeException.

quiz.q: When does finally run?
quiz.why: It runs whether the try completed, threw or returned.

quiz.q: What does an annotation do by itself?
quiz.why: It is metadata for compilers, processors and frameworks.

blocks.text: A collection is an object that holds other objects. List keeps order and allows duplicates. Set keeps unique items. Map stores key and value pairs.
Generics put the element type in angle brackets, as in List<String>, so the compiler stops you adding the wrong thing.
Streams describe a pipeline (filter, map, sum) instead of a hand-written loop.
Why it matters
Almost every screen is a list of something. Picking the right collection decides whether a lookup takes one step or a scan through ten thousand items.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: List is a numbered queue. Set is a guest list where each name appears once. Map is a dictionary: look up the word, get the meaning.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
ArrayList is Array, HashMap is Dictionary, HashSet is Set. Swift collections are value types with copy-on-write; Java collections are shared mutable objects.
Swift
Java generics are erased at runtime: List<String> and List<Integer> are the same class once compiled. Swift keeps generic type information.
Flutter
Dart List, Set and Map map one to one. Dart keeps generic types at runtime, so is List<String> works in Dart and does not in Java.

blocks.text: qty.merge(item, 1, Integer::sum)

items: Hash the key to find its bucket
Key absent: store 1
Key present: call Integer.sum(oldValue, 1) and store the result

blocks.text: Walkthrough

blocks.code: static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> items)
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: A generic method. T can be any type that knows how to compare itself, so the same code works for Integer and String.
The diamond <> lets the compiler infer String on the right-hand side.
Copies the list into a set, which drops the duplicate "milk".
TreeMap keeps keys sorted, so the printed order is stable. HashMap order is not guaranteed.
Keeps items starting with m, converts each to its length and adds them: 4 + 4 = 8.
What happens when it runs

items: Three adds give a list of size 3.
The set keeps 2 unique items.
The loop builds counts in a HashMap; TreeMap sorts them for printing.
The stream runs only when sum() is called. Streams are lazy until a terminal operation.

blocks.text: Memory

items: ArrayList wraps an array and grows by about half when full, copying the old contents.
HashMap<Integer, X> boxes every key. Android offers SparseArray and ArrayMap for small maps with less overhead.
A stream allocates pipeline objects. In code that runs every frame, such as onDraw or onBindViewHolder, a plain loop is the safer choice.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: The debugger shows collection contents expanded. Right-click a collection and choose Filter to narrow it.
Add .peek(System.out::println) in a stream temporarily, or use the Stream Trace button in the debugger.

blocks.text: In production

items: RecyclerView adapters hold a List of items. DiffUtil compares the old and new lists using equals, which is why correct equals and hashCode matter.
Caches keyed by id are HashMaps. LruCache in the Android SDK is a LinkedHashMap with eviction.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Query results arrive as Lists; lookups by id use Maps; de-duplication uses Sets. Choosing HashMap over a list scan is the difference between a fast endpoint and a slow one under load.
Collections shared between request threads must be concurrent ones.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Removing from a list inside a for-each loop, which throws ConcurrentModificationException.
Use removeIf, an Iterator with remove(), or build a new list.
Using a mutable object as a HashMap key and then changing it.
Keys must have stable equals and hashCode. Prefer immutable keys.
Raw types such as List items.
Always give the type argument so the compiler can check it.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Group a list of product names by their first letter into a Map<Character, List<String>>.
blocks.text: Hint: computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(name)

blocks.title: Write a generic method <T> T firstOrDefault(List<T> items, T fallback).
Rewrite the stream pipeline as a for loop. Which is easier to read? Which allocates less?

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does HashMap work internally?
blocks.text: It keeps an array of buckets. The hashCode of the key picks a bucket; equals finds the exact entry inside it. Collisions are chained in a linked list that becomes a balanced tree once a bucket holds 8 or more entries and the table has at least 64 buckets. When the load factor (0.75 by default) is exceeded the table doubles and entries are redistributed.

blocks.title: ArrayList or LinkedList?
blocks.text: ArrayList for almost everything: index access is constant time and iteration is cache friendly. LinkedList only wins for frequent inserts or removals at the ends, and ArrayDeque usually beats it there too.

blocks.title: What are wildcards ? extends T and ? super T for?
blocks.text: They make generic APIs flexible. A producer of values is declared with extends (you can read T out). A consumer is declared with super (you can put T in). The mnemonic is PECS: producer extends, consumer super.

quiz.q: Which collection would you use to check quickly whether a product id is already in the cart?
quiz.why: HashSet.contains is constant time on average. Lists need a scan.

quiz.q: What does type erasure mean?
options: Collections are cleared by the garbage collector
quiz.why: The compiler checks generic types, then removes them. At runtime a List<String> is just a List.

quiz.q: What order does HashMap iteration follow?
quiz.why: Use LinkedHashMap for insertion order or TreeMap for sorted order.

blocks.text: Generics let a class or method work with a type that is chosen later. Box<T> is a box of "some type T"; Box<String> is a box of strings.
The compiler then checks that you only put strings in and gives you strings back, with no casts.
A wildcard, written ?, means "some type I do not need to name". ? extends Number accepts a list of any kind of number.
Why it matters

Without generics a list holds Object, anything can be added, and every read needs a cast that may fail at runtime. Generics move that failure to compile time and let one piece of code serve many types.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Labelled storage boxes. A box labelled "shoes" will only accept shoes, and you know what you will find inside without opening it and checking.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
Java generics are erased: at runtime a List<String> is just a List. Swift keeps the type, so you can ask "is this [String]" and Java cannot.
Swift
<T extends Comparable<T>> is <T: Comparable>. Wildcards have no direct Swift form; Swift expresses the same flexibility with generic parameters or "some" and "any".
Flutter
Dart generics are kept at runtime and are covariant by default, which is convenient and less safe. Java generics are invariant unless you use a wildcard.

blocks.text: What the compiler does with List<String>

items: Checks every add: only String is allowed
Inserts a cast to String at every get
Removes the type argument: the class file says List
At runtime the JVM sees a plain List of objects

blocks.text: Kotlin states variance once, where the type is declared (out, in), and can keep a type at runtime with reified.
Walkthrough
T is a type parameter. It stands for whatever the user of Box supplies.
A generic method with its own parameter R, declared before the return type.

blocks.code: static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(T a, T b)
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: A bound: T may be any type that can compare itself to another T.

blocks.code: static double sum(List<? extends Number> numbers)
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: The method only reads, so it can accept a list of any Number subtype.

blocks.code: static void fill(List<? super Integer> target)
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: The method only writes Integers, so any list that can hold an Integer will do.
True. Both are ArrayList at runtime. That is erasure.
Arrays are covariant and checked when written, so this compiles and fails at runtime. Generic lists reject it at compile time.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output: "milk 4"; "9 banana"; 6.0 and 4.0 from sum over an Integer list and a Double list; [1, 2] [1, 2] from fill; "same class at runtime: true"; and the ArrayStoreException from the array.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Generics add no runtime cost: there is one ArrayList class however many element types you use.
Type arguments must be objects, so List<Integer> boxes every number.
Because of erasure you cannot write new T(), new T[10] or instanceof List<String>.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: A ClassCastException on a line with no visible cast is a compiler-inserted cast: something of the wrong type entered a generic container through a raw type.
Hover a generic call in the IDE to see what the compiler inferred for T.
When inference fails, state the type explicitly: Collections.<String>emptyList().

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: LiveData<T>, List<T> in adapters, Retrofit Call<T> and callbacks such as Callback<T> are all generic.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Repositories and services are generic over the entity: CrudRepository<User, Long>. Response wrappers such as ApiResponse<T> and Page<T> are standard.
JSON libraries need the full type at runtime, which erasure removes. That is why you pass TypeReference<List<User>> or a TypeToken.
Wildcards appear in library signatures you read daily, for example Comparator<? super T>.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Raw types: List items = new ArrayList();
Always give the type argument. Raw types switch the checking off.
Expecting List<Integer> to be accepted where List<Number> is required.
Generics are invariant. Declare the parameter as List<? extends Number>.
Trying to add to a List<? extends Number>.
The compiler cannot know which subtype it holds. Use ? super when writing.
Suppressing "unchecked" warnings without understanding them.
Each one marks a place where a ClassCastException can appear far from its cause.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Write a generic Pair<A, B> with a swap() method returning Pair<B, A>.
Write static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dst, List<? extends T> src) and explain each wildcard.
Explain why this does not compile: List<Object> a = new ArrayList<String>();

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Explain PECS.
blocks.text: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. If a parameter only produces values for you to read, declare it ? extends T so more specific collections are accepted. If it only consumes values you write, declare it ? super T so more general collections are accepted. If you do both, use plain T.

blocks.title: What are the consequences of type erasure?
blocks.text: No runtime check of type arguments, no generic array creation, no instanceof with a parameterised type, overloads that differ only in type argument clash, and reflection-based libraries need a type token to know the full type.

blocks.title: Why are arrays covariant and generics invariant?
blocks.text: Arrays were made covariant in Java 1.0 so methods such as sort(Object[]) could exist before generics, at the price of a runtime check on every store. Generics came later and chose compile-time safety, since erasure makes a runtime check impossible.

quiz.q: What does type erasure mean?
options: Generic types are removed at runtime
quiz.why: The compiler checks them and then drops them from the bytecode.

quiz.q: Which parameter type accepts a List<Integer> for reading numbers?
quiz.why: extends admits any subtype of Number for reading.

quiz.q: Why is List<int> not allowed?
options: Type arguments must be reference types
quiz.why: Generics work on objects, so primitives are boxed as Integer.

lessons.title: Lambdas, functional interfaces, streams and Optional

blocks.text: A lambda is a short way to write a function as a value: item -> item.getPrice() < 10000.
A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method. A lambda can be used wherever one is expected.
A stream is a pipeline over a collection: filter this, transform that, collect the result. You say what you want, not how to loop.
Optional is a box that either holds a value or is empty, used as a return type to say "there may be no result".
Why it matters

Before Java 8, passing behaviour meant writing an anonymous class of six lines for one line of logic. Lambdas made that one line, and streams made common collection work, such as filter, group and sum, readable and hard to get wrong.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A stream is an assembly line. Items enter one at a time; each station filters or changes them; the last station packs the result. Nothing moves until the packer at the end starts pulling.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
A Java lambda is a Swift closure. Java has no function types, so a lambda always needs an interface such as Function or Predicate to give it a type.
Swift
stream().filter().map().collect() is filter and map on a Swift sequence. Java streams are lazy like lazy sequences, and single use.
Swift
Optional<T> is a library class, not part of the type system. Nothing stops a method returning a null Optional or a null plain value. Kotlin and Swift check nullability in the compiler.

blocks.text: findFirst on a filtered stream

items: findFirst asks the pipeline for one item
The source hands over Milk
peek prints it, filter accepts it
findFirst has its answer and stops
Ghee, Bread and Cake are never visited

blocks.text: Kotlin gets the same results with collection functions and null, without streams or Optional.
Walkthrough
One abstract method. The annotation makes the compiler enforce that.
The lambda becomes the body of apply.
Predicate is the built-in interface for "takes a T, returns boolean".
A method reference, shorthand for item -> item.getName().
Groups by category into a sorted map and sums prices within each group.
Transforms the value if present, and supplies a default if not.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output: Rs 108; [Bread, Milk]; {bakery=39500, dairy=68000}; total 107500; Ghee; "nothing false" for the empty Optional; and a single "visiting Milk" line, proving the stream stopped early.

blocks.text: Memory

items: A lambda that captures no variables is created once and reused. One that captures variables is a new object each time the line runs.
Captured local variables must be effectively final: the lambda holds a copy.
A stream pipeline allocates several small objects. In very hot code a plain loop is cheaper.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Insert .peek(x -> System.out.println(x)) between stages to see what flows through.
IntelliJ and Android Studio have a Trace Current Stream Chain button in the debugger that shows each stage.
When a pipeline is too clever to debug, rewrite it as a loop, fix it, then decide whether to convert back.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: click listeners and callbacks are lambdas. Streams need API 24 or desugaring; in list code that runs every frame, loops are still preferred.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Streams are everywhere in service code: mapping entities to response objects, grouping rows for a report, filtering by permission.
Repository methods return Optional<User> so callers must decide what "not found" means: orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(id)).
Functional interfaces define extension points such as retry policies, validators and event handlers.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Reusing a stream after a terminal operation.
A stream can be consumed once. Create a new one from the collection.
optional.get() without checking.
It throws when empty. Use orElse, orElseGet, map or ifPresent.
Changing outside variables from inside a stream lambda.
Return a result with collect or reduce. Side effects break with parallel streams and are hard to read.
Optional as a field or a method parameter.
It is designed for return values. Use overloads or nullable fields.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: From a list of items, produce a comma-separated string of the three most expensive names.
blocks.text: Hint: sorted(Comparator.comparingLong(Item::getPrice).reversed()).limit(3)

blocks.title: Write a method that returns Optional<Item> for the cheapest item in a category.
Write your own functional interface Validator<T> and combine two validators with a default method and(...).

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How is a lambda different from an anonymous inner class?
blocks.text: A lambda can only implement a functional interface, has no this of its own (this refers to the enclosing object), and is compiled with invokedynamic, so no extra class file is created per lambda. An anonymous class can implement any interface or extend a class and has its own this and state.

blocks.title: map versus flatMap?
blocks.text: map turns each element into one result. flatMap turns each element into a stream of results and flattens them into one stream, for example orders into all their line items. Optional has both with the same meaning.

blocks.title: When should you not use parallel streams?
blocks.text: When the work is small, when the source splits poorly (LinkedList, I/O), when operations have side effects or depend on order, and inside servers, because parallel streams share the common ForkJoinPool with everything else in the process and one slow task starves the rest.

blocks.title: What is Optional for, and what is it not for?
blocks.text: It is a return type that makes "no result" explicit and offers map, filter and orElse to handle it. It is not a general replacement for null: it should not be used for fields, parameters or collections, and it is not serialisable.

quiz.q: When does a stream pipeline start executing?
quiz.why: Intermediate operations only describe the pipeline.

quiz.q: What makes an interface functional?
quiz.why: The annotation is optional; the single abstract method is the rule.

quiz.q: What does Optional.orElse("x") return when the Optional is empty?
quiz.why: It supplies the given default.

modules.title: Advanced Java
modules.summary: JVM internals, concurrency, and a backend branch: REST, layers, SQL, auth, testing, deployment, and a Spring Boot project that runs.

lessons.title: Inside the JVM: bytecode, class loading, memory and garbage collection

blocks.text: Java source is compiled by javac into bytecode, stored in .class files. Bytecode is not for any one processor; it is for the Java Virtual Machine, a program that runs it.
The JRE is the JVM plus the standard library: enough to run programs. The JDK is the JRE plus tools such as javac: enough to build them.
The JVM gives each thread a stack for method calls and gives the whole program one heap for objects. A garbage collector finds objects nothing refers to any more and frees them.
Why it matters

"Write once, run anywhere": the same .class file runs on any machine with a JVM. Managed memory removes whole classes of bugs, such as use-after-free. Knowing what happens underneath is how you explain a memory leak, a slow start or a pause.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Bytecode is sheet music and the JVM is the musician: the same score plays on any instrument that has a player. The heap is a shared warehouse; the garbage collector is the cleaner who removes anything with no label pointing to it.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift

Swift compiles straight to machine code and frees memory by reference counting, at a predictable moment. Java frees by tracing garbage collection, at a moment the JVM chooses. Java has no retain cycles; it has leaks through references you forgot.
iOS
Reflection in Java is far more capable than Swift Mirror: you can create objects, call private methods and read annotations by name. Frameworks depend on it.
Flutter
Dart also uses a VM with a garbage collector in debug mode and compiles ahead of time for release, much like ART on Android.

blocks.text: What makes an object collectable

items: Start from the roots: local variables on every thread stack, static fields, live threads
Follow every reference from the roots
Everything reached is alive
Everything not reached is garbage, whatever refers to it
The collector frees it at some later time

blocks.text: There is no Kotlin file for this lesson: Kotlin compiles to the same bytecode and runs on the same JVM, so everything here applies to it unchanged.
Walkthrough
null means the bootstrap loader, which loads the core library.
Loads a class from its name at runtime. The $ separates a nested class from its outer class.
Reflection can bypass private. Frameworks use this; application code rarely should.
Each call added a frame until the thread stack was full. Caught here only to demonstrate it.
A weak reference does not keep its object alive, so it lets you observe collection.
A request. The JVM may ignore it. Never rely on it in real code.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output: String loaded by null; this class loaded by "app"; 2 fields found by reflection; the private method called; a stack overflow after more than a thousand frames; and the weakly referenced object collected on this run. Collection timing is the JVM's decision, so that last line is usual, not guaranteed.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Stack: one per thread, holds frames with parameters and local variables, freed automatically when a method returns.
Heap: all objects and arrays, shared by all threads, split into a young generation for new objects and an old generation for survivors.
Most objects die young, so collecting the young generation is fast and frequent. Collecting the old generation is slower.
A memory leak in Java is an object that is still reachable but no longer needed: a growing static list, a listener never removed, a cache with no limit.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: javap -c Cart.class prints the bytecode of a class.
A heap dump shows every object and what holds it. Open it in Android Studio's profiler or Eclipse MAT and look at the path to a GC root.
jstack <pid> (or an ANR trace on Android) prints every thread stack.
java -Xlog:gc prints each garbage collection with its pause time.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: the build converts .class files to DEX, and ART runs DEX with its own collector. The ideas are the same: stacks, a heap, GC roots, and leaks through long-lived references to an Activity.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Server JVMs are tuned with flags: -Xmx for the heap limit, a collector choice such as G1 or ZGC, and container-aware settings.
Long GC pauses appear as latency spikes, so services watch pause times and allocation rates.
Spring, Hibernate and Jackson rely on class loading, reflection and annotations to wire and map objects at startup, which is why big services start slowly.
OutOfMemoryError in production is diagnosed from a heap dump taken with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Assuming setting a variable to null frees the object immediately.
It only removes one reference. The object is freed later, and only if nothing else refers to it.
Unbounded static maps used as caches.
Statics are GC roots. Bound the cache, or use weak references or a cache library.
Heavy reflection in hot paths.
Reflective calls are slower and defeat some optimisations. Look up once and reuse, or generate code.
Calling System.gc() to "fix" memory use.
It is a hint that often causes a long pause. Find the reference that keeps the objects alive.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Run javap -c on the compiled Variables class and find the instruction that adds two ints.
Write a program that leaks memory by adding to a static list in a loop, and watch it end in OutOfMemoryError with -Xmx32m.
Use reflection to print the name and type of every field of java.lang.String.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does garbage collection work in the JVM?
blocks.text: It is tracing and generational. From the GC roots it marks every reachable object; the rest is garbage. New objects go to the young generation, which is collected often by copying the few survivors; long-lived objects are promoted to the old generation, collected less often. Modern collectors such as G1 and ZGC do most work concurrently to keep pauses short.

blocks.title: Explain class loading.
blocks.text: A class is loaded the first time it is needed. Loaders form a parent chain: bootstrap, platform, application. A loader asks its parent first, so core classes cannot be replaced. After loading, the class is verified, its static fields get default values, and its static initialisers run once, thread-safely.

blocks.title: What is the difference between stack and heap memory?
blocks.text: Each thread has its own stack of frames for method calls; it holds parameters, local primitives and references, and is reclaimed when methods return. The heap is shared, holds all objects, and is reclaimed by the collector. StackOverflowError means too many frames; OutOfMemoryError means the heap (or another memory area) is exhausted.

blocks.title: What is the JIT compiler?
blocks.text: The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode and counts how often methods and loops run. Hot code is compiled to optimised machine code while the program runs, using what it observed, such as which implementation a call really uses. This is why Java code speeds up after warm-up.

quiz.q: What does javac produce?
quiz.why: Bytecode is run by a JVM, or converted to DEX for Android.

quiz.q: Where do objects live?
quiz.why: The stack holds references and primitives of local variables; objects are on the heap.

quiz.q: When can an object be garbage collected?
options: When no chain of references from a root reaches it
quiz.why: Reachability from GC roots is the only test.

quiz.q: JDK versus JRE?
options: JDK adds development tools such as the compiler
quiz.why: The JRE runs programs; the JDK also builds them.

blocks.text: A thread is a separate line of execution inside your app. Several threads can run at the same time on different CPU cores.
An ExecutorService owns a pool of threads. You hand it tasks and it gives back a Future, a ticket for the result.
When two threads change the same variable without coordination, updates get lost. That is a race condition.
Why it matters

Android draws the UI on one thread, the main thread. Anything slow, such as network, disk or heavy maths, must run elsewhere or the screen freezes and the system shows an Application Not Responding dialog.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A kitchen with one head chef plating dishes (the main thread) and several cooks (the pool). If the chef goes off to chop onions, no plates leave the kitchen.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
ExecutorService is close to a DispatchQueue or OperationQueue. Future.get() blocks, which is like calling semaphore.wait(); it is not like await.
Swift
synchronized and AtomicInteger do by hand what Swift actors do by design. Java has no compiler-checked data race safety.
Flutter
Dart runs your code on one isolate with an event loop, so shared-memory races do not exist there. Java threads share the heap, so they do.

blocks.text: Why unsafeCount++ loses updates

items: Thread A reads 41
Thread B reads 41
Thread A writes 42
Thread B writes 42: one increment is gone

blocks.text: Kotlin coroutines are not threads. They are shown here as the modern Android answer to the same problem and get their own lesson.
Walkthrough
Creates four reusable worker threads. Creating a raw Thread per task is wasteful.
Looks like one step. It is three: read, add one, write back. Another thread can slip in between.
Uses a CPU compare-and-swap instruction so the three steps behave as one.
Blocks the calling thread until the task finishes. Never do this on the Android main thread.
Without this the worker threads keep the JVM alive.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output from one run on this Mac: safe=2000000, unsafe lost updates: true. The exact value of unsafeCount differs on every run, which is the point.
The third task runs on a pool thread while main waits up to one second in get(1, SECONDS).

blocks.text: Memory

items: Each thread reserves its own stack, typically around 1 MB on Android. Thousands of threads exhaust memory.
The Java Memory Model lets a thread keep a stale cached copy of a field. volatile forces reads and writes to be visible across threads; it does not make ++ atomic.
A running thread is a garbage collection root. A thread that references an Activity keeps it alive until the thread ends.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: The Threads tab in the debugger lists every thread and its stack. A deadlock shows two threads each WAITING on a monitor the other holds.
adb shell kill -3 <pid> or an ANR trace file prints every thread stack. Look for the "main" thread first.
StrictMode.setThreadPolicy(...detectAll()) reports disk and network use on the main thread during development.

blocks.text: In production

items: OkHttp runs calls on its own dispatcher thread pool. Room refuses to run queries on the main thread unless you opt in.
Legacy Java codebases use Executors plus Handler to return to the main thread. Modern Kotlin code uses coroutines on Dispatchers.IO, which is itself backed by a thread pool.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: A server is a thread pool by design: each request runs on a pool thread, and the pool size limits how many are served at once.
Blocking calls to databases and other services hold a thread. Timeouts and bounded pools keep one slow dependency from taking the service down.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Touching a View from a background thread, which throws CalledFromWrongThreadException.
Post back to the main thread with runOnUiThread, Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()) or a main-dispatcher coroutine.
Calling Future.get() or Thread.sleep() on the main thread.
Deliver results with a callback, LiveData or a coroutine.
Assuming volatile int count makes count++ safe.
Use AtomicInteger, synchronized or a lock for compound actions.
Two threads taking the same two locks in opposite order, which deadlocks.
Always acquire locks in one global order, or avoid nested locks.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Fix unsafeCount with a synchronized block. Then measure both versions. Which is faster and why?
Write two threads that deadlock by locking A then B and B then A. Read the thread dump.
Replace the two Future.get() calls with CompletableFuture.allOf(...).thenRun(...). What changed about blocking?

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is the difference between synchronized, volatile and AtomicInteger?
blocks.text: synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility for a block of code. volatile gives visibility for a single field, nothing more. Atomic classes give lock-free atomic updates of a single value using compare-and-swap.

blocks.title: What causes an ANR and how do you investigate one?
blocks.text: The main thread did not respond in time: about 5 seconds for an input event, with shorter limits for BroadcastReceivers and Service start. Pull the ANR trace from Play Console or /data/anr, find the main thread stack and see what it is blocked on: disk or network I/O, a lock held by another thread, a long loop or a binder call.

blocks.title: Explain Handler, Looper and MessageQueue.
blocks.text: A Looper runs a loop on one thread, pulling Messages and Runnables from its MessageQueue. A Handler posts work to that queue. The main thread has a Looper created by the system, which is how other threads hand work back to the UI.

blocks.title: What is a thread pool and how do you size one?
blocks.text: A set of reusable threads fed from a queue. CPU-bound work wants about as many threads as cores. I/O-bound work can use more, because threads spend their time waiting. Unbounded pools risk memory exhaustion.

quiz.q: Two threads each run count++ 1,000 times on a plain int. What is the final value?
quiz.why: Increments can be lost whenever two threads interleave. With extreme interleaving the result can be far below 2000.

quiz.q: What does volatile guarantee?
options: Visibility of the latest write to other threads
quiz.why: volatile is about visibility and ordering, not atomicity.

quiz.q: Why must network calls stay off the Android main thread?
options: It blocks drawing and input handling
The main thread has no internet permission
quiz.why: The main thread processes input and draws frames. Blocking it for about 5 seconds during input triggers an ANR; Android also throws NetworkOnMainThreadException.

lessons.title: Synchronization, locks, volatile and concurrent collections

blocks.text: When two threads change the same data at once, results go wrong. The cure is to make sure only one thread touches it at a time, or to use data structures built for sharing.
synchronized marks a block that only one thread may be inside. A Lock does the same with more control.
volatile on a field guarantees that every thread sees the latest value written to it.
Classes such as ConcurrentHashMap and AtomicInteger are designed to be used by many threads safely.
Why it matters

Servers and apps run on many cores and handle many things at once. Shared mutable state without coordination produces bugs that appear rarely, cannot be reproduced on demand, and corrupt data silently.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A single-occupancy changing room. synchronized is the door lock: one person in, others wait. volatile is a noticeboard everyone is required to re-read every time, not trust from memory.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
synchronized and locks are what NSLock or a serial DispatchQueue give you. Swift actors make the compiler enforce one-at-a-time access; Java has no such check.
Swift
AtomicInteger is ManagedAtomic from swift-atomics. ConcurrentHashMap has no standard Swift counterpart; you would protect a Dictionary with an actor.
Flutter
Dart isolates share no memory, so none of this exists there. Kotlin coroutines on several threads have the same problems and use Mutex.

blocks.text: Two threads meet at synchronized (monitor)

items: Thread A acquires the monitor and enters
Thread B arrives and blocks
Thread A changes the shared data and leaves, releasing the monitor
Thread B wakes, acquires the monitor and enters
B is guaranteed to see everything A wrote

blocks.text: The Kotlin file is not a translation. It shows the coroutine tools for the same problems: Mutex in place of locks, Channel in place of a BlockingQueue.
Walkthrough
Only one thread at a time can run this block for this monitor object.
An explicit lock. unlock belongs in finally, or an exception would leave it locked forever.
One atomic read-modify-write inside the map. get followed by put would lose updates.
Without volatile the worker thread may keep a cached copy and never notice the change.
A CountDownLatch lets one thread wait until others have finished.
Gives up after a timeout instead of waiting forever, which is one way to avoid deadlock.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output from one run: synchronized, lock and concurrent map all reach exactly 200000. The unprotected counter lost updates on this run. The worker saw the volatile flag and stopped. The exact shortfall of the plain counter changes every run.

blocks.text: Memory

items: The Java Memory Model says when one thread is guaranteed to see another's writes: after a lock release and acquire, after a volatile write and read, and after thread start and join.
Without such a "happens-before" edge the JVM may reorder or cache, and a thread can read stale data indefinitely.
An uncontended lock is cheap. A contended lock parks threads, which is expensive and limits how far you scale.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: A thread dump (jstack or an ANR trace) shows which threads are BLOCKED and which lock each waits for. Deadlocks are reported explicitly.
Concurrency bugs rarely reproduce under a debugger, because pausing changes the timing. Add logging with thread names.
Stress tests that run the suspect code from many threads thousands of times find races that a single run hides.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: the main thread must not block on a lock held by a thread doing I/O; that is a classic ANR. Handlers, executors and coroutines confine state to one thread to avoid locks altogether.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: A server handles each request on a pool thread, so anything shared between requests, such as caches, counters and connection pools, must be thread-safe.
Stateless services with immutable request data avoid most locking. Shared state is pushed into the database, which provides transactions.
In-memory caches are ConcurrentHashMap or a cache library. Rate limiters use Semaphore or atomics. Fan-out to other services uses CompletableFuture.
Java 21 virtual threads make blocking code cheap, which changes pool sizing but not the rules about shared state.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v) on a ConcurrentHashMap.
Two safe calls are not one safe operation. Use putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent or merge.
Locking on different objects for the same data.
Every access to a piece of shared state must use the same lock.
Taking two locks in different orders in different methods.
That is a deadlock waiting to happen. Fix a global order, or use tryLock.
Believing volatile makes count++ safe.
volatile gives visibility, not atomicity. Use AtomicInteger or a lock.
Calling unknown code, such as a listener, while holding a lock.
It may take another lock or block. Copy what you need, release, then call.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Remove the synchronized block and see how far the synced counter falls short. Then replace it with AtomicInteger.
Write a deadlock with two locks, capture a thread dump, and fix it with a lock order.
Build a bounded producer and consumer with ArrayBlockingQueue.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: synchronized versus ReentrantLock?
blocks.text: Both give mutual exclusion and are reentrant. synchronized is simpler and released automatically. ReentrantLock adds tryLock with timeout, interruptible waiting, optional fairness and several Condition objects, at the cost of having to unlock in finally.

blocks.title: What is a deadlock and how do you prevent one?
blocks.text: Two or more threads each hold a lock the other needs, so none can proceed. Prevent it by acquiring locks in one global order, holding as few locks as possible for as short as possible, using tryLock with a timeout, and never calling outside code while holding a lock.

blocks.title: How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety?
blocks.text: Reads are lock-free. Writes lock only the bucket being changed, using compare-and-swap for empty buckets and a small synchronized section otherwise, so threads working on different buckets do not block each other. Iterators are weakly consistent and never throw ConcurrentModificationException.

blocks.title: What does the Java Memory Model guarantee?
blocks.text: It defines happens-before relationships. If action A happens-before B, B sees A's effects. Such edges come from locks, volatile, thread start and join, and final fields after construction. Without one, visibility and ordering between threads are not guaranteed, even if the code looks sequential.

quiz.q: What does synchronized guarantee?
options: One thread at a time in the block, and visibility of its writes
quiz.why: Mutual exclusion plus a happens-before edge on release and acquire.

quiz.q: Is count++ on a volatile int thread-safe?
quiz.why: It is three steps. volatile only makes each read and write visible.

quiz.q: Why put unlock() in finally?
options: So the lock is released even if the body throws
quiz.why: Otherwise an exception leaves the lock held and other threads wait forever.

quiz.q: Which is a single atomic operation on ConcurrentHashMap?
quiz.why: merge, compute and putIfAbsent are atomic; sequences of calls are not.

lessons.title: Java on the backend: an HTTP service with only the JDK

blocks.text: A backend service is a program that waits for requests over the network and answers them. The Android app you write is its client.
A request has a method (GET, POST), a path (/products/2) and maybe a body. A response has a status code (200, 404), headers and a body, usually JSON.
This lesson builds one with nothing but the JDK, so you can see every part. Real services use a framework such as Spring Boot that does the same things with less code.
Why it matters

Knowing what the server does makes you a better client developer: you understand status codes, timeouts, threads and why an API behaves as it does. It also shows that backend Java is the same core language you have been learning, pointed at a different job.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A takeaway counter. Customers (clients) hand in order slips (requests). A fixed number of cooks (the thread pool) each take one slip, look things up in the storeroom (the data), and hand back a bag with a receipt number (response and status code).
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
This is the server side of what URLSession talks to. The Swift counterpart of this code would be a small Vapor or Hummingbird service.
iOS
On mobile you learn to keep work off the main thread. On a server there is no main thread; every request runs on a pool thread, and the concern becomes shared state between requests.
Flutter
A Dart shelf server has the same shape: a handler from request to response. Dart handles requests on one event loop; Java uses a thread per request.

blocks.text: GET /products/abc

items: The server accepts the connection and hands the exchange to a pool thread
The handler splits the path into parts
The method is GET, so it continues
Integer.parseInt("abc") throws NumberFormatException
The handler answers 400 with a JSON error body
The response is written and the stream closed

blocks.text: One file contains both the server and a client that calls it, so it runs by itself. Kotlin services are written the same way on the JVM, usually with Ktor or Spring Boot.
Walkthrough
Listen on this machine only, on any free port. A real service uses a fixed port such as 8080.
At most four requests are handled at once. Others wait in a queue.
Handlers run on several threads, so shared data must be thread-safe.
Registers a handler for every path starting with /products. The lambda implements HttpHandler.
The status code is how the client learns the outcome without reading the body.
Status and headers go first, then the body. The length tells the client how much to read.
try-with-resources closes the stream, which completes the response.
The client half. On Android, Retrofit and OkHttp do this for you.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output from this Mac: GET /products returns 200 with both products as a JSON array; /products/2 returns 200 with Bread; /products/9 returns 404; /products/abc returns 400; POST /products returns 405.
These are exactly the outcomes the Retrofit lesson teaches the Android side to handle.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Each pool thread has its own stack. Objects created for a request become garbage once the response is sent.
Anything stored in a static field or a singleton is shared by all requests and lives for the life of the service.
A service with no bound on its request queue or cache grows until it runs out of memory under load.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: curl -i http://localhost:8080/products/2 shows the status line, headers and body exactly as the client receives them.
Log one line per request: method, path, status, duration. Most production questions are answered from that line.
A thread dump shows what every pool thread is doing when the service stops responding.
For "works on my machine": compare the request the client really sent (headers, body encoding) with what you tested.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: this is what your Retrofit interface is talking to. The status codes map to HttpException, and no response at all maps to IOException.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Real services use Spring Boot: @RestController and @GetMapping("/products/{id}") replace the routing code, Jackson replaces the JSON code, and Tomcat or Netty replaces HttpServer.
Data lives in a database reached through JDBC, JPA and Hibernate, or jOOQ, with a connection pool such as HikariCP.
Build with Maven or Gradle, package as a jar, run in a container. Add health checks, metrics, structured logs and tracing.
