What to learn next for backend work: Spring Boot, SQL and transactions, REST design, authentication with OAuth and JWT, testing with JUnit and Testcontainers, and messaging with Kafka. None of that is built in this academy yet.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Building JSON by concatenating strings, as this teaching sample does.
It breaks as soon as a name contains a quote. Use a JSON library such as Jackson.
Returning 200 with {"error": ...} in the body.
Use the status code. Clients, proxies and monitoring all read it.
Sharing a HashMap or a SimpleDateFormat between request threads.
Use thread-safe classes or keep the object local to the request.
Trusting input: parsing ids and sizes without validation.
Validate every field and answer 400. Never pass raw input into SQL or file paths.
Blocking pool threads on slow calls with no timeout.
Set timeouts on every outbound call, or one slow dependency exhausts the pool.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add POST /products that reads a name from the body, stores it under the next id and answers 201.
blocks.text: Hint: new String(exchange.getRequestBody().readAllBytes(), UTF_8) and an AtomicInteger for the id

blocks.title: Add DELETE /products/{id}. Which status codes can it return?
Run the server on port 8080 without the client part and call it with curl.
Rewrite the product endpoints in Spring Boot and compare the line count.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What happens when a server receives an HTTP request?
blocks.text: The connection is accepted, the request line, headers and body are parsed, and the request is dispatched to a worker thread. Routing picks a handler by method and path. The handler authenticates, validates, runs business logic, usually talks to a database, and builds a response with a status code, headers and a serialised body, which is written back before the thread returns to the pool.

blocks.title: How do you design REST endpoints for a product catalogue?
blocks.text: Nouns for resources and HTTP methods for actions: GET /products (list, with paging and filters as query parameters), GET /products/{id}, POST /products (201 with a Location header), PUT or PATCH /products/{id}, DELETE /products/{id}. Consistent error bodies, correct status codes, and versioning in the path or a header.

blocks.title: What makes an operation idempotent, and why does a mobile client care?
blocks.text: Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are meant to be; POST is not. Mobile networks drop responses, so the client retries: a retried non-idempotent "place order" can create two orders. The fix is an idempotency key the server remembers.

blocks.title: Thread-per-request versus event loop?
blocks.text: Thread-per-request is simple to write and debug, since code blocks naturally, but each waiting request holds a thread. An event loop handles many connections on few threads and never blocks, which scales for I/O-heavy loads but needs asynchronous code. Virtual threads in Java 21 aim to give the simple style with the scalable cost.

blocks.title: As a mobile developer, what do you want from a backend API?
blocks.text: Stable contracts with versioning, correct status codes and machine-readable errors, pagination, fields that are never removed without notice, tolerance for old app versions, idempotent writes, small payloads, and clear nullability. Old clients stay in use for years, so the server must not break them.

quiz.q: What does status 404 tell the client?
options: The thing asked for does not exist
quiz.why: 404 is Not Found. Malformed input is 400, a server failure is 500.

quiz.q: Why must the products map be thread-safe?
options: Handlers run on several pool threads at once
quiz.why: Concurrent requests read and write it from different threads.

quiz.q: What does a fixed pool of 4 threads mean for a fifth simultaneous request?
options: It waits until a thread is free
quiz.why: The executor queues it.

quiz.q: Which side decides the status code?
quiz.why: The handler sets it to report the outcome.

lessons.title: Backend: designing a REST API with validation and errors

blocks.text: A REST API exposes things (resources) at addresses (paths), such as /products and /products/2.
The HTTP method says what to do: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, DELETE removes.
The server checks everything it receives. Bad input gets a clear error with a status code and a machine-readable reason. Good input gets the result.
Why it matters

An API is a contract used by apps you cannot update on demand: an Android release from two years ago still calls it. Predictable paths, correct status codes and one consistent error shape are what let clients handle every outcome without guessing.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A post office counter with clearly labelled windows. Each window (path) deals with one kind of thing, the form you hand over (method and body) says what you want, and every rejection slip has the same layout so you always know where to look for the reason.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
This is the other end of URLSession. The error body here is what you decode into a Swift Decodable error type on a non-2xx response.
iOS
On iOS a 404 is not thrown by URLSession; you check statusCode yourself. Retrofit on Android throws HttpException for it. Both depend on the server choosing the right code.
Flutter
dio raises DioException with the response attached for 4xx and 5xx. A consistent error JSON lets one interceptor handle all of them.

blocks.text: POST /products with an empty name

items: The body is read as text
route sees POST on the collection path
validated() finds name is blank
It throws ApiException(400, "invalid_name", ...)
The handler catches it and builds the standard error body
The client receives 400 and can show a message for invalid_name

blocks.text: JDK only, Java 17 (records and switch expressions). The server and a client that exercises it are in one file, so it runs by itself.
The same resource in Spring Boot
What you would write at work. Routing, JSON and validation become annotations. From the shop-service project, which was built and run here.
Error mapping in Spring Boot
Walkthrough

blocks.code: record Product(int id, String name, long pricePaise)
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: A record is an immutable data class: constructor, accessors, equals and toString are generated.
One exception type carries the status and a stable error code. Throwing it anywhere produces a correct response.

blocks.code: static ApiResponse route(String method, String path, String query, String body)
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: Routing is a plain function with no HTTP objects, so it can be checked without starting a server.
A switch expression: each arm yields the response. Unknown methods become 405.
201 Created, with the new resource including the id the server chose.
204 No Content: it worked and there is nothing to send back.
Unexpected failures return a generic 500. Stack traces and SQL never go to the client; they go to the log.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output from this Mac: two POSTs return 201 with ids 1 and 2; an empty name and a non-numeric price return 400 with different error codes; GET with limit=1 returns one item; PUT returns the updated product; DELETE returns 204; reading the deleted product returns 404; PATCH returns 405; an unknown path returns 404.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Request and response objects are short-lived garbage once the response is written.
The store map and id counter are shared by every request thread, so they are a ConcurrentHashMap and an AtomicInteger.
Reading the whole body into memory is fine for small JSON. Uploads must be streamed, with a size limit.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: curl -i -X POST localhost:8080/products -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"Milk","pricePaise":6000}' shows exactly what a client sees.
Give every request an id, return it in a header, and include it in each log line. A user-reported failure can then be found in the logs.
When a client says "the API is broken", get the exact method, path, body and status first. Most reports are a 4xx the client did not read.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: these codes are what your Retrofit layer maps. 400 means fix the request, 401 means refresh or sign in again, 404 means the thing is gone, 409 means refresh your state, 5xx or no response means retry with backoff.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Spring Boot: @RestController, @GetMapping and @PostMapping do the routing; @Valid with annotations on a record does validation; @RestControllerAdvice maps exceptions to error bodies.
APIs are documented with OpenAPI, and client code can be generated from it.
Write operations that may be retried take an idempotency key so a repeated POST does not create two orders.
Rate limiting, authentication and request logging sit in filters in front of every handler.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Verbs in paths: POST /createProduct, GET /getProducts.
Nouns for resources, methods for verbs: POST /products, GET /products.
A different error format per endpoint.
One shape everywhere, with a stable code clients can switch on and a message for humans.
Trusting client input because "our app always sends it right".
Anyone can call your API. Validate on the server every time.
Removing or renaming a response field.
Old app versions break. Only add fields; version the API for breaking changes.
Returning unbounded lists.
Always page: a limit with a default and a maximum, and a cursor or offset.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add PATCH /products/{id} that changes only the fields present in the body.
Add a maximum of 100 to limit, and return 400 for limit=0.
Make POST idempotent: accept an Idempotency-Key header and return the same response for a repeated key.
blocks.text: Hint: A ConcurrentHashMap from key to the ApiResponse already sent

blocks.title: Write the error codes of this API as a table a mobile developer could work from.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: PUT versus PATCH versus POST?
blocks.text: POST creates a resource under a collection or triggers an action, and is not idempotent. PUT replaces the resource at a known address with the body sent, and is idempotent. PATCH applies a partial change. Use PUT when the client sends the full state, PATCH when it sends only what changed.

blocks.title: How do you version an API?
blocks.text: Avoid needing to: only make additive changes, and have clients ignore unknown fields. For breaking changes, put a version in the path (/v2/products) or a header, run both versions until old clients are gone, and measure usage of the old one before removing it.

blocks.title: How do you paginate a large collection?
blocks.text: Offset and limit is simple but slow on deep pages and unstable when rows are inserted. Cursor pagination returns an opaque token for "after this item", based on an indexed sort key, and stays fast and stable. Always cap the page size.

blocks.title: What makes a good error response?
blocks.text: The right status code, a stable machine-readable code, a human-readable message, field-level details for validation failures, and a request id for support. No stack traces or internal names. The same structure on every endpoint.

quiz.q: Which status fits a successful POST that created a product?
quiz.why: 201 Created.

quiz.q: A client sends a price of "free". Which status?
quiz.why: The request is malformed, so it is the client's to fix.

quiz.q: Why keep an error code separate from the message?
options: Clients branch on a stable code; messages may change or be translated
quiz.why: Text is for people, codes are for programs.

quiz.q: What should a 500 response contain?
options: A generic message, with details only in the server log
quiz.why: Internals help attackers and mean nothing to clients.

lessons.title: Backend: controllers, services, repositories and Spring Boot

blocks.text: Backend code is split into three kinds of class. A controller speaks HTTP. A service holds the business rules. A repository reads and writes data.
Each one only talks to the next: controller to service, service to repository.
Something has to create these objects and hand each one what it needs. You can do it by hand in main. Spring Boot does it for you: that is dependency injection.
Why it matters

Mixing HTTP, rules and SQL in one method makes each impossible to change or test alone. With layers, the rule "free delivery from Rs 500" lives in one class that can be tested in milliseconds with no server and no database.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A restaurant. The waiter (controller) takes orders and brings plates but does not cook. The chef (service) cooks to the recipes but does not go to market. The storekeeper (repository) fetches ingredients and knows nothing about recipes.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
Server-side Swift (Vapor) uses the same split: route handlers, services and repositories. On iOS the nearest shape is view model, use case and repository.
iOS
Spring's container is a dependency injection framework like Swinject or Factory, with much more: it also provides web, data and transaction support.
Flutter
This is the presentation, domain and data layering you already use in Flutter, with HTTP in place of widgets.

blocks.text: Placing an order

items: Controller receives the lines and calls service.place
Service loads each product through the repository
Service checks stock and adds up the price
Service saves the reduced stock and the order
Service returns the Order
Controller turns it into a 201 response

blocks.text: All layers are in one file and wired by hand in main, so you can see what a framework automates.
The service layer with Spring Boot

@RestController, @Service and the repository interface are found by Spring at startup and connected through their constructors. From the shop-service project, which was built and run here. The lesson "A Spring Boot project you build and run" shows every file.
Walkthrough

blocks.code: interface ProductRepository { Optional<Product> findById(int id); void save(Product product); }
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: The service depends on this interface, not on a database.
Constructor injection. The service never creates its own collaborators.
The service reports problems as domain exceptions. It does not know about 404.
A business rule, in exactly one place.

blocks.code: catch (OutOfStockException e) { return new Response(409, e.getMessage()); }
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: The controller owns the translation from domain failure to HTTP status.
The composition root. Spring's container does this, in the right order, for hundreds of classes.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output: the first order is 201 with delivery 4900; the second is 201 with free delivery because items total 68000; ordering Ghee again is 409 because stock is now 0; an unknown product is 404; an empty order is 400; and three units of milk have been taken from stock.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Controllers, services and repositories are created once and shared by all request threads, so they must hold no per-request state in fields.
Per-request data lives in local variables and method parameters, on each thread's own stack.
The in-memory repositories here are not thread-safe; a real repository delegates to the database, which is.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: A wrong response: decide which layer first. Call the service method directly with the same input; if it is right, the bug is in the controller mapping.
Spring startup failures name the bean that could not be created and the dependency it was missing. Read the last "Caused by".
Log at layer boundaries with the request id, not inside every method.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: the same separation as ViewModel, use case and repository. Recognising it makes backend code easy to read, and helps you tell the backend team which layer a bug is probably in.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Spring Boot scans for @RestController, @Service and @Repository, creates one instance of each, and injects them by constructor.
@Transactional on a service method makes it one database transaction.
Configuration classes with @Bean methods create objects you do not own, such as an HTTP client or a clock.
Other entry points, such as Kafka consumers and scheduled jobs, call the same services as the controllers.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Business rules in the controller.
They cannot be reused by another entry point, such as a message consumer or a scheduled job. Put them in the service.
A service method returning ResponseEntity or taking HttpServletRequest.
That ties rules to HTTP. Pass and return plain objects.
Storing the current user or request in a field of a singleton service.
Every request thread shares that field. Pass it as a parameter.
Field injection with @Autowired on private fields.
Use constructor injection: dependencies are visible, final, and the class can be created in a plain unit check.
Returning database entities straight from the API.
Map to response objects so a schema change does not change the API.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add a second entry point, a "nightly restock" method, that reuses OrderService or a new StockService without touching the controller.
Write a FailingProductRepository that throws, and decide which status the controller should return.
Move the delivery rule into its own DeliveryPolicy interface so it can vary by city.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What does Spring's dependency injection container do?
blocks.text: At startup it finds classes marked as components, works out the dependency graph from their constructors, creates each object once in the right order, and passes dependencies in. It can also wrap objects in proxies to add behaviour such as transactions, security checks and caching.

blocks.title: Constructor injection versus field injection?
blocks.text: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and final, allows creating the object without the framework, and fails at startup if something is missing. Field injection hides dependencies, needs reflection, and permits half-built objects. Constructor injection is the recommended style.

blocks.title: What is a bean scope?
blocks.text: How long the container keeps an instance. Singleton, the default, is one per application. Prototype is a new one per injection. Request and session scopes are one per HTTP request or session. Most beans are stateless singletons.

blocks.title: How is a backend service layer like an Android architecture?
blocks.text: Controller corresponds to the UI layer and ViewModel, service to the domain layer and use cases, repository to the data layer. Both point dependencies at the rules and inject implementations. The main difference is concurrency: a server shares each object among many request threads.

quiz.q: Which layer decides that out-of-stock becomes HTTP 409?
quiz.why: Only the controller knows about HTTP.

quiz.q: Why does the service depend on a repository interface?
options: So storage can change and be faked in checks
quiz.why: The rules do not care where data lives.

quiz.q: Why must a singleton service keep no request data in fields?
options: All request threads share the one instance
quiz.why: One user's data would leak into another's request.

blocks.text: A relational database stores data in tables of rows and columns. SQL is the language for asking questions of it and changing it.
JDBC is the part of Java that sends SQL to a database and reads the rows that come back.
A transaction groups several changes so that either all of them happen or none do.
Why it matters

A server's memory is lost on every restart and is not shared between the several copies of a service that run at once. The database is the one place where data is durable, shared and consistent. Transactions are what stop money or stock disappearing when something fails halfway.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A bank transfer. Money leaving one account and arriving in another are two steps. A transaction is the promise that you never see one without the other, even if the power fails in between.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: iOS
You know SQL from the SQLite inside Core Data and GRDB. A server database such as PostgreSQL is the same language with many clients connected at once, so locking and isolation matter far more.
Swift
JDBC is the low-level driver API. JPA and Hibernate sit above it as an object mapper, in the position Core Data or SwiftData occupy.
Flutter
Room on Android and drift in Flutter wrap a local SQLite file. The SQL in this lesson is the same; the server version adds connection pools and concurrent transactions.

blocks.text: placeOrder as one transaction

items: Borrow a connection and turn auto-commit off
UPDATE stock, only if enough is left
No row updated: throw, which leads to rollback
INSERT the order and read its generated id
INSERT the order line
commit: all three become visible to everyone at once
On any SQLException: rollback, so none of them happened

blocks.text: JDBC is in the JDK, so this file was compiled here. It was not run, because running needs a database driver that is not on this Mac.
The SQL itself, run for real with sqlite3
These statements ran on this Mac in an in-memory SQLite database. The lines starting with a dot are sqlite3 shell commands, not SQL.
The same data access with Spring Data JPA: the entity
An @Entity class and a repository interface replace the hand-written SQL for simple cases. From the shop-service project, which was built and run here.
The repository interface
Walkthrough
try-with-resources closes both. Closing a pooled connection returns it to the pool.
The value travels separately from the SQL text, so it can never be executed as SQL.
A ResultSet is a cursor. next() moves to the next row and says whether there was one.
Starts a transaction. By default every statement commits by itself.

blocks.code: "UPDATE products SET stock = stock - ? WHERE id = ? AND stock >= ?"
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: The check and the change are one statement, so two buyers cannot both take the last item.

blocks.code: if (take.executeUpdate() == 0) throw new SQLException("Not enough stock");
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: executeUpdate returns how many rows changed. Zero means the condition failed.
Commit makes the changes permanent and visible. Rollback discards them.
What happens when it runs

items: Real sqlite3 output: Milk and Ghee are in stock; the join lists four order lines; asha has 2 orders totalling 98000 and ravi 1 totalling 6000; after the committed transaction Milk stock is 7; after the rolled-back one Ghee stock is still 1; and the query plan changes from "SCAN orders" to "SEARCH orders USING COVERING INDEX" once the index exists.
SQLite stands in for a server database here. The SQL shown is standard and works the same on PostgreSQL or MySQL; EXPLAIN output differs between databases.

blocks.text: Memory

items: A database connection is expensive: a network socket and server-side memory. Services keep a small pool, often 10 to 20, and share it.
A request that holds a connection while doing something slow starves the others. Borrow late, return early.
Reading a huge result into a List can exhaust the heap. Page the query or stream it.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Run the exact SQL by hand in a database console with the same parameters. Most data bugs are visible at once.
EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE on PostgreSQL) shows whether a query uses an index or scans the table.
Turn on SQL logging in development to see what an object mapper really sends, including how many queries one request makes.
"Connection is not available, request timed out" means the pool is exhausted: look for leaked or long-held connections.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: Room is this same SQL with compile-time checking, and the same advice applies: parameters not concatenation, transactions for multi-step changes, indexes for filtered columns.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Most Java services use Spring Data JPA with Hibernate for ordinary reads and writes, and plain SQL (JdbcTemplate or jOOQ) for reports and performance-critical queries.
@Transactional on a service method begins a transaction, commits on normal return and rolls back on an unchecked exception.
Schema changes are versioned scripts applied by Flyway or Liquibase, never by hand and never by the app's object mapper in production.
Isolation levels decide what concurrent transactions see of each other. Read committed is the usual default; know that it permits a lost update unless you lock or check.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"
That is SQL injection. Always use ? parameters with PreparedStatement.
Reading stock in one statement and writing it in another with no protection.
Two requests interleave and oversell. Use a conditional UPDATE, a row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), or optimistic locking with a version column.
Forgetting to close a connection on the error path.
The pool runs dry and every request hangs. Use try-with-resources.
One query per row in a loop (the N+1 problem).
Fetch with a join or an IN (...) query. With JPA, use a fetch join or an entity graph.
A transaction left open while calling another service.
Locks are held for the whole call. Keep transactions short and database-only.
Filtering on a column with no index in a large table.
The database scans every row. Add an index, and confirm with EXPLAIN.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add a query to shop.sql that lists products never ordered.
blocks.text: Hint: LEFT JOIN order_lines ... WHERE order_lines.product_id IS NULL

blocks.title: Add a version column to products and write the UPDATE that only succeeds if the version is unchanged.
Write a JDBC method that returns the top three customers by spend, using the aggregate query from shop.sql.
Install a database driver in a real project and run ProductJdbcRepository against it.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Explain ACID.
blocks.text: Atomicity: a transaction's changes all happen or none do. Consistency: constraints hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work, to a degree set by the isolation level. Durability: once committed, changes survive a crash.

blocks.title: What are the isolation levels and the problems they prevent?
blocks.text: Read uncommitted allows dirty reads. Read committed prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads. Repeatable read keeps rows you have read stable but may allow phantom rows. Serializable behaves as if transactions ran one at a time. Higher levels cost more locking or more retries.

blocks.title: Optimistic versus pessimistic locking?
blocks.text: Pessimistic: lock the row when you read it (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) so nobody else can change it until you commit. Optimistic: read a version number, and make the update conditional on the version being unchanged; if zero rows update, someone else got there first and you retry or report a conflict. Optimistic suits rare conflicts; pessimistic suits frequent ones.

blocks.title: What is the N+1 query problem?
blocks.text: Loading a list with one query and then issuing one more query per item for a related object, which turns one request into hundreds of round trips. It usually comes from lazy loading in an object mapper. Fix with a join fetch, a batch size, or a dedicated query.

blocks.title: JDBC, JPA or something in between?
blocks.text: JDBC gives full control and full boilerplate. JPA with Hibernate maps objects to tables, tracks changes and writes SQL for you, which is productive for ordinary operations and opaque when performance matters. JdbcTemplate and jOOQ sit between: you write the SQL, they remove the plumbing. Many teams use JPA by default and SQL for the hard queries.

quiz.q: Why use PreparedStatement parameters?
quiz.why: Values are sent as data, never parsed as SQL.

quiz.q: What does rollback do?
options: Discards the changes made in the current transaction
quiz.why: The database returns to how it was before the transaction began.

quiz.q: What is a connection pool for?
options: Reusing a limited set of open connections
Running SQL in parallel on one connection
quiz.why: Opening a connection per request is slow and the database allows only so many.

quiz.q: A query plan says SCAN on a table of ten million rows. What is likely missing?
options: An index on the filtered column
quiz.why: Without an index every row is read.

lessons.title: Backend: authentication, password hashing and tokens

blocks.text: Authentication answers "who are you?". Authorization answers "are you allowed to do this?".
A server never stores passwords. It stores a hash: the result of a slow one-way function. At login it hashes what you typed and compares.
After login the server gives the client a token. The client sends it with every request so it does not have to log in each time.
A signed token carries a signature made with a secret only the server knows, so the server can tell if anyone changed it.
Why it matters

HTTP has no memory: every request arrives alone. Tokens are how a server recognises a returning user. Hashing limits the damage when a database leaks, which does happen. Getting either wrong exposes every user at once.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A wristband at an event. You show ID once at the gate (login) and get a band (token) that staff can check at a glance. The band has a tamper-proof seal (signature) and is only valid for today (expiry). A staff-only band opens doors a guest band does not (authorization).
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: iOS
On the client you store the token in the Keychain; on Android, encrypted with a Keystore key. This lesson is the server side that issues and checks it.
Swift
CryptoKit's HMAC<SHA256> is the Mac class here. The base64url header.payload.signature layout is the same JWT your iOS app already carries.
Flutter
A dio interceptor that adds Authorization: Bearer and refreshes on 401 is the client half of this protocol.

blocks.text: Verifying a token

items: Split into header, payload and signature
Recompute the signature over header.payload with the server secret
Compare in constant time. Different: reject
Decode the payload and read the expiry
Expired: reject
Otherwise trust the subject and role inside

blocks.text: JDK only, to show the mechanics. In production use a maintained library for password hashing and tokens; do not ship hand-written crypto code.
Walkthrough
PBKDF2 runs the hash many thousands of times so that each guess is slow for an attacker. Use the iteration count currently recommended for your algorithm, or a library offering Argon2id or bcrypt.
A random salt per user means two users with the same password get different hashes.
A constant-time comparison. A normal equals returns early on the first different byte, which leaks timing.
The JWT layout. The first two parts are only encoded, not encrypted: anyone can read them.

blocks.code: if (now >= claims.expiresAt()) throw new SecurityException("token expired");
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: A token is valid only for a short time, so a stolen one is useful only briefly.
Authentication succeeded. Authorization is a separate check.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output: the right password matches and a near-miss does not; the token has 3 segments and its payload is readable by anyone; changing the role to admin without the secret is rejected with "bad signature"; 16 minutes later the token is expired; and the admin endpoint returns 401 with no token, 403 with a customer token and 200 with an admin token.

blocks.text: Memory

items: A signed token lets the server stay stateless: nothing is stored per login, so any server instance can check any request.
The cost of stateless tokens is that they cannot be cancelled before expiry without a server-side list. Short lifetimes and refresh tokens are the usual answer.
Secrets belong in configuration supplied at runtime, never in source code. The one in this teaching file is only there so the example runs.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Decode a token's payload (it is only base64url) to see its subject, role and expiry when a request is refused.
A burst of 401s after a deploy usually means the signing secret or key changed, invalidating existing tokens.
Clock differences between servers cause "expired" or "not yet valid" errors. Allow a few seconds of leeway and keep clocks synchronised.
Log authentication failures with the reason, but never log passwords or full tokens.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: store the refresh token encrypted with a Keystore key, send the access token in an Authorization header from an OkHttp interceptor, and refresh on 401 through an Authenticator, with a lock so parallel requests refresh once.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Spring Security provides the filter chain: it parses the token, sets the current user, and enforces rules such as @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')").
Login for real products is usually delegated: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect with an identity provider, which issues tokens signed with a private key that services verify with the public key.
Session cookies are the alternative to tokens for browser apps: the server keeps session state, which makes logout and revocation simple.
Everything here assumes HTTPS. Without it, passwords and tokens travel in the clear.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Storing passwords in plain text or with a fast hash such as MD5 or SHA-256 alone.
Use a slow, salted password hash: Argon2id, bcrypt or PBKDF2 with a high iteration count.
Putting sensitive data in a token payload.
The payload is readable by anyone who holds the token. Put identifiers in it, nothing secret.
Trusting a user id or role sent by the client in the body.
Take identity only from the verified token.
Checking only that the user is logged in before returning /orders/{id}.
Also check the order belongs to that user. Missing ownership checks are among the most common API vulnerabilities.
Tokens that never expire.
Short-lived access tokens, with a refresh token that can be revoked.
Accepting whatever algorithm the token header names.
Fix the algorithm on the server. Tokens claiming "none" or a different algorithm must be rejected.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add a refresh token: a random value stored server-side that can be exchanged for a new access token and revoked.
Add an ownership check: a customer may read only their own order, an admin any order.
Change one character of the token signature and of the payload, and observe each failure.
Explain why the server must use the same secret on every instance, and what happens during a secret rotation.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Sessions versus tokens?
blocks.text: A session keeps state on the server and gives the client an opaque id, usually in a cookie: easy to revoke, needs shared session storage across servers. A signed token carries the state itself: no server lookup and easy to scale, but hard to revoke before it expires and larger on every request. Browsers often use sessions; mobile apps and service-to-service calls usually use tokens.

blocks.title: How does a JWT work, and what are its risks?
blocks.text: It is three base64url parts: a header naming the algorithm, a payload of claims such as subject and expiry, and a signature over the first two. The server verifies the signature and expiry and then trusts the claims. Risks: the payload is readable, tokens cannot be revoked without extra state, algorithm confusion if the server trusts the header, and long lifetimes turning a leak into lasting access.

blocks.title: How should passwords be stored?
blocks.text: With a password hashing function designed to be slow and salted per user: Argon2id is the current preference, bcrypt and scrypt are established, PBKDF2 is acceptable with a high iteration count. Store the algorithm, parameters and salt with the hash so settings can be raised later and old hashes upgraded at next login.

blocks.title: Describe the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE for a mobile app.
blocks.text: The app opens the provider's login page in the system browser with a code challenge derived from a random verifier. The user signs in there, and the provider redirects back to the app with a one-time code. The app exchanges the code plus the original verifier for tokens. PKCE stops another app that intercepts the code from using it, and the app never sees the password.

blocks.title: What is the difference between authentication and authorization, with an example of a bug in each?
blocks.text: Authentication establishes identity; a bug is accepting an expired or unsigned token. Authorization decides permission; a bug is letting any logged-in user fetch /orders/123 without checking that order 123 is theirs. The second kind is more common and harder for tests to notice.

quiz.q: What does a server store for a password?
options: An encrypted password it can decrypt
quiz.why: A hash cannot be reversed, and the salt and slowness make guessing expensive.

quiz.q: A valid customer token calls an admin-only endpoint. Which status?
quiz.why: The user is known but not permitted.

quiz.q: Can a client read the payload of a signed token?
quiz.why: Signing proves it was not changed. It does not hide it.

quiz.q: Why give tokens a short lifetime?
options: To limit how long a stolen token works
quiz.why: Stateless tokens cannot easily be cancelled, so they are made to expire soon.

blocks.text: A test is a small program that calls your code with known input and checks the result. It passes or fails with no human looking.
Every test has three steps: arrange the starting situation, act by calling the code, assert that the result is what you expected.
To test one class alone, replace the things it depends on (a database, a clock) with stand-ins you control. These are called fakes or mocks.
Why it matters

A backend change ships to every user at once. Tests are what let you change code and know within seconds whether the rules still hold, without clicking through an app or waiting for a customer to find out.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A pilot's pre-flight checklist. Each item is small, the same every time, and gives a clear yes or no. Nobody relies on "it flew fine yesterday".
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
JUnit is XCTest: @Test methods are test functions, assertEquals is XCTAssertEqual, and assertThrows is XCTAssertThrowsError.
iOS
Mockito generates stand-ins at runtime from an interface. Swift has no runtime mocking, so iOS developers write fakes by hand, exactly as the runnable file in this lesson does.
Flutter
package:test with mocktail maps directly: test(), expect(), when().thenReturn().

blocks.text: One unit test

items: Arrange: a fake repository that knows milk costs 6000, and a clock fixed at noon
Act: call quote("milk", 10)
Assert: the result equals 54000
Equal: pass, and say nothing
Different: fail, printing expected and actual

blocks.text: A test harness in thirty lines of plain Java, so you can see there is no magic. It was compiled and run here. Its last check fails on purpose to show what a failure looks like.
The same idea with JUnit 5 and Mockito
What you would write at work. This is a real test class in the shop-service project.
A web-layer test
Starts only the controller and sends it fake HTTP requests.
Walkthrough
The service receives its dependencies. That is the only thing that makes it testable.

blocks.code: ProductRepository fakeRepository = name -> name.equals("milk") ? Optional.of(6_000L) : Optional.empty();
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: A fake: a tiny implementation the check controls. No database is involved.
Time is a dependency too. A real clock would make the result depend on when you ran it.
Arrange, act and assert in one line. The expected value is written out, not computed.
Failure cases are checked as carefully as successes.
Mockito: program a generated stand-in instead of writing a fake class.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output: five checks PASS, and the sixth reports "FAIL a wrong expectation fails loudly: expected 1 but was 6000". A good failure message names what was checked, the expected value and the actual value.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Unit tests create a few small objects and need no server, database or network, which is why thousands run in seconds.
Each test builds its own objects. State shared between tests makes them pass or fail depending on order.
Integration tests start real infrastructure, so they are slower and are kept fewer.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Read the failure message before the code: expected versus actual usually names the bug.
Run the single failing test alone. If it passes alone and fails in the suite, another test is leaving state behind.
A test that never fails is not proof: break the code on purpose once and confirm the test notices.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: the same pyramid. ViewModels and use cases get JVM unit tests with fakes; Room DAOs and UI get instrumented tests. The dependency-injection habits from this lesson are what make either possible.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: JUnit 5 runs the tests; Mockito or hand-written fakes isolate a class; AssertJ gives readable assertions.
Spring offers slices: @WebMvcTest starts only the web layer with MockMvc, @DataJpaTest only the persistence layer.
Testcontainers starts a real PostgreSQL or Kafka in Docker for integration tests, so SQL is checked against the database you ship with.
Tests run on every commit in CI, and a failing build blocks the merge.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Tests that call the real clock, network or a shared database.
Inject a clock, fake the network, and give each test its own data.
Asserting on how the code works, with a verify for every internal call.
Assert on results. Tests that mirror the implementation break on every refactor.
One enormous test covering ten cases.
One behaviour per test, named for what it checks.
Only testing the success path.
Bad input, missing data and failing dependencies are where production bugs are.
Mocking the class under test, or mocking simple value objects.
Mock collaborators at the boundary. Use real objects for values.
Ignoring a test that fails "sometimes".
A flaky test hides a real race or a shared-state bug. Find the cause or delete the test.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add a rule: orders over 20 items are refused. Write the check first, watch it fail, then write the code.
Make the last check pass by fixing the expectation, then make a real bug in quote() and see which checks catch it.
Write a fake repository that throws, and decide what quote() should do.
In a real project, convert ServiceChecks to JUnit 5.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Mock, stub, fake, spy: what is the difference?
blocks.text: A stub returns canned answers. A mock also records calls so you can verify interactions. A fake is a real but simplified implementation, such as an in-memory repository. A spy wraps a real object and records calls. Prefer fakes and stubs with assertions on results; use interaction verification where the interaction is the behaviour, such as "an email was sent".

blocks.title: What makes code testable?
blocks.text: Dependencies passed in through the constructor, behind interfaces at the boundaries; no static or global state; time, randomness and I/O treated as dependencies; and small methods that return values. Code that is hard to test is usually telling you about a design problem.

blocks.title: Unit test or integration test for a repository?
blocks.text: Integration. A repository's job is its interaction with the database, so mocking the database tests nothing. Run it against the same database engine used in production, in a container, with a clean schema per test.

blocks.title: How do you deal with flaky tests?
blocks.text: Treat them as bugs. Typical causes: shared state between tests, dependence on timing or real time, test order, and external services. Reproduce by running the test repeatedly, remove the nondeterminism by injecting it, and do not paper over it with retries.

blocks.title: What does code coverage tell you, and what does it not?
blocks.text: It tells you which lines ran during tests, so it finds code with no tests at all. It does not tell you whether the assertions were meaningful. High coverage with weak assertions is false comfort; use it to find gaps, not as a target.

quiz.q: What are the three parts of a test?
quiz.why: Set up, call the code, check the result.

quiz.q: Why pass a Clock into the service?
options: So a test can fix the time
quiz.why: A real clock makes results depend on when the test runs.

quiz.q: Which tests should there be most of?
quiz.why: They are fast and point directly at the failing class.

quiz.q: What is a fake?
options: A simple working implementation used in place of a real dependency
quiz.why: For example an in-memory repository.

lessons.title: Backend: building, configuring and running a service

blocks.text: A build tool (Maven or Gradle) downloads the libraries your service needs, compiles it, runs the tests and packages everything into one file, a jar.
The same jar runs everywhere. What differs between your laptop, the test environment and production is configuration, supplied from outside as environment variables.
A running service must tell the platform whether it is alive and whether it is ready for traffic, write logs someone can search, and shut down without dropping requests.
Why it matters

Code that works on your machine is not a service. A service is built the same way every time, configured per environment without rebuilding, observable when something goes wrong at night, and replaceable with a new version without users noticing.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Opening a shop, not just baking bread. You need a repeatable recipe (the build), settings that differ per branch such as opening hours (configuration), a sign that says open or closed (health and readiness), a ledger (logs), and a closing routine that serves the customers already inside (graceful shutdown).
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: iOS
Maven and Gradle are Swift Package Manager plus xcodebuild. A jar is the archive you ship; a container image is closer to an .ipa that also carries its runtime.
iOS
Environment variables per environment play the role of xcconfig files and build configurations, with one difference: the binary is identical and the values are read at start.
Flutter
An app release goes through store review and users update when they choose. A backend release reaches everyone immediately, so rollout and rollback are part of the design.

blocks.text: A rolling update

items: A new instance starts with the new version
It reads configuration and refuses to start if something required is missing
/ready returns 503 until the database connection and caches are up
/ready returns 200 and the load balancer sends it traffic
An old instance is told to stop
It stops accepting requests, finishes those in flight, closes its pool and exits

blocks.text: JDK only. Configuration, a health and a readiness endpoint, a structured log line and a shutdown hook, compiled and run here.
Maven build file
The build file of the shop-service project. The parent supplies tested versions for every Spring dependency, which is why they carry no version numbers.
Spring Boot configuration
Container image
Not built here. A two-stage build: the first stage has Maven and the JDK, the second has only a JRE and the jar.
Walkthrough
Read from the environment, with a sensible default for local runs.

blocks.code: if (dbUrl == null) throw new IllegalStateException("APP_DB_URL is required");
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: Fail fast. A service that starts with broken configuration fails later, in a more confusing way.
Liveness: the process is running and can answer.
Readiness: 503 until the instance can really serve requests.
Runs when the process is asked to stop, which is the moment to finish in-flight work and release resources.
One line per event, as key=value pairs, with a request id to connect the lines of one request.
A starter is one dependency that pulls in everything needed for a job, here the web server and JSON.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output: the default configuration; the overridden one; two refusals to start, for a missing database URL and a non-numeric port; /health 200 and /ready 503 while starting; /ready 200 after warm-up; one structured log line; and the shutdown hook message printed as the program exits.

blocks.text: Memory

items: In a container the JVM must be told how much of the container's memory to use for the heap, for example -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75, leaving the rest for thread stacks and native memory.
Exceeding the container limit gets the process killed by the platform with no Java exception and no heap dump.
Several small identical instances are preferred to one large one: a failure or a deploy then affects only part of the capacity.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Start from the request id: find every log line for it across services.
Three questions for any incident: what changed (deploy, configuration, traffic), what do the error rate and latency graphs show, and is one instance or all of them affected.
A service that restarts in a loop: read the last lines of its log before the restart. It is usually missing configuration or an unreachable dependency.
Take a thread dump when a service hangs and a heap dump when memory climbs.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: staged rollout, feature flags and crash-rate monitoring are the mobile versions of rolling updates, configuration and observability. The difference is that you cannot roll an installed app back, which is why the backend has to stay compatible with old versions.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: Spring Boot packages the service and its web server into one runnable jar; spring-boot-starter-actuator provides health and metrics endpoints.
CI builds, tests and publishes an image on every merge. CD deploys it, usually instance by instance, watching health and error rates.
Kubernetes is the common platform: it runs the containers, probes liveness and readiness, restarts failures and performs rolling updates.
Observability means three things: logs for what happened, metrics for how much and how fast, traces for where time went across services.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Secrets and environment-specific URLs committed in source.
Supply them at runtime from environment variables or a secret manager.
A different build per environment.
Build once, promote the same artefact from test to production, change only configuration.
A liveness check that queries the database.
A database outage then restarts every instance repeatedly. Put dependency checks in readiness.
Logging with System.out and free-form text, or logging passwords and tokens.
Use a logging library with levels and structured fields, and keep secrets and personal data out.
Killing instances without a grace period.
Requests in flight fail. Handle the stop signal: stop accepting, finish, close, exit.
No timeouts on calls to other services.
One slow dependency ties up every thread. Set timeouts, and add retries with backoff only for safe operations.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add APP_LOG_LEVEL to Config with allowed values DEBUG, INFO and WARN, refusing anything else.
Add a /ready check that becomes false again when a simulated database flag is turned off.
Explain each line of the Dockerfile, and why the build has two stages.
In examples/spring/shop-service, run mvn package and start the jar with a different APP_PORT without rebuilding.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Liveness versus readiness probes?
blocks.text: Liveness asks whether the process should be restarted; it should check only that the process itself can respond. Readiness asks whether the instance should receive traffic; it may check dependencies and warm-up. Failing liveness causes a restart, failing readiness only removes the instance from the load balancer.

blocks.title: How do you manage configuration and secrets?
blocks.text: Keep configuration out of the artefact and supply it at runtime: environment variables, mounted files or a configuration service. Secrets come from a secret manager with access control and rotation, never from source control or the image. Validate everything at startup and fail fast.

blocks.title: How do you deploy without downtime?
blocks.text: Run several instances behind a load balancer. Replace them one at a time (rolling), or bring up a full new set and switch (blue-green), or send a small share of traffic to the new version first (canary). All require readiness checks, graceful shutdown, and database changes that both the old and the new version can work with.

blocks.title: What would you monitor for a service?
blocks.text: Request rate, error rate and latency percentiles per endpoint; saturation of threads, connection pool, memory and CPU; garbage collection pauses; and the health of each dependency. Alerts should be on symptoms users feel, such as error rate and latency, not on every internal metric.

blocks.title: Maven or Gradle?
blocks.text: Both resolve dependencies, compile, test and package. Maven is declarative XML with a fixed lifecycle: predictable and uniform. Gradle uses a Kotlin or Groovy build script: more flexible and faster with caching, which is why Android uses it. Backend teams use either; what matters is a reproducible build with pinned versions.

quiz.q: What should differ between test and production?
quiz.why: Build once, configure per environment.

quiz.q: What should an instance return from /ready while its database connection is not up yet?
quiz.why: Not ready: alive, but must not receive traffic.

quiz.q: Why fail at startup on missing configuration?
options: So the problem is found immediately, not at the first request that needs it
quiz.why: A bad instance never reaches users.

quiz.q: What does graceful shutdown do?
options: Stops taking new requests and finishes those in flight
quiz.why: So a deploy does not fail user requests.

lessons.title: Backend: a Spring Boot project you build and run

blocks.text: This is a complete Spring Boot service, not a sketch. It lives in the examples/spring/shop-service folder of this academy's project, and it was built with Maven, started, and called over HTTP on this Mac.

It has four endpoints: list products, get one product, create a product, and a health check. The data is kept in H2, a database that lives in memory, so you need nothing installed except Java 17 and Maven.
Each class has one job and its own file: the application entry point, an entity, a repository, a service, a controller, and one class that turns errors into responses.
Why it matters

The earlier backend lessons build each idea by hand in plain Java so you can see how it works. At work you will use a framework. This lesson shows the same ideas in the form you will actually write, in a project you can run, change and break yourself.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: The earlier lessons were cooking each dish from raw ingredients to learn the technique. Spring Boot is a professional kitchen: the ovens, the pass and the suppliers are already in place. You write the recipes (controller, service, repository) and the kitchen runs them.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: iOS
pom.xml is Package.swift: it names the libraries. Maven downloads them to ~/.m2 the first time, as SwiftPM does into its cache.
Swift
@RestController with @GetMapping is close to a Vapor route collection. The difference is that Spring finds the class by scanning the package; you do not register it.
Flutter
Spring's container plays the role of get_it or Riverpod providers: it creates each object once and passes it to whoever asks for it in a constructor.
iOS
The Product entity with a repository interface is the server-side counterpart of a Core Data or SwiftData model with a fetch request.

blocks.text: POST /products with a valid body

items: The embedded Tomcat server accepts the connection and hands the request to Spring
Spring matches POST /products to ProductController.create
Jackson turns the JSON body into a CreateProductRequest record
@Valid checks @NotBlank and @Positive; a failure stops here with 400
The controller calls ProductService.create, which opens a transaction
ProductRepository.save runs an INSERT and the database assigns the id
The transaction commits and the Product is returned
Jackson turns the Product into JSON and the response is 201 Created

blocks.text: The whole entry point. Below it are the real responses the running service gave. They were recorded by this project's check script, which builds the jar, starts it on a free port, sends these seven requests and stops it.
Controller: HTTP in, HTTP out
Request body and its validation rules
Service: rules and transactions
Entity: one row of the products table
The fields are private with getters. Jackson builds the JSON from the getters, and JPA needs the no-argument constructor.
Repository: an interface with no implementation
Errors: exceptions to responses, in one place
Build file
Maven downloaded Spring Boot and the other libraries into ~/.m2 on the first build. Later builds work offline.
Configuration
Table and starting rows
Spring runs schema.sql and then data.sql at startup, for the in-memory database only. Hibernate then checks that the table matches the entity (ddl-auto: validate).
A unit test of the service
A web-layer test of the controller
Walkthrough
Three things in one: this is a configuration class, turn on auto-configuration, and scan this package for annotated classes.
Creates every object, connects them, runs the SQL files, starts Tomcat on the port, and then waits for requests.
Spring sees the constructor needs a ProductService, finds the @Service class, and passes it in.
The {id} part of the path becomes the parameter. /products/abc gives 400 without any code from you.
@RequestBody: build the record from JSON. @Valid: check its annotations before the method runs.

blocks.code: record CreateProductRequest(@NotBlank String name, @Positive long pricePaise)
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: The rules sit on the data they describe.
Spring Data reads the method name and writes the query: where upper(name) like upper(?) with a trailing %.
Spring wraps the method: begin before it, commit when it returns, roll back if it throws an unchecked exception.
Any controller that lets this exception escape gets a 404 with the same body shape.
A starter pulls in a working set: here Hibernate, Spring Data and a connection pool. No version is given because the parent sets it.
What happens when it runs

items: To run it yourself: open a terminal in examples/spring/shop-service and run mvn spring-boot:run. The first run downloads the libraries. Then call it with curl from another terminal; the commands are in the README in that folder.

The recorded responses, in order: health is UP; the list has the two rows from data.sql; product 1 is Milk; the POST returns 201 and the database gave the new product id 3; the prefix search for "g" finds only Ghee, ignoring case; product 99 is 404 with the not_found body; and a blank name with a negative price is 400, naming both fields.
What was not done here: the two test classes were compiled by Maven but not run, the container image was not built, and the service was only run against H2, not PostgreSQL.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Spring creates one ProductController, one ProductService and one repository, and every request thread shares them. That is why they hold only final references and no per-request data.

Tomcat serves requests from a thread pool (200 threads by default). The database connection pool is smaller (10 here), so at most 10 requests can be inside the database at once; the others wait for a connection.

Inside a transaction, Hibernate keeps the entities it loaded in a per-transaction cache and compares them with the database at commit. Loading thousands of entities in one transaction holds them all in memory.
The H2 database here is in the heap of the same process. Stop the service and the data is gone, which is what you want for a lesson and never for production.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: The service will not start: read the first "Caused by" from the bottom of the stack trace. It is usually a missing bean (a class not scanned or not annotated), a schema mismatch reported by validate, or a port already in use.
A request gives 404 for a path you wrote: check the class is in or under the application's package and has @RestController, then check the HTTP method.
A request gives 400 or 415: the body did not parse, or the Content-Type header is not application/json.
To see the SQL that Hibernate runs, start with --logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=debug. Never leave it on in production.
Port 8080 is taken: start with APP_PORT=8081 mvn spring-boot:run, or pass --server.port=8081 to the jar.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: this is the server your Retrofit interface talks to. The JSON field names here (id, name, pricePaise) are the contract your data classes must match, and the 400 and 404 bodies are what your error handling parses.
When the mobile and backend teams disagree about a response, running the service locally and calling it with curl settles it in a minute.

blocks.text: On the backend

items: A production version of this service adds: PostgreSQL with migrations, response records separate from entities, pagination on the list, authentication, request logging with a request id, and tests that run in CI on every change.
The H2 default exists so the project runs anywhere. Setting APP_DB_URL, APP_DB_USER and APP_DB_PASSWORD switches it to PostgreSQL without rebuilding.
New Spring Boot projects are usually generated at start.spring.io, which produces this same layout: pom.xml, src/main/java, src/main/resources, src/test/java.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Entity fields with no getters, then wondering why the JSON is empty or the request fails.
Jackson reads public getters (or record components). Better still, return a separate response record so the API does not change when the table does.
ddl-auto: update or create against a shared database.
Hibernate will change or drop tables. Use validate, and change the schema with migrations (Flyway or Liquibase).
Putting classes outside the package of the @SpringBootApplication class.
Scanning starts at that package. A controller elsewhere is silently not found, and every request to it is 404.
@Transactional on a private method, or calling a transactional method from another method of the same class.
The transaction is added by a wrapper around the object, so it only applies to calls that come in from outside through a public method.
Leaving open-in-view at its default.
It keeps a database connection for the whole request, including while JSON is written. Turn it off and load what you need inside the service.
Returning the framework's default error body for some errors and your own for others.
Handle them in one @RestControllerAdvice so clients see one shape.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Run the service and repeat the seven recorded requests with curl. Check each response against the one shown here.
Add DELETE /products/{id} that returns 204, and 404 when the product does not exist.
blocks.text: Hint: A service method that calls get(id) first, then repository.delete

blocks.title: Add a stock column: change schema.sql, data.sql and Product together. Then change only Product and read the startup error that validate gives you.
Return a ProductResponse record from the controller, not the entity, with the price as rupees and paise.
Make a duplicate product name return 409.
blocks.text: Hint: A unique constraint in schema.sql, and a handler for DataIntegrityViolationException in ApiErrors

blocks.title: Call the service from the Retrofit interface in the Android networking lesson, using http://10.0.2.2:8080 from the emulator.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What does @SpringBootApplication do?
blocks.text: It combines three annotations. @Configuration marks the class as a source of bean definitions. @EnableAutoConfiguration configures what it finds on the classpath: with spring-web present it sets up an embedded server and JSON conversion, with a JDBC driver and JPA present it sets up a connection pool and Hibernate. @ComponentScan finds annotated classes in this package and below.

blocks.title: Constructor injection versus field injection?
blocks.text: With constructor injection the dependencies are parameters: they can be final, the object is never half-built, and a test can create the class with new and pass in fakes. Field injection hides dependencies, needs reflection to set them, and makes it easy for a class to collect too many. Constructor injection is the recommended form; with a single constructor no annotation is needed.

blocks.title: How does @Transactional work, and when does it silently not work?
blocks.text: Spring wraps the bean in a proxy. A call through the proxy begins a transaction, runs the method, and commits, or rolls back on an unchecked exception. It does nothing when the call does not pass through the proxy: a method calling another method of the same object, or a private method. By default checked exceptions do not cause a rollback.

blocks.title: Why should a controller not return JPA entities?
blocks.text: It ties the API to the table: renaming a column changes the JSON, and new columns leak out without a decision. Lazy relations can trigger queries during serialisation or fail outside a transaction. Accepting entities as request bodies lets a client set fields it should not. Map to request and response records at the boundary.

blocks.title: What happens between an HTTP request arriving and your controller method running?
blocks.text: The embedded server accepts the connection and takes a thread from its pool. The request passes through filters (security, logging), then the DispatcherServlet finds the handler method whose mapping matches the path and method. Argument resolvers build the parameters: path variables are converted, the body is read by Jackson, and @Valid arguments are validated. Then the method is called, and its return value is written back as JSON. Exceptions at any step go to the exception handlers.

blocks.title: How would you move this service from H2 to PostgreSQL safely?
blocks.text: Add a migration tool and make the current schema the first migration. Run the same engine in tests as in production, for example with Testcontainers, because H2 does not behave identically. Supply the connection settings from the environment, keep ddl-auto on validate, and size the connection pool against the database's connection limit multiplied by the number of instances.

quiz.q: Who creates the ProductService object?
quiz.why: The container creates one and injects it through the controller's constructor.

quiz.q: Where is the code for findByNameStartingWithIgnoreCase?
options: Nowhere: Spring Data generates it from the method name
quiz.why: The repository is an interface; the implementation is created at startup.

quiz.q: POST /products with a blank name returned 400. Which code produced that status?
options: An if statement in the controller
@Valid on the parameter, then the handler in ApiErrors
quiz.why: Validation fails before the controller method runs, and ApiErrors shapes the body.

quiz.q: What does ddl-auto: validate do at startup?
options: Checks the tables match the entities and refuses to start if not
quiz.why: It reads the schema and never changes it.

quiz.q: Why does the new product get id 3?
options: The database assigns it, after the two rows from data.sql
quiz.why: GenerationType.IDENTITY leaves id generation to the database.

modules.title: Kotlin Fundamentals
modules.summary: Null safety, control flow, functions, classes, objects, collections, generics.

blocks.text: val declares a name you cannot reassign. var declares one you can. The compiler works out the type from the value.
A normal type such as String can never hold null. Add a question mark, String?, and it can.
The compiler will not let you use a nullable value until you have dealt with the null case, using ?. (safe call), ?: (fallback) or an if check.
Why it matters
NullPointerException was the most common crash in Java Android apps. Kotlin moves that check from runtime, where users see it, to compile time, where only you see it.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A parcel that may be empty is stamped "may be empty". You are not allowed to use the contents until you have opened it and looked.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
Almost identical to Swift optionals. let is val, var is var, String? is String?, ?. is ?., ?: is ??, and !! is the force-unwrap !.
Swift
There is no if let. A plain if (x != null) smart-casts x inside the block, or you write x?.let { ... }.
Swift
Swift Optional is an enum you can pattern-match. A Kotlin nullable type is a compiler-tracked flag on an ordinary reference, with no wrapper object.
Flutter
Dart sound null safety works the same way: String?, ?. and ??. Dart ! is Kotlin !!.

blocks.text: Choosing an operator

items: Can the value be absent at all? If not, use a non-null type
Need a member of it? Use ?.
Need a default? Add ?:
Need to run a block only when present? Use ?.let { }
Certain it is non-null and want a crash if wrong? Use !! and write down why

blocks.text: Walkthrough

blocks.code: data class User(val name: String, val email: String?)
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: name is required. email is allowed to be missing, and the type says so.
Each ?. stops and yields null if the thing on its left is null.
The Elvis operator supplies a value when the left side is null.
Smart cast: inside the block the compiler treats email as String, not String?.
String templates: $name inserts a variable, ${expr} inserts an expression.
The Java version needs explicit checks, and nothing forces you to write them.
What happens when it runs

items: emailDomain(asha) walks the chain and returns example.com.
emailDomain(guest) stops at email and falls back.
emailDomain(null) stops at user and falls back.
guest.email is null, so the else branch prints.

blocks.text: Memory

items: String? costs nothing extra at runtime: it is the same reference, which may be null.
Int? is different. A nullable Int compiles to java.lang.Integer, a boxed object. Int compiles to the primitive int.
val makes the reference read-only. The object behind it can still be mutable.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: A NullPointerException in Kotlin almost always comes from !!, from Java interop, or from lateinit. Search the stack trace line for those three.
Android Studio greys out safe calls that are never needed. Treat that as a hint the type can be made non-null.

blocks.text: In production

items: JSON models mark optional API fields as nullable, so the compiler forces every screen to handle a missing value.
findViewById returns a platform type. ViewBinding generates non-null properties for views that exist in every layout variant and nullable ones otherwise.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Scattering !! to silence the compiler.
Each !! is a possible crash. Use ?: with a sensible default, return early, or make the type non-null at its source.
lateinit var for values that may never be set.
lateinit throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException on early access. Use a nullable type or by lazy when initialisation is not guaranteed.
Trusting values that come from Java.
Java types without nullability annotations arrive as platform types (String!). The compiler does not check them. Declare the type you expect explicitly.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Write fun displayName(user: User?): String that returns the name, or "Guest" when user is null, in one expression.
Given val prices: List<Int?>, compute the sum of the non-null values.
blocks.text: Hint: filterNotNull()

blocks.title: Convert the Java cityOf method to Kotlin without looking at the solution, then compare.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does Kotlin null safety work, and where can a NullPointerException still occur?
blocks.text: Nullability is part of the type. The compiler rejects dereferencing a nullable type without a check. NPEs can still come from !!, from Java code returning null through a platform type, from lateinit accessed too early, and from using this in a constructor before fields are initialised.

blocks.title: What is the difference between lateinit and by lazy?
blocks.text: lateinit is for a non-null var that is assigned later, for example by dependency injection or in onCreate. by lazy is for a val computed on first access and cached. lazy is thread-safe by default; lateinit has no synchronisation.

blocks.title: val versus const val?
blocks.text: val is assigned at runtime and read through a getter. const val is a compile-time constant of a primitive or String type, declared at top level or in an object, and inlined at use sites.

quiz.q: What is the type of user?.email when user is User? and email is String?
quiz.why: A safe call always produces a nullable result.

quiz.q: What does val list = mutableListOf(1) allow?
quiz.why: val fixes the reference. The list object is still mutable.

quiz.q: When does x!! throw?
options: When x is not a String
quiz.why: !! converts to a non-null type and throws NullPointerException if the value is null.

lessons.title: Basics: types, strings, conditions and loops

blocks.text: Kotlin has the usual basic types: Int, Long, Double, Boolean, Char, String. You rarely write them, because the compiler works them out from the value.
if and when choose what happens. In Kotlin they are expressions: they produce a value you can assign or return.
for walks over a range (1..5) or a collection. while repeats until a condition is false.
A string can contain values directly: "total = $total". This is called a string template.
Why it matters
These are the words every other Kotlin feature is built from. Kotlin's versions are shorter than Java's and, because if and when return values, they remove a lot of temporary variables.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: when is a sorting office: a parcel comes in and goes down the first chute whose label matches. A range is a ruler: 1..5 marks both ends, and "until" stops just before the end.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
when is switch: exhaustive when used as an expression, no fall-through, and able to match types and ranges. 1..5 is 1...5, and 1 until 5 is 1..<5.
Swift
String templates use $name and ${expression} where Swift uses \(expression).
Flutter
Dart uses the same $name and ${expr} templates. Dart 3 switch expressions are close to when.

blocks.text: How when picks a branch

items: Evaluate the subject once
Check the branches top to bottom
Run the first branch that matches and stop
No match: run else
As an expression, the chosen branch's last value is the result

blocks.text: The two files compute the same results. Compare how much of the Java is ceremony.
Strings and arrays in both languages, compiled and run
Walkthrough
An if with an else is an expression. There is no ternary operator because this replaces it.
Each branch is a value. No break is needed and nothing falls through.
After the is check, x is treated as a String inside the branch: a smart cast.
1..5 includes both 1 and 5.
Ranges can count down and skip.
withIndex gives the position and the value together.
== compares content. === compares identity. This is the opposite of Java's == on objects.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output includes: the three grades; "an Int, a String of length 4, a known Double"; countdown 10 5 0; "index 1 is over 100"; steps = 111; and from the strings file "== true, === false".

blocks.text: Memory

items: Int compiles to a JVM int with no object. Int? must be able to hold null, so it becomes a boxed Integer.
A range in a for loop is compiled to a plain counting loop; no range object is created.
String templates compile to a StringBuilder.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Hover a val in the IDE, or press the inlay hints shortcut, to see the type the compiler inferred.
If a when unexpectedly hits else, print the subject with its class: println("$x ${x::class}").
Evaluate Expression in the debugger accepts Kotlin, including string templates.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: when over a sealed UiState decides what a screen shows; ranges and for loops drive list building; string templates build log messages (user-visible text still comes from resources).

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Using when as an expression without covering every case.
Add else, or switch over a sealed type or enum so the compiler can check completeness.
Writing 0..list.size as a loop range.
That includes size and goes out of bounds. Use list.indices or 0 until list.size.
Expecting Java-style implicit widening: val x: Long = 5 + someInt.
Kotlin never converts numbers silently. Call toLong().
Using Array<Int> for numbers in hot code.
That boxes every element. Use IntArray.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Write fun fizzBuzz(n: Int): String using when with no subject.
Print the numbers from 20 down to 0 in steps of 4.
Convert the Java grade method to Kotlin three ways: if expression, when with ranges, when with conditions.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does when differ from Java switch?
blocks.text: It is an expression, has no fall-through, accepts any type as subject, and its branches can be values, ranges (in 1..10), type checks (is String) or arbitrary conditions when used without a subject. Used as an expression it must be exhaustive, which the compiler verifies for enums and sealed types.

blocks.title: Does Kotlin have primitive types?
blocks.text: Not in the language: Int and Double are classes with methods. The compiler represents them as JVM primitives wherever possible and boxes them only when needed, such as for nullable types (Int?) and generic arguments (List<Int>). IntArray and friends give primitive arrays.

blocks.title: What is a smart cast and when does it not work?
blocks.text: After a check such as is String or != null, the compiler treats the value as that type without an explicit cast. It only works when the value cannot change between the check and the use: local val or var not captured in a lambda that modifies it, and val properties without a custom getter in the same module. For a var property, copy it to a local val first.

quiz.q: What does 1 until 5 contain?
quiz.why: until excludes the end. 1..5 includes it.

quiz.q: What does == do on two Kotlin strings?
quiz.why: It calls equals. === compares identity.

quiz.q: Why does Kotlin have no ternary operator?
quiz.why: val x = if (a) b else c does the same job.

blocks.text: A function is declared with fun. If the body is one expression you can write it after an equals sign.
Parameters can have default values, and callers can name the arguments they pass.
A lambda is a function written as a value, inside curly braces. A function that takes or returns another function is called a higher-order function.
Why it matters
