Defaults remove the pile of overloaded methods Java needs. Lambdas let you pass behaviour, such as what to do on click or how to filter a list, without declaring an interface and a class for each case.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Ordering coffee. "A coffee" uses the defaults. "A coffee, size large" changes one thing by name. A lambda is handing the barista your own recipe card.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
Kotlin has no argument labels. Any parameter can be named at the call site, and names are optional. Trailing lambda syntax is the same idea as Swift trailing closures.
Swift
it is the implicit single parameter, like $0 in Swift.
Swift

Kotlin lambdas capture references strongly and there is no [weak self]. The garbage collector handles cycles, so leaks come from lifetime (a long-lived object holding a lambda that captured an Activity), not from retain cycles.
Flutter
Dart has named and optional parameters with similar goals. Kotlin does not need the required keyword: a parameter without a default is required.

blocks.text: applyTwice(5) { it + 10 }

items: The lambda becomes the op argument
Inner call: op(5) returns 15
Outer call: op(15) returns 25
25 is returned to the caller

blocks.text: The Java file shows the anonymous-class style that Kotlin lambdas replace.
Walkthrough

blocks.code: fun price(base: Int, qty: Int = 1, discountPct: Int = 0): Int =
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: Two parameters have defaults. An expression body needs no braces and no return.
Named arguments let you skip qty and keep its default.
A function type: takes an Int, returns an Int.
A lambda stored in a variable. it is the single parameter.
When the last parameter is a function, the lambda can move outside the parentheses.
What happens when it runs

items: price(120) → 120, price(120, qty = 3) → 360, with a 10% discount → 108.
applyTwice doubles 5 twice → 20, then adds 10 twice → 25.
filter then map leaves [BREAD].

blocks.text: Memory

items: A lambda that captures variables is an object on the heap. A lambda that captures nothing is a shared singleton.
Marking a higher-order function inline copies the lambda body into the call site, so no object is allocated. That is why forEach, map and filter cost about the same as a loop.
Default arguments compile to an extra synthetic method. Java callers do not see the defaults unless you add @JvmOverloads.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Breakpoints can be set inside a lambda on the same line: Android Studio asks whether you mean the line or the lambda.
Tools → Kotlin → Show Kotlin Bytecode → Decompile shows the Java that Kotlin generated, which settles most "what does this really do" questions.

blocks.text: In production

items: Click handlers: button.setOnClickListener { viewModel.onAddClicked() }.
Compose is built on this: every composable takes content: @Composable () -> Unit as a trailing lambda.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: A lambda stored in a singleton that captured an Activity or View.
Clear the listener in onDestroy or onDestroyView, or scope the work to the lifecycle.
return inside a lambda passed to an inline function, which returns from the enclosing function.
Use a labelled return such as return@forEach when you only mean to skip one item.
Long chains of map and filter on huge lists.
Each step allocates a list. Switch to asSequence() or a single loop.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Write fun retry(times: Int = 3, block: () -> Boolean): Boolean that calls block until it returns true or the attempts run out.
Add @JvmOverloads to price and list the overloads Java can now call.
Write an inline function measure(label: String, block: () -> Unit) that prints the elapsed milliseconds.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What do inline, noinline and crossinline do?
blocks.text: inline copies the function body and its lambda arguments into the call site, removing the lambda allocation and allowing non-local return. noinline opts one lambda parameter out so it can be stored or passed on. crossinline keeps a lambda inlined but forbids non-local return, which is needed when the lambda is invoked from another execution context.

blocks.title: How do Kotlin lambdas interoperate with Java interfaces?
blocks.text: A Java interface with one abstract method accepts a Kotlin lambda through SAM conversion. For Kotlin interfaces you must declare fun interface to get the same conversion.

blocks.title: How are default arguments exposed to Java?
blocks.text: They are not, by default: Java sees one method with all parameters. @JvmOverloads generates overloads that drop trailing defaulted parameters.

quiz.q: What does price(120, discountPct = 50) return?
quiz.why: qty keeps its default of 1: 120 × 1 × 50 / 100 = 60.

quiz.q: What is it?
options: The implicit name of a single lambda parameter
quiz.why: When a lambda has exactly one parameter you may omit its declaration and call it it.

quiz.q: Why mark a higher-order function inline?
options: To avoid allocating a lambda object per call
To run it on another thread
quiz.why: The compiler pastes the function and lambda bodies at the call site.

lessons.title: Classes, data classes and sealed types

blocks.text: A Kotlin class declares its properties in the header: class Product(val id: Int).
A data class also gets equals, hashCode, toString, copy and destructuring generated from those properties.
A sealed type has a fixed, known set of subtypes. A when over it must cover every one, and the compiler tells you if you forget.
Why it matters
Screen state is the main use. A screen is loading, or showing content, or showing an error. A sealed type makes those three cases explicit and makes impossible combinations unrepresentable.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A traffic light has exactly three states. A form that only offers red, amber and green can never be filled in with "purple".
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
A sealed class or interface is a Swift enum with associated values. when is switch, and both are checked for exhaustiveness.
Swift
A data class looks like a struct but it is a reference type. Assigning it does not copy; you call copy() explicitly.
Swift
A Kotlin enum class is closer to a simple Swift enum without associated values. Each constant is a singleton object.
Flutter
Dart 3 sealed classes with switch patterns are the same idea. copy() is what copyWith does in freezed.

Fix each one

blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: One line replaces the constructor, getters, equals, hashCode and toString a Java class needs.
A singleton state with no data. data gives it a readable toString.
After the is check, state is smart-cast to Loaded, so items is available.
Creates a new object with one property changed. The original is untouched.
Destructuring reads properties by position through generated component1() and component2().
Java 8 style cannot prove the if chain is complete, so it needs a fallback that should never run.
What happens when it runs

items: println(milk) uses the generated toString.
milk == Product(1, "Milk", 6_000) is true: == calls equals, which compares properties.
render is called with each state and each branch runs once.

blocks.text: Memory

items: copy() is shallow. A copied object shares any lists or nested objects with the original.
Only properties in the primary constructor take part in equals and hashCode. A var declared in the class body is ignored.
data object and object are created once, lazily, and live for the life of the process.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Generated toString makes logs readable: Log.d(TAG, "state=$state") prints every property.
If DiffUtil or Compose misses a change, check whether the changed property is outside the primary constructor.

blocks.text: In production

items: sealed interface UiState { Loading, Success(data), Error(message) } exposed from a ViewModel as StateFlow is the standard MVVM screen contract.
Network layers return a sealed Result so callers handle success and failure without exceptions crossing layers.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Adding else to a when over a sealed type.
Leave it out so the compiler flags new subtypes.
var properties in a data class used as a map key or in a StateFlow.
Use val and copy(). Mutating an object in place does not notify observers and breaks hash lookups.
One state class with isLoading, data and error fields that can all be set at once.
Model mutually exclusive states as a sealed type.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add data object Empty to CartState and update render. Note where the compiler stops you.
Model a payment result: Success(orderId), Declined(reason), NeedsOtp(reference).
Create a data class with a List property, copy() it, mutate the list through one copy and observe the other.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Sealed class, sealed interface or enum: when do you use each?
blocks.text: enum when every case is a constant with the same shape. sealed class or interface when cases carry different data. Prefer sealed interface unless subtypes need shared state or a common constructor, because a class can implement several interfaces.

blocks.title: What are the limits of data classes?
blocks.text: They cannot be open, abstract, sealed or inner. Only primary constructor properties count for equality. copy is shallow. Arrays as properties compare by reference, so use List.

blocks.title: == versus === in Kotlin?
blocks.text: == calls equals (structural equality) with null handled for you. === compares references. This is the reverse of Java, where == on objects is reference equality.

quiz.q: What does a.copy() on a data class produce?
options: A new object with the same property references
quiz.why: copy is shallow: a new instance whose properties point at the same objects.

quiz.q: Why omit else when switching over a sealed type?
options: So the compiler reports missing cases when a subtype is added
quiz.why: Exhaustiveness checking only helps if there is no catch-all branch.

quiz.q: Which methods does a data class generate?
quiz.why: All five are derived from the primary constructor properties.

blocks.text: object declares a class and its single instance in one go: a singleton.
A companion object is an object inside a class. Its members are called on the class name, which is how Kotlin does what Java does with static.
Delegation means handing a job to another object. "by" does it for you: by lazy computes a value on first use, and Logger by logger forwards an interface to an existing implementation.
operator fun lets your own types use symbols such as + and *. Destructuring unpacks an object into several variables.
Why it matters

Singletons, factory methods, lazy initialisation and wrapping one object in another are patterns every codebase needs. Kotlin turns each from a page of boilerplate into a keyword, and makes them thread-safe by default.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Delegation is a manager who signs for a parcel and passes it straight to the right person. by lazy is a kettle you only boil when someone first asks for tea, and then keep hot.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
object is a class with static let shared. A companion object's members are Swift static members. const val is a static let of a literal.
Swift
by lazy is lazy var. Delegates.observable is didSet. Property delegates in general are Swift property wrappers.
Swift
operator fun plus is static func +. Destructuring a data class has no direct Swift form beyond tuples.
Flutter
Dart has factory constructors, late final for lazy values and operator overloading, but no interface delegation with by.

blocks.text: Reading a by lazy property

items: First read: take a lock
Run the initialiser block
Store the result
Release the lock and return the value
Every later read returns the stored value with no block and no lock

blocks.text: The Java file shows the static members that a companion object replaces. Delegation and operator overloading have no Java equivalent.
Enums and exceptions in both languages, compiled and run
Kotlin enums can carry properties and methods. try is an expression, and there are no checked exceptions.
Walkthrough
One instance, created safely the first time it is used.
The constructor is private, so the only way to create one is the factory in the companion.
A compile-time constant, inlined wherever it is used.

blocks.code: operator fun plus(other: Money) = Money(paise + other.paise)
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: Lets you write a + b. Only a fixed set of operator names is allowed.

blocks.code: class OrderService(logger: Logger) : Logger by logger
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: OrderService implements Logger by forwarding every call to the object it was given.

blocks.code: val taxTable: Map<String, Int> by lazy { ... }
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: The block runs once, on first access, and the result is cached.

blocks.code: var status: String by Delegates.observable("new") { _, old, new -> ... }
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: The lambda runs after every assignment.
Destructuring a map entry into key and value.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output: events: 2; "Milk 6000 max=40"; "Rs 165 true" from the operators; "log: created"; "building tax table" printed once although the table is read twice; "log: status new -> paid"; then the cart lines.

blocks.text: Memory

items: An object lives from first use until the process ends. It must not hold short-lived things such as an Activity.
A companion object is one extra object per class. Use const val and @JvmStatic to get true JVM statics when Java calls it.
by lazy holds its lambda, and whatever the lambda captured, until first access.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Decompile to Java to see what a delegate or companion really generated.
A lazy value computed "too early" is being read by something at startup: put a breakpoint inside the lazy block and read the stack.
If Java cannot see a companion function as static, it is missing @JvmStatic.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: by viewModels() and by lazy are property delegates; Fragment newInstance factories and constants live in companion objects; sealed class cases with no data are data objects; Compose uses by remember { mutableStateOf(...) }.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Making every helper an object.
Stateless functions belong at the top level of a file. Use object when there is state or an interface to implement.
Overloading operators with surprising meanings.
Use + only where addition is the obvious reading, as with Money or vectors.
by lazy for something that needs a Context from an object.
The lazy value will capture and keep that Context. Pass applicationContext, or do not make it a singleton.
Storing mutable global state in an object and testing against it.
Tests then affect each other. Inject the dependency so each test gets a fresh one.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Write a delegate-free and a by lazy version of an expensive property, and prove with a println which runs when.
Add operator fun minus and operator fun compareTo use to Money, then sort a list of Money.
Wrap a MutableList<String> in a class that logs every add, using interface delegation so you override only add.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: object, companion object and top-level declarations: how do you choose?
blocks.text: Top-level functions and constants for utilities with no natural owner. A companion object for factories and constants that belong to a class or need access to its private constructor. An object for a real singleton that holds state or implements an interface. From Java, top-level members appear on a FileKt class and companion members need @JvmStatic to be static.

blocks.title: How does by lazy work and is it thread-safe?
blocks.text: It creates a Lazy<T> holder. The default mode, SYNCHRONIZED, uses a lock so the initialiser runs at most once even with several threads. PUBLICATION may run it several times and keep the first result. NONE has no locking and is for single-thread use, such as the Android main thread.

blocks.title: What is a property delegate?
blocks.text: An object with getValue (and setValue for var) operator functions. Writing val x by delegate makes the compiler route every read and write of x through it. lazy, observable, vetoable, map-backed properties, viewModels and Compose's remember all use this mechanism.

blocks.title: Composition by delegation versus inheritance?
blocks.text: Inheritance fixes the parent at compile time and exposes you to changes in its internals. Delegating an interface to a held object keeps the two independent, lets the delegate be swapped or faked, and works with final classes, which Kotlin classes are by default.

quiz.q: How many instances does an object declaration have?
quiz.why: It is a singleton created on first use.

quiz.q: When does a by lazy block run?
options: On first read of the property
quiz.why: Once, on first access; the value is then cached.

quiz.q: What does class A(b: B) : I by b do?
options: Forwards the members of I to b
Makes A a subclass of B
quiz.why: Interface delegation generates forwarding functions.

blocks.text: An extension function adds a function to a type you do not own, such as Long or String, without subclassing it.

Scope functions (let, run, with, apply, also) run a block of code "on" an object. They differ in two ways: whether the object is called this or it inside the block, and whether the block returns the object or its last line.
Why it matters
Extensions replace the StringUtils and ViewUtils helper classes of Java codebases with code that reads as part of the type. Scope functions cut repetition when configuring or null-checking an object.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: An extension is a clip-on lens for a camera you did not build. A scope function is saying "while you are holding that, also do this".
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
A Kotlin extension is a Swift extension, with limits: it cannot add stored properties and cannot make a type conform to an interface.
Swift
x?.let { } is the idiom closest to if let x. apply { } has no direct Swift equivalent; it is used where Swift would use a configuration closure.
Flutter
Dart extension methods are the same feature. apply covers most uses of the Dart cascade operator (..).

blocks.text: How 12_550L.asRupees() is compiled

items: The compiler emits a static method asRupees(long receiver)
The call becomes ExtensionsKt.asRupees(12550L)
Nothing is added to the Long class
So it is resolved by the declared type, not the runtime type

blocks.text: Java has no equivalent of extensions or scope functions. The closest Java pattern is a static helper: Money.asRupees(value).
Walkthrough
Long is the receiver type. Inside the function, this is the Long it was called on.
An extension property. It must be computed; it cannot store anything.
Inside apply, this is the new Request, so its properties are set directly. apply returns the Request.
token is null, so the block does not run. This is the null-check idiom.
with is a plain function taking the object as an argument. It returns the last expression.
What happens when it runs

items: 12550 paise formats as Rs 125.50.
"asha rao".initials yields AR.
apply configures the request; also adds one header; the let on the null token is skipped.
The summary reports one header because Authorization was never added.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Extensions are static methods: no object, no allocation.
Scope functions are inline, so the lambdas disappear at compile time.
An extension cannot read private members of the class it extends.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Ctrl+click or Cmd+click an extension call to see which file supplies it. Wrong imports are a common cause of surprising behaviour.
Step Into on a scope function enters your lambda directly because the function itself is inlined.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android KTX is a library of extensions: view.isVisible = true, bundleOf("id" to 1), sharedPreferences.edit { putInt("k", 1) }.
Compose Modifier chains are extension functions: Modifier.padding(16.dp).fillMaxWidth().

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Nesting scope functions until nobody can tell what it or this refers to.
One level is enough. Name the lambda parameter, or use a local variable.
Expecting an extension to be overridden by a subclass.
Extensions are resolved statically from the declared type. If you need polymorphism, use a member function.
Declaring an extension with the same signature as a member.
The member always wins and the extension is silently ignored.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Write fun String.isValidPin(): Boolean for a six-digit Indian PIN code.
Rewrite the Request setup without scope functions and compare readability.
Write an extension on List<Int> called secondLargest() returning Int?.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How are extension functions implemented, and what follows from that?
blocks.text: As static methods with the receiver as the first parameter. Therefore they are dispatched statically on the declared type, cannot be overridden, cannot access private members, and lose to a member with the same signature.

blocks.title: Explain the difference between let, run, with, apply and also.
blocks.text: Two axes. Context object: this for run, with and apply; it for let and also. Return value: the object for apply and also; the lambda result for let, run and with. Use apply to configure, also for side effects, let for null checks and transforms, run and with to compute something from an object.

blocks.title: When would you not use an extension?
blocks.text: When the behaviour needs private state, needs to be polymorphic, or is core to the type and you own the class. Overusing extensions on common types such as String also pollutes autocomplete across the codebase.

quiz.q: What does apply return?
options: The last line of the block
The object it was called on
quiz.why: apply and also return the receiver. let, run and with return the block result.

quiz.q: Can an extension function access private fields of the class?
quiz.why: It is a static function outside the class and sees only the public API.

quiz.q: Inside x.let { ... }, how do you refer to x?
quiz.why: let and also expose the object as the lambda parameter it.

blocks.text: Kotlin has List, Set and Map. Each comes in two forms: read-only (List) and changeable (MutableList).
Collections come with a large set of functions that take a lambda: filter, map, groupBy, sortedBy, sumOf, first and many more.
A Sequence does the same work lazily: one element travels through the whole chain before the next one starts, and it can stop early.
Why it matters
Most app code is "take this list and turn it into that list". These functions say what you want in one readable line and remove the loops, counters and temporary lists where bugs live.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: List operations are a kitchen that finishes each step for every dish before starting the next step. A sequence is a conveyor belt: each dish goes through every station in turn, and the belt stops as soon as enough dishes are done.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
The same vocabulary: filter, map, reduce (fold), first(where:) is firstOrNull, Dictionary(grouping:) is groupBy. A Sequence is Swift's .lazy.
Swift
Swift collections are value types, so let makes them immutable. A Kotlin List is a read-only view of an object that someone else may still be changing.
Flutter
Dart's where and map return lazy Iterables by default, like Kotlin sequences. Kotlin's List functions are eager.

blocks.text: Eager list versus lazy sequence for filter then first

items: List: filter visits all four items and builds a new list
List: first takes element 0 of that list
Sequence: first asks for one element
Sequence: Milk passes the filter, so the work stops
Sequence: the other three items are never visited

blocks.text: Java needs streams, collectors and Optional for what Kotlin does with functions on the collection and null.
Walkthrough
Three steps, each returning a new list. The original is untouched.
Builds a Map from category to the list of items in it.
Returns null when nothing matches, which the safe call and Elvis operator handle. first() would throw.
Splits into two lists in one pass and destructures the pair.
Builds a Map from each element. "to" creates a Pair.
toMutableList made a copy, so the original list still has four items.
Lazy: only as many elements are processed as the final step needs.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output: [Bread, Milk]; {bakery=39500, dairy=68000}; total 107500; Ghee; none; "2 cheap, 2 dear"; the name-to-price map; the chunked lists; "4 5" showing the copy; and one "visiting Milk" line from the sequence.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Every eager step allocates a new list. For a few hundred items this is irrelevant; for large data or long chains, use a sequence.
The collection functions are inline, so the lambdas cost nothing.
List<Int> stores boxed integers. Use IntArray for large numeric data.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Insert .onEach { println(it) } between steps to see the data at that point.
Split a long chain into named vals. Each can be inspected in the debugger.
If results are in an unexpected order, check whether a HashMap or HashSet from Java entered the chain.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: mapping API models to UI models (dtos.map { it.toUi() }), filtering lists for search, grouping rows into sections, and combining lists inside a Flow with map.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Treating List as immutable.
It is read-only through that reference. Whoever holds the MutableList can still change it. Copy with toList() when you need a snapshot.
Using first() or single() on a list that may be empty.
They throw. Use firstOrNull() and handle null.
Turning everything into a sequence "for performance".
Sequences have overhead per element. They win for large data, long chains or early exit.
Building a sequence and never calling a terminal operation.
Nothing runs until toList, first, sum or similar is called.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: From the items, build a string such as "bakery: Bread, Cake; dairy: Ghee, Milk".
Find the most expensive item per category.
blocks.text: Hint: groupBy then mapValues { it.value.maxByOrNull { item -> item.price } }

blocks.title: Generate the first ten even squares with generateSequence, lazily.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: List versus MutableList, and is List immutable?
blocks.text: List exposes only read operations; MutableList adds add, remove and set. List is read-only, not immutable: the same object may be referenced as a MutableList elsewhere and change underneath you, and Java code can always mutate it. For real immutability, copy defensively or use kotlinx.collections.immutable.

blocks.title: Collection operations versus Sequence versus Java Stream?
blocks.text: Collection operations are eager and build a list per step. Sequences are lazy, processed element by element, and stop early. Java streams are also lazy, add parallelism, and are single-use. In Kotlin code prefer collection functions for small data and sequences for large or short-circuiting pipelines.

blocks.title: map, flatMap, fold, reduce?
blocks.text: map transforms each element to one result. flatMap transforms each to a collection and flattens. fold combines all elements starting from an initial value, so it works on an empty collection and can return a different type. reduce starts from the first element and throws on an empty collection.

quiz.q: What does listOf(1, 2, 3).map { it * 2 } return?
quiz.why: Collection functions return new collections.

quiz.q: What does firstOrNull return when nothing matches?
quiz.why: first() throws; firstOrNull() returns null.

quiz.q: When is a Sequence the better choice?
options: Large data, long chains, or early exit
quiz.why: Laziness avoids intermediate lists and unnecessary work.

blocks.text: Generics let a class or function work with a type chosen by the caller: Box<T>.
Variance answers the question "is a Box<Int> also a Box<Number>?" out T says yes, for types that only hand T out. in T says the reverse, for types that only take T in.
An inline function is copied into the place it is called. Marking its type parameter reified lets the function know the real type at runtime.
Why it matters

Variance is what lets you pass a List<Int> to a function wanting List<Number> safely. reified removes the need to pass Class objects around, which is why Kotlin APIs such as filterIsInstance<String>() read so cleanly.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A vending machine only hands things out. A machine that vends cola is also a machine that vends drinks: that is out. A recycling bin only takes things in. A bin for any rubbish can serve as a bin for cans: that is in.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
Swift has no variance annotations for your own types; only built-in collections are covariant. Kotlin lets you declare out and in.
Swift
Swift keeps generic types at runtime, so T.self always works. Kotlin on the JVM erases them, and reified is the way to get T::class.
Swift
<T : Comparable<T>> is <T: Comparable>. A where clause exists in both for several constraints.

blocks.text: What inline with reified does

items: You call mixed.only<Int>()
The compiler copies the function body to the call site
It replaces T with Int in the copy
The copy contains a real check: is Int
No type information had to survive to runtime

blocks.text: Java puts wildcards at every use (? extends, ? super). Kotlin declares variance once on the type.
Walkthrough
A generic class. Box("milk") infers T as String.

blocks.code: fun <T : Comparable<T>> max(a: T, b: T): T
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: An upper bound: T must be comparable with itself.

blocks.code: interface Source<out T> { fun next(): T }
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: out promises T is only produced. The compiler rejects a function that takes a T parameter.
Allowed because of out. With an invariant type this would not compile.
Allowed because of in: something that accepts any Number can accept Ints.

blocks.code: inline fun <reified T> List<Any>.only(): List<T> = filterIsInstance<T>()
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: reified needs inline. Inside, T can be used in is checks and T::class.
Star projection: a list whose element type you do not know or care about. You can read Any? from it.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output: "milk 4"; "9 banana"; 6.0 and 4.0; 42 from the covariant source; [7] from the contravariant sink; "[1, 3] [two] Double" from the reified functions; and 4.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Like Java, generics are erased on the JVM: there is one Box class for all T.
inline copies the function body to every call site, which removes the lambda object and the call, but grows the code. Keep inline functions small.
reified adds no runtime cost; the type is written into each copied call site.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Read variance errors literally: "Type parameter T is declared as out but occurs in in position" names the offending function.
Tools → Kotlin → Show Kotlin Bytecode → Decompile shows what an inline function became at the call site.
When inference picks a surprising type, state the type argument explicitly.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: by viewModels<CartViewModel>(), Gson and kotlinx.serialization helpers such as Json.decodeFromString<User>(text), and navigation toRoute<ProductDetail>() are all inline reified functions. StateFlow<out T> and List<out E> are covariant.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Declaring out T and then writing fun add(item: T).
A producer cannot consume. Either drop out, or remove the function.
Marking large functions inline for speed.
inline pays off for functions taking lambdas or needing reified. Otherwise it only bloats bytecode.
Trying to call a reified inline function from Java.
Java cannot. Provide an overload that takes a Class<T>.
Checking list is List<String>.
Erasure makes that impossible. Check elements, or use a reified helper.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Write inline fun <reified T> Any.isA(): Boolean and test it with several types.
Declare interface Mapper<in A, out B> with one function, and explain each modifier.
Explain why MutableList<Int> cannot be passed where MutableList<Number> is expected, with a line of code that would break.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Explain declaration-site and use-site variance.
blocks.text: Declaration-site: the class states its variance once, interface Source<out T>, and every use benefits. Use-site: variance is stated where the type is used, as with Java wildcards or Kotlin projections such as Array<out Any>. Kotlin supports both; Java has only use-site.

blocks.title: What can and cannot be done with reified type parameters?
blocks.text: Inside the function you can use T in is and as checks, get T::class, and call other reified functions with it. You cannot create an instance with T(), the function must be inline, it cannot be called from Java, and it cannot be virtual.

blocks.title: What is the cost of inline?
blocks.text: The body is duplicated at every call site, increasing code size, and a public inline function cannot use non-public declarations. In exchange you avoid a lambda allocation and a call, gain non-local return, and can use reified. The standard library's collection functions are inline for this reason.

quiz.q: What does out T allow?
options: T only as a return type
quiz.why: A covariant type may only produce T.

quiz.q: Why must a reified function be inline?
options: So the real type can be written into the call site
quiz.why: Erasure removes T from a normal function; inlining substitutes it.

quiz.q: Is List<Int> accepted where List<Number> is required?
options: Yes, because List is declared out
quiz.why: List<out E> is covariant. MutableList is not.

modules.title: Advanced Kotlin
modules.summary: Coroutines: basics, supervisors, exceptions, Mutex and Channel.

blocks.text: A coroutine is a piece of work that can pause without blocking the thread it runs on, and continue later.
A suspend function is one that may pause. It can only be called from a coroutine or another suspend function.
launch starts a coroutine that returns nothing. async starts one that returns a result you collect with await.
Coroutines are started inside a scope. When the scope is cancelled, everything started in it is cancelled. This is called structured concurrency.
Why it matters

Android needs slow work kept off the main thread and results delivered back on it. Threads and callbacks can do that, but the code becomes nested and cancellation is easy to forget. Coroutines let you write the same logic top to bottom, and cancellation follows the screen lifecycle.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A cook starts the rice, and while it simmers moves on to chop vegetables instead of staring at the pot. One cook, several dishes in progress. The cook is the thread; each dish is a coroutine.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
suspend fun is async func. Calling one needs no await keyword in Kotlin; the suspension point is shown by an icon in the editor gutter.
Swift
async { } with await() is async let. coroutineScope { } is a TaskGroup. launch is Task { }, with one big difference: launch always needs a scope, so there is no unstructured default.
Swift
Dispatchers.Main is @MainActor. Kotlin has no actors in the language and no compiler data-race checking; shared mutable state still needs a Mutex or single-thread confinement.
Swift
Cancellation is cooperative in both. Kotlin throws CancellationException at the next suspension point; Swift sets a flag that you check or that try await surfaces.
Flutter
A Dart Future with async and await reads the same, but Dart runs on a single isolate. Kotlin coroutines can run in parallel across threads, so shared state needs care.

blocks.text: What happens at delay(100)

items: The coroutine saves where it is and its local variables in a continuation object
It returns the thread to the dispatcher
The thread runs other coroutines or UI work
After 100 ms the continuation is scheduled again
The coroutine carries on from the next line

blocks.text: Java has no coroutines. The Java file shows the closest standard tools, a thread pool and Future, which block threads instead of suspending. Java 21 virtual threads are closer in cost but are not available to Android apps.
Walkthrough
suspend marks a function that can pause. The compiler adds a hidden continuation parameter.
Bridges normal code into coroutines by blocking the current thread until the block finishes. Never use it on the Android main thread.
Starts a child coroutine and returns a Job immediately. The child does not run until the parent suspends, because both share the one thread.
Starts a child that produces a value. Two async blocks run concurrently.
Suspends until each result is ready. Both delays overlap, so the wait is about 100 ms, not 200.
Moves the block to the IO thread pool and suspends the caller. When the block ends, execution returns to the original context.
Requests cancellation and waits. delay notices and throws CancellationException, so the finally block runs.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output from this Mac: start on main, banner loaded, total = 90, io work ran on DefaultDispatcher, slow job cleaned up, done on main.
Dispatchers.IO and Dispatchers.Default share worker threads named DefaultDispatcher-worker-N, which is why the IO block reports that name.

blocks.text: Memory

items: A suspended coroutine is a small heap object holding its local variables and resume point. It has no thread stack, so hundreds of thousands can exist at once.
A coroutine keeps whatever it captured alive until it completes or is cancelled. One launched in GlobalScope that captured a ViewModel or View leaks it.
viewModelScope is cancelled in onCleared. lifecycleScope is cancelled when the Lifecycle is destroyed. Use these, not a hand-made scope.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Add -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug to JVM arguments to append the coroutine name to Thread.currentThread().name.
The Coroutines tab in the Android Studio debugger lists running and suspended coroutines with their stacks.
Stack traces stop at the last suspension point. Log at the boundaries of your suspend functions to rebuild the path.
In tests use runTest from kotlinx-coroutines-test: delays are skipped using virtual time.

blocks.text: In production

items: A ViewModel calls viewModelScope.launch { _state.value = Loaded(repository.loadCart()) }. The repository function is suspend and switches to Dispatchers.IO internally, so it is safe to call from the main thread.
Retrofit and Room both generate suspend functions that are main-safe.
Loading several endpoints for one screen uses coroutineScope with two or three async calls, exactly as in this example.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: GlobalScope.launch { } from a screen.
Use viewModelScope or lifecycleScope so the work stops with the screen.
Blocking calls inside a coroutine on Dispatchers.Main, such as Thread.sleep or a synchronous database read.
Wrap blocking work in withContext(Dispatchers.IO). A suspend modifier alone does not move anything off the main thread.
catch (e: Exception) that swallows CancellationException.
Rethrow it, or catch specific exceptions. Swallowing it breaks cancellation.
Wrapping await() in try/catch to handle a failing async child.
A failed async child cancels its parent scope first. Wrap the group in coroutineScope { } and catch around that, or use supervisorScope.
A tight loop with no suspension point that never notices cancellation.
Call ensureActive() or yield() inside long loops.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Change both async calls to sequential calls. Predict the total time, then measure with measureTimeMillis.
Make fetchPrice("bread") throw. What happens to milk and to the banner job? Then try supervisorScope.
Write a loop that prints a counter every 200 ms and cancel it after 1 second with withTimeout.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do coroutines differ from threads?
blocks.text: A thread is an operating system resource with its own stack, scheduled by the kernel. A coroutine is a compiler-generated state machine that runs on threads and gives the thread back whenever it suspends. Many coroutines share few threads, switching is cheap, and cancellation and parent-child structure are built in.

blocks.title: What is structured concurrency?
blocks.text: Every coroutine runs in a scope and has a parent. A parent does not complete until its children do, cancelling a parent cancels the children, and a failing child cancels its parent and siblings unless a SupervisorJob is used. Work cannot leak past the scope that started it.

blocks.title: launch versus async?
blocks.text: launch returns a Job and is for work with no result; an uncaught exception goes to the scope handler immediately. async returns Deferred and holds its exception until await, though it still cancels the parent on failure in a regular scope.

blocks.title: How does cancellation work, and how can it fail?
blocks.text: cancel() marks the Job as cancelling. The coroutine notices at its next suspension point, where a CancellationException is thrown and finally blocks run. It fails to stop if the code never suspends, or catches and swallows CancellationException. Cleanup that must suspend goes in withContext(NonCancellable).

blocks.title: Dispatchers.IO versus Dispatchers.Default?
blocks.text: Default is sized to the CPU core count, for computation. IO allows many more threads (64 by default, or the core count if larger) because they spend their time blocked. They share one pool, so switching between them often needs no thread hop.

quiz.q: Two async blocks each delay(100). Roughly how long until both await calls return?
quiz.why: They run concurrently, so the delays overlap.

quiz.q: What does delay do to the thread?
options: Releases it to do other work
quiz.why: delay suspends the coroutine only. Thread.sleep is the blocking call.

quiz.q: What does withContext(Dispatchers.IO) return to?
options: The caller context once the block ends
quiz.why: It runs the block in the given context and then resumes the caller in its original one.

quiz.q: Where should a ViewModel start coroutines?
quiz.why: viewModelScope is cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared.

lessons.title: Coroutines in depth: Job, supervisors, exceptions, Mutex and Channel

blocks.text: Every coroutine has a Job, which is its handle: you can wait for it or cancel it. Jobs form a family tree: a coroutine started inside another is its child.
By default, if a child fails, its parent and all its siblings are cancelled. Under a supervisor, a failing child affects nobody else.
A Mutex lets only one coroutine at a time run a block, for protecting shared data. A Channel is a pipe: one coroutine sends values in, another takes them out.
Why it matters

Real screens start several things at once. You need to decide, on purpose, what happens when one of them fails: should the others stop or carry on? And when coroutines run on several threads, shared state needs the same protection as with threads.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A team on a job. In an ordinary team, if one member reports a disaster, everyone downs tools. A supervisor is a manager who lets the others finish and notes the one failure. A Mutex is a single key to the stockroom. A Channel is a serving hatch between kitchen and dining room.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
coroutineScope with children is a throwing TaskGroup: one failure cancels the rest. supervisorScope has no direct equivalent; you catch inside each child task.
Swift
A Mutex protects state the way an actor does, but by convention: nothing forces you to take it. A Channel is close to AsyncStream with a continuation.
Swift
Cancellation is cooperative in both. Kotlin throws CancellationException at suspension points; Swift requires checking or try await.

blocks.text: A child fails inside coroutineScope

items: The child throws IllegalStateException
Its Job is marked failed and tells the parent
The parent cancels its other children
Each sibling gets CancellationException at its next suspension point and runs finally
When all children have finished, coroutineScope rethrows the original exception

blocks.text: Java has no coroutines. The Java file shows the thread tools for the same needs: locks where Kotlin uses Mutex, and a latch and executor where Kotlin uses structured scopes.
Walkthrough

blocks.code: coroutineScope { launch { ... }; launch { load("prices", fail = true) } }
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: Both children belong to this scope. The second one failing cancels the first.
finally runs during cancellation. isActive is false by then.

blocks.code: supervisorScope { val banner = async { ... }; val offers = async { ... } }
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: Here a failure in offers does not cancel banner.
With async, the exception surfaces at await, where you can handle it.
A scope you own. SupervisorJob keeps it usable after a child fails; the handler receives uncaught exceptions from launch.
Only one coroutine at a time runs the block. Unlike synchronized, waiting suspends instead of blocking a thread.
With the default channel, send suspends until a receiver takes the value: a rendezvous.
Cancels the block when time runs out and returns null.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output: in section 1 the sibling is cancelled and the exception is caught; in section 2 banner succeeds while offers fails; in section 3 the handler receives the failure and the scope is still active; the Mutex counter is exactly 10000; the three orders arrive in order; and the timeout gives "fast: fast, slow: null".

blocks.text: Memory

items: A Job holds its children until they complete. A scope you create yourself must be cancelled by you, or its coroutines and everything they captured live on.
A suspended coroutine waiting on a Mutex or a Channel uses no thread, only a small object.
A buffered Channel holds undelivered items; an unlimited one can grow without bound if the receiver is slow.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Give coroutines names with CoroutineName("sync") and run with -Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug to see them in thread names and logs.
job.children and job.isActive, isCancelled, isCompleted show the state of the tree in the debugger.
A coroutine that never finishes is usually waiting on a Channel nobody closes or a Mutex never released: check for send without a receiver.

blocks.text: In production

items: Android: viewModelScope is a SupervisorJob on Dispatchers.Main.immediate, so one failed launch does not kill the others. Loading several independent sections of a home screen uses supervisorScope; loading parts that are useless without each other uses coroutineScope. One-off UI events are often sent through a Channel.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: try { launch { risky() } } catch (e: Exception) { }
launch returns at once, so the try catches nothing. Catch inside the coroutine, or wrap a coroutineScope.
Passing SupervisorJob() as an argument to launch to "protect" it.
That breaks the parent link, so cancellation no longer reaches it. Use supervisorScope { }.
Expecting CoroutineExceptionHandler to catch exceptions in a child coroutine or in async.
It only sees uncaught exceptions of root coroutines started with launch.
Using synchronized or a ReentrantLock around a suspending call.
The coroutine may resume on another thread and the lock is tied to the first. Use Mutex.
Catching Exception around suspend calls and carrying on.
That swallows CancellationException. Rethrow it, or catch specific types.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: In section 1, change coroutineScope to supervisorScope and predict the output before running.
Remove the Mutex and run it several times. Then fix it another way, with a single-threaded dispatcher.
blocks.text: Hint: Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)

blocks.title: Give the Channel a capacity of 2 and add printlns around send to see when the producer suspends.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Job versus SupervisorJob?
blocks.text: With a Job, a failing child cancels the parent, which cancels all other children: all or nothing. With a SupervisorJob, a child's failure is its own and siblings continue. Cancellation of the parent still cancels all children in both. Use coroutineScope when the results only make sense together, supervisorScope when they are independent.

blocks.title: How do exceptions propagate in coroutines?
blocks.text: In launch, an uncaught exception goes up to the parent Job; at the root it is passed to the CoroutineExceptionHandler, or the thread's uncaught handler, which on Android crashes the app. In async, the exception is stored and thrown at await, but in a non-supervisor scope it still cancels the parent. CancellationException is special: it is normal termination and is not propagated as a failure.

blocks.title: How do you protect shared mutable state in coroutines?
blocks.text: Best: do not share; keep state in one coroutine or confine it to a single-threaded dispatcher. Otherwise use atomic types or MutableStateFlow.update for single values, and Mutex.withLock for compound changes. Avoid thread locks around suspension points.

blocks.title: Channel versus Flow?
blocks.text: A Channel is a hot communication primitive between coroutines: each value is received by exactly one receiver, and it exists whether or not anyone is listening. A Flow is a cold description that runs per collector. Use a Channel for hand-offs and one-off events, a Flow for streams of data, and SharedFlow or StateFlow to broadcast to several collectors.

blocks.title: What is the difference between cancel(), cancelAndJoin() and withTimeout?
blocks.text: cancel() requests cancellation and returns immediately. cancelAndJoin() also suspends until the coroutine has actually finished, including its finally blocks. withTimeout runs a block and cancels it by throwing TimeoutCancellationException when time is up; withTimeoutOrNull returns null instead of throwing.

quiz.q: A child fails inside coroutineScope. What happens to its siblings?
quiz.why: With a regular Job, failure propagates to the parent, which cancels the other children.

quiz.q: Where does an exception from async show up?
quiz.why: Deferred holds the failure until awaited.

quiz.q: Why use Mutex instead of synchronized in coroutines?
options: It suspends instead of blocking and works across thread switches
It is required by the compiler
quiz.why: A coroutine can resume on a different thread, which thread-bound locks do not allow.

quiz.q: What does a rendezvous Channel do on send?
options: Suspends until a receiver takes it
quiz.why: The default capacity is zero, so sender and receiver meet.

modules.title: Android Architecture Overview
modules.summary: Kernel to app, processes, Binder, Zygote and the main thread loop.

lessons.title: How Android works: kernel to app, process to main thread

blocks.text: Android is a stack of layers. At the bottom is the Linux kernel, which talks to the hardware. At the top is your app. Each layer uses only the one below it.

Every app runs in its own process, as its own Linux user, with its own private files. Apps cannot touch each other. When they need something from the system or from another app, they ask through a channel called Binder.

Inside your process there is one special thread, the main thread. It runs a loop that takes one message at a time from a queue: a touch, a lifecycle callback, a request to draw a frame. Everything on screen depends on that loop staying free.
Why it matters

Almost every Android rule you will meet follows from this design. You cannot do network on the main thread because it blocks the loop. Your process can vanish in the background because the system owns the memory. State must be saved because the Activity record lives in another process. Knowing the layers turns a list of rules into one picture.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: An apartment building. The kernel is the foundations and utilities. The system server is the building manager who holds every key and decides who gets the lift. Each app is a locked flat. To get anything outside your flat you ring the manager on the intercom, which is Binder. Inside your flat there is one front door with a single queue of visitors, the main thread.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: iOS

Both run each app in a sandboxed process over a Unix-like kernel (Linux here, XNU there). Android's Binder corresponds to Mach messages and XPC. The system server corresponds to SpringBoard plus daemons such as backboardd and runningboardd.
iOS

ART is a managed runtime with garbage collection and a mix of interpretation, JIT and ahead-of-time compilation. iOS runs native code compiled ahead of time, with reference counting. This is why Android has GC pauses and iOS has retain cycles.
UIKit
The main Looper is the main RunLoop. Handler.post is DispatchQueue.main.async. An ANR is the watchdog termination that iOS reports as 0x8badf00d.
iOS
Zygote has no iOS counterpart. Android forks every app from a process that already has the framework loaded; iOS launches each app with dyld and a shared cache.
Flutter

A Flutter app is still one Android process with a main thread. The Dart UI isolate runs on its own thread, and platform channels hop to the Android main thread, which is why a slow channel handler janks the native side.

blocks.text: From tapping the icon to the first frame

items: Launcher sends startActivity to the system server over Binder
The system server finds no process for the app and asks Zygote to fork one
The new process starts ActivityThread.main, which creates the main Looper
The process tells the system server it is ready (attachApplication)
The system server tells it to create the Application: onCreate runs
The system server tells it to launch the Activity: onCreate, onStart, onResume
The view tree is measured, laid out and drawn, and the first frame is shown

blocks.text: The Java file is a runnable model of the main thread written with plain JDK classes, so you can see the mechanism. The Kotlin file is how you use the real thing on Android.
Walkthrough

blocks.code: static final BlockingQueue<Runnable> queue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>();
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: The model's MessageQueue. Any thread may add to it.
The loop sleeps here when there is nothing to do, using no CPU. The real Looper does the same.
Messages run one at a time. While one runs, everything behind it waits, including drawing.

blocks.code: post("click handler that blocks for 100 ms", () -> sleep(100));
blocks.caption: Java

blocks.text: A slow handler. The "draw frame" message posted after it cannot start until it returns.
A worker thread does not touch the UI. It posts a message, and the main thread runs it.
A Handler bound to the main thread's Looper. Posting to it queues work for the main thread.
The coroutine version of the same hand-off: work off the main thread, then resume on it.
Reports disk and network access on the main thread while you develop.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output of the model: onCreate, then the blocking click handler, then draw frame, which reports it waited at least 100 ms, then the result posted from worker-1. Every line is printed by the thread named main.
That is the whole reason for the rule "never block the main thread": the frame could not be drawn while the click handler slept.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Each app process has its own heap with a size limit set by the device (often a few hundred megabytes). Exceeding it throws OutOfMemoryError in your process only.
Zygote loads the framework classes and resources once. Forked app processes share those memory pages until they write to them, which is why dozens of apps can stay cached.
The system orders processes by importance (foreground, visible, service, cached) and the kernel low memory killer removes the least important first.
A Binder transaction copies its data into a buffer of about 1 MB shared by all transactions in flight for your process. Large Intent extras or saved state throw TransactionTooLargeException.
ART compiles hot code ahead of time using profiles collected on the device or shipped as a Baseline Profile, so later runs start faster.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: adb shell dumpsys activity processes lists processes with their importance and why (adj values).
adb shell dumpsys meminfo <package> shows the heap, native memory and view counts of your process.
An ANR writes every thread stack to a trace file. Open it from Play Console or a bug report and read the thread named "main" first.
Perfetto or the Android Studio CPU profiler with a system trace shows the main thread's messages, frame deadlines and Binder calls on one timeline.
adb shell am start -W <package>/<activity> prints launch time. Logcat's "Displayed" line gives time to first frame.

blocks.text: In production

items: Cold start work is measured and budgeted: Application.onCreate, dependency graph creation and the first screen each get a share.
Calls to system services are Binder calls and can be slow. Hot paths avoid calling PackageManager or reading settings repeatedly.
Multi-process apps (a separate process for a media player or a WebView) pay with a second Application.onCreate and no shared memory. Use them only for isolation.
Crash and ANR rates are tracked per release as Android vitals in Play Console, and bad rates reduce store visibility.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Assuming the app keeps running in the background like a desktop program.
Assume the process can end at any moment once the user leaves. Persist what matters and schedule real background work with WorkManager.
Doing heavy work in Application.onCreate.
It runs before any screen and for every entry point, including a broadcast or a push message. Initialise lazily.
Keeping app state in static fields or singletons and expecting it after a return from the background.
After process death they are empty while the UI is restored mid-flow. Reload from saved state or storage.
Passing a bitmap or a long list through an Intent.
Pass an id or a content URI. Binder has a size limit.
Updating a View from a background thread.
Post to the main thread. The framework throws CalledFromWrongThreadException for most view changes.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: In LooperModel.java, change the blocking handler to sleep 6 seconds. Which real Android failure does this model, and what would the user see?
Add a second worker that posts 100 messages. Does the order of their output ever interleave within one message? Why not?
On a device, run adb shell dumpsys activity processes before and after pressing Home. Find your process and read how its state changed.
Draw the stack from memory, then mark which layers a call to startActivity passes through.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Walk through what happens when the user taps an app icon.
blocks.text: Launcher calls startActivity, a Binder call to the system server. ActivityTaskManager resolves the Intent, sees no process and asks Zygote to fork one. The new process runs ActivityThread.main, prepares the main Looper and attaches to the system server. The system server then instructs it to bind the Application (ContentProviders are created, then Application.onCreate) and to launch the Activity. The Activity is created, started and resumed, the view tree is attached to a window, and after the first traversal a frame is submitted and shown.

blocks.title: What is Binder and why did Android need it?
blocks.text: A kernel driver providing fast inter-process calls with one copy of the data and with the caller's identity (UID and PID) attached by the kernel, so services can check permissions reliably. It supports object references across processes, death notifications and a thread pool in each process to serve incoming calls. Android builds system services, Intents, ContentProviders and AIDL on it.

blocks.title: Explain Looper, MessageQueue and Handler.
blocks.text: A Looper owns a MessageQueue for one thread and loops forever taking messages. A Handler is the object that posts messages or Runnables to a Looper and handles them when they are dequeued. The main thread's Looper is created for you; a HandlerThread gives a background thread one.

blocks.title: How does Android decide which process to kill?
blocks.text: Each process gets an importance from the components running in it: foreground (resumed Activity, foreground service, executing receiver), visible, service, and cached. The system translates that into an oom_adj score and the low memory killer removes the highest scores first. Among cached processes, least recently used goes first.

blocks.title: What is the application sandbox?
blocks.text: Each app is installed as a distinct Linux user with a private data directory, runs in its own process, and is confined by SELinux. Access to anything outside, such as the camera, contacts or another app's data, goes through a system service that checks permissions, or through a component the other app explicitly exports.

blocks.title: How does ART differ from Dalvik and from a desktop JVM?
blocks.text: Dalvik interpreted DEX with a JIT. ART added ahead-of-time compilation, a better garbage collector and profile-guided compilation: it interprets and JIT-compiles first, records hot methods, and compiles them ahead of time when the device is idle. Unlike a desktop JVM it runs DEX, a register-based format designed for small memory, not stack-based class files.

quiz.q: What is Zygote for?
options: A pre-warmed process that app processes are forked from
quiz.why: Forking a process that already has the framework loaded makes app starts fast and shares memory.

quiz.q: How does your app talk to the system server?
options: It runs in the same process
quiz.why: Every system service call is a Binder transaction to another process.

quiz.q: What causes an ANR?
options: The main thread not responding to input in time
A crash in a background thread
quiz.why: The system detects that the main thread did not handle an input event within about 5 seconds.

quiz.q: Which process is killed first under memory pressure?
quiz.why: Cached processes hold nothing the user can currently see or hear.

quiz.q: What does ART execute?
options: DEX bytecode, interpreted, JIT-compiled or compiled ahead of time
quiz.why: Class files are converted to DEX at build time, and ART runs DEX.

modules.title: Android SDK Fundamentals
modules.summary: Manifest, the four components, Context, Intents and resources.

blocks.text: An Android app is not one program with one starting point. It is a set of components, and the system can start any of them: an Activity (a screen), a Service (work with no screen), a BroadcastReceiver (a reaction to an event), a ContentProvider (shared data).
The manifest is the file where you declare every component and every permission. If it is not in the manifest, the system does not know it exists.
An Intent is a message that says "start this" or "someone please do this". A Context is your handle to the app's surroundings: resources, files, system services, starting components.
Why it matters

The system, not your code, creates and destroys components, so it must know about them before the app runs. Intents let apps cooperate without knowing each other: your app can ask for "something that can share text" and any installed app may answer. Context exists because everything environmental, from a string resource to the vibration service, depends on which app and which screen is asking.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: The manifest is a company's entry in the phone directory: who works there and which lines are public. An explicit Intent is dialling a known extension. An implicit Intent is asking the operator for "anyone who repairs printers". Context is your staff badge: it proves who you are and opens the doors you are allowed through.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: iOS
The manifest combines what iOS splits across Info.plist, entitlements and the app delegate. Android also lists every screen there; iOS does not list view controllers anywhere.
iOS

An explicit Intent is like presenting a view controller you instantiate. An implicit Intent covers what URL schemes, Universal Links, UIActivityViewController and app extensions do on iOS, in one mechanism.
UIKit
There is no Context on iOS. Its jobs are spread over Bundle.main, UIApplication.shared, FileManager and trait collections.
iOS
Resource qualifiers (values-hi, drawable-night, layout-sw600dp) do what asset catalog variants and .lproj folders do, extended to any resource and many more axes.
Flutter
A Flutter app still ships an AndroidManifest.xml with one Activity. Plugins such as url_launcher and share_plus are wrappers that build Intents.

blocks.text: startActivity with an implicit Intent

items: Your code builds an Intent with an action and data
startActivity sends it to the system server
PackageManager compares it with the intent filters of every installed, visible app
No match: ActivityNotFoundException
One match: that Activity starts
Several matches: the user chooses, unless a verified App Link or a default decides

blocks.text: The manifest those Activities are declared in
Intent resolution as a model, compiled and run
A simplified version of the matching the system performs. Real matching also compares host, path and MIME type.
Walkthrough
An explicit Intent names the exact class. No matching happens.
Extras are a key-value Bundle. Keep them small: they cross a process boundary.
An implicit Intent describes the job. Any app whose filter matches can take it.
Always shows the system share sheet, so the user picks each time.
Nothing on the device can handle the Intent. Without this catch the app crashes.
The modern way to get a result back. It must be registered before the Activity is started, so do it as a property.
In the manifest. Other apps and the system may start this component. Required to be stated for any component with an intent filter since Android 12.
The receiving side reads extras from the Intent that started it. The Intent is redelivered after recreation.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output of the resolution model: the explicit Intent goes straight to its component. VIEW https matches two apps. SEND matches the mail app. VIEW geo matches nothing, which on a device is ActivityNotFoundException.

The last line is the instructive one: MAIN matches nothing, because startActivity adds the DEFAULT category to every implicit Intent and the launcher filter does not list it. An Activity you want reachable by implicit Intents must declare DEFAULT.

blocks.text: Memory

items: An Activity is a Context. A reference to it from a singleton, a static field or a long-running thread keeps the whole screen and its views alive.
applicationContext lives as long as the process and is safe to hold, but it has no theme and cannot show dialogs.
Intent extras and results travel through Binder. Large payloads throw TransactionTooLargeException, sometimes only on the return trip.
Resources are loaded per configuration. On a configuration change the Activity is recreated so that strings, layouts and dimensions for the new configuration are picked.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Start any exported component from the terminal: adb shell am start -n <package>/.ProductActivity --el order_id 9001.
Fire an implicit Intent: adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "https://shop.example.com/product/42".
See what would handle an Intent: adb shell cmd package query-activities -a android.intent.action.SEND -t text/plain.
Build errors that mention "Manifest merger failed" list the two conflicting declarations. The Merged Manifest tab shows where each line came from.
adb shell dumpsys package <package> prints the declared components, filters and granted permissions as the system sees them.

blocks.text: In production

items: Single-Activity apps declare one launcher Activity and a few others for special entry points such as share targets and payment redirects.
Share sheets, opening maps, the dialler, email and the system photo picker are all implicit Intents; none need a permission.
Product flavors and build types contribute their own manifest fragments, for example a debug-only Activity or a different app name.
Deep links, push notification taps and app shortcuts all arrive as Intents at an exported Activity, which validates them and hands off to navigation.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Creating an Activity class and forgetting to declare it.
Add an <activity> entry. Starting an undeclared Activity throws ActivityNotFoundException.
android:exported="true" on an internal screen, or with no validation of incoming data.
Export only real entry points. Treat every extra and URL from outside as untrusted input.
Calling startActivity with an implicit Intent and no handling for "no app found".
Catch ActivityNotFoundException, or use a chooser, and show a message.
Using applicationContext to inflate a layout.
The theme is lost and views look wrong. Inflate with the Activity context.
Hard-coding user-facing text and sizes in code.
Put text in strings.xml and sizes in dimens.xml so they can vary by language, screen and theme.
Checking for other apps with queryIntentActivities and getting an empty list on Android 11 and later.
Package visibility is filtered. Declare a <queries> element for the intents or packages you need to see.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: In IntentResolution.kt, add an app that handles VIEW for the geo scheme and run it again. Then make the launcher filter reachable by an implicit MAIN Intent.
Write the Intent that opens the dialler with a phone number filled in, and say whether it needs a permission.
blocks.text: Hint: Intent(Intent.ACTION_DIAL, Uri.parse("tel:..."))

blocks.title: Add a values-hi/strings.xml with one translated string and switch the device language. What was recreated?
Find the merged manifest of any app you have and list three entries that came from libraries.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is the manifest for, and what goes wrong without it?
blocks.text: It declares the app's components, permissions, hardware requirements and application-level settings so that the system and the store can know them without running the app. Components not declared cannot be started; permissions not declared are denied; intent filters not declared mean other apps and links cannot reach you.

blocks.title: Explain Intent filters and how an implicit Intent is resolved.
blocks.text: A filter lists actions, categories and data (scheme, host, path, MIME type). An implicit Intent matches when its action is in the filter, every one of its categories is in the filter, and its data matches. startActivity adds CATEGORY_DEFAULT, so an Activity must list DEFAULT to receive implicit Intents. If several match, the system shows a chooser unless a default or a verified App Link applies.

blocks.title: What are the different Contexts and how do they differ?
blocks.text: Application, Activity and Service are all Contexts. The Activity context is themed and tied to one screen's lifetime; use it for anything visual. The application context lasts for the process and is safe to keep, but it cannot start an Activity without FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK and inflates with the default theme. ContextWrapper lets classes such as ContextThemeWrapper adjust one.

blocks.title: What does android:exported mean and why is it a security topic?
blocks.text: An exported component can be started by other apps. Any app can then send it arbitrary Intents. Exported Activities must validate extras and URLs, exported Services and Receivers should require a permission where possible, and ContentProviders should be unexported or protected with read and write permissions.

blocks.title: What is a PendingIntent?
blocks.text: A token wrapping an Intent that another app or the system can fire later as if it were your app, with your identity and permissions. Notifications, alarms and widgets use them. Since Android 12 you must declare FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE; immutable is the default choice so the holder cannot alter the Intent.

blocks.title: How does the resource system choose a resource?
blocks.text: Resources live in folders with qualifiers: language and region, night mode, screen density, smallest width, orientation, API level. At runtime the system removes folders that contradict the device configuration and picks the best remaining match by qualifier precedence. A configuration change invalidates those choices, which is why the Activity is recreated.

quiz.q: Which is not one of the four app components?
quiz.why: ViewModel is a Jetpack class. The four components are Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver and ContentProvider.

quiz.q: What happens if an implicit Intent matches no Activity?
options: A system dialog offers to install an app
quiz.why: startActivity throws, and an uncaught exception crashes the app.

quiz.q: Since Android 12, what must a component with an intent filter declare?
quiz.why: The value must be stated explicitly or the app fails to install.

quiz.q: Which Context should a singleton hold?
quiz.why: It lives as long as the process, so holding it leaks nothing.

quiz.q: What decides which string a user sees for R.string.add?
options: The resource qualifier that best matches the device configuration
quiz.why: The resource system picks from folders such as values, values-hi and values-night.

modules.title: Activity Lifecycle
modules.summary: Callbacks, rotation, process death, state restoration, with a simulator.

blocks.text: An Activity is one screen of an Android app. You do not create it or destroy it yourself. The system does, and it tells you what is happening by calling methods on your class in a fixed order.

There are three levels. Created: the object exists. Started: it is visible. Resumed: it is in front and receiving touches. Going up calls onCreate, onStart, onResume. Coming down calls onPause, onStop, onDestroy.

Two things surprise developers from other platforms. Rotating the phone destroys the Activity and builds a new one. And while your app is in the background the system may kill the whole process without calling anything.
Why it matters

Phones have limited memory and many apps. Android keeps the right to reclaim any screen the user cannot see. The lifecycle callbacks are your chance to start work when the screen appears, release resources when it goes away, and save what the user was doing so it can be rebuilt.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A stage actor. The stage manager calls "places" (onCreate), raises the curtain (onStart), turns on your spotlight (onResume). The spotlight can move away (onPause), the curtain can fall (onStop), and the set can be struck (onDestroy). You act when called. You never raise the curtain yourself.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: UIKit
A UIViewController lives for as long as it is on the navigation stack. An Activity can be destroyed and recreated while it is still on the back stack, with a new object each time.
iOS

iOS also terminates suspended apps to free memory, and by default the app then starts fresh. Android expects you to restore: the system keeps the back stack and a saved state Bundle per Activity and replays them when the user returns.
UIKit

Rotation on iOS calls viewWillTransition(to:with:) on the same controller. On Android an unhandled configuration change (rotation, dark mode, locale, font scale, window resize) recreates the Activity.
SwiftUI
scenePhase (.active, .inactive, .background) lines up with resumed, paused and stopped. @SceneStorage is the counterpart of saved instance state.
Flutter

A Flutter app usually runs inside one Activity whose manifest declares configChanges, so rotation does not recreate it and Dart state survives. Process death still wipes Dart memory. AppLifecycleState mirrors the Android states.

blocks.text: Cold start to first frame

items: User taps the launcher icon
System forks a new process from Zygote
Application.onCreate runs
Activity is constructed and onCreate(null) runs: set the content view
onStart: the Activity is visible
onResume: the Activity has focus and takes input
The first frame is drawn

blocks.text: The Java version saves state by hand in onSaveInstanceState. The Kotlin version shows the modern approach: a ViewModel with SavedStateHandle.
Walkthrough
Every lifecycle override must call super. The framework throws SuperNotCalledException if you forget.
The Bundle is null on a fresh launch and non-null after rotation or process death. This is where the old value comes back.
Called when the Activity may be destroyed and later restored. Write small values only: the Bundle crosses a process boundary.
Inside onDestroy these tell you why. finishing means gone for good. changingConfigurations means a new instance is coming right away.

blocks.code: private val viewModel: CounterViewModel by viewModels()
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: Returns the same ViewModel to the old and new Activity across a rotation. The default factory supplies the SavedStateHandle.
SavedStateHandle is a map that the library writes into the saved state Bundle for you.
An ordinary field belongs to one Activity object and is gone as soon as that object is.
Called once, when the Activity finishes for good. It is not called on rotation.
What happens when it runs

items: Launch: onCreate, onStart, onResume.
Home button: onPause, onStop, then onSaveInstanceState.
Return: onRestart, onStart, onResume.
Rotation: onPause, onStop, onSaveInstanceState, onDestroy on the old object, then onCreate(bundle), onStart, onRestoreInstanceState, onResume on a new object.
Use the simulator below to run these and the less obvious cases.

blocks.text: Memory

items: The system holds the Activity. Anything else that holds it after onDestroy (a static field, a singleton listener, a running thread, a long-lived coroutine) leaks the Activity together with its whole view tree.
A ViewModel outlives the Activity object across rotation, so it must never hold a View, an Activity or a Fragment. Use AndroidViewModel only when you need the application Context.

A process in the background is kept in memory as a cached process and can be killed at any time when memory is needed. The system does not call onDestroy first. Any state that is only in memory is lost.

The saved state Bundle is sent to the system process over Binder, whose transaction buffer is 1 MB shared across the whole process. Large bundles throw TransactionTooLargeException. Keep it to ids and small values.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Log every callback, as the example does, and filter Logcat by tag:MainActivity.

Test process death properly: put the app in the background with Home, run adb shell am kill <your.package>, then reopen it from Recents. The Stop button in Android Studio is a force stop and discards saved state, so it does not test restoration.
Developer options → "Don't keep activities" destroys every Activity as soon as you leave it. It exercises onSaveInstanceState and restoration, though it does not kill the process.
adb shell dumpsys activity activities shows the back stack and the state of every Activity record.
