To see why the process last died, call ActivityManager.getHistoricalProcessExitReasons (API 30+).

blocks.text: In production

items: A checkout screen keeps the entered address in SavedStateHandle, the cart in a Room database, and the in-flight payment call in viewModelScope. Rotation keeps all three. Process death keeps the first two, and the payment status is re-queried from the server on return.
Camera, location updates and sensors are acquired in onStart or onResume and released in onStop or onPause, or handed to a lifecycle-aware component that does it for you.
Analytics screen-view events fire in onResume. Firing them in onCreate double counts after every rotation.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Saving data in onDestroy or onStop only.
onDestroy is not called on process death. Persist user data when it changes, or at the latest in onPause or onStop, and use saved state for transient UI state.
Starting a network call in onCreate with no ViewModel, so every rotation fires it again.
Start the work in a ViewModel. The new Activity instance observes the same result.
Registering a listener in onCreate and unregistering in onStop.
Pair symmetrically: onCreate with onDestroy, onStart with onStop, onResume with onPause. Otherwise the second onStart runs with no listener.
Putting a list of items or a bitmap in the saved state Bundle.
Save the id or the query. Reload the data from the repository or database.
Setting android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize" to "fix" rotation bugs.
That hides the bug for rotation only. Dark mode, locale change, multi-window resize and process death still lose the state.
Assuming onPause means the screen is hidden.
In multi-window, or under a permission dialog, a paused Activity is still fully visible. Keep video and animations running until onStop.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: In the simulator: launch, tap + three times, rotate. Which of the three counters kept its value and why?
Launch, tap + twice, press Home, kill the process, reopen. Explain each counter value.
Open the detail screen, press Home, kill the process, reopen, then press Back. In what order are the two Activities recreated?
Build MainActivity in Android Studio from the code above. Reproduce the rotation and adb am kill sequences and compare Logcat with the simulator.
Add a LifecycleObserver (DefaultLifecycleObserver) that logs the same events without overriding any Activity method.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Walk through the Activity lifecycle.
blocks.text: onCreate: build the UI and restore state. onStart: visible. onResume: in the foreground with input focus. onPause: losing focus, may still be visible. onStop: no longer visible. onDestroy: finishing or being recreated. onRestart runs before onStart when returning from the stopped state. The pairs are symmetric: create and destroy, start and stop, resume and pause.

blocks.title: What happens on a configuration change, and how do you keep state?
blocks.text: The Activity is destroyed and recreated so resources can be reloaded for the new configuration. Three tools, by lifetime: ViewModel keeps in-memory objects across the recreation; saved instance state (or SavedStateHandle, or rememberSaveable in Compose) keeps small values across recreation and process death; persistent storage keeps real data across everything.

blocks.title: What is process death and how do you handle it?
blocks.text: While the app is in the background the system may kill its process to reclaim memory. No callback runs. The system keeps the task, the back stack and each Activity's saved state Bundle. When the user returns, a new process starts, Application.onCreate runs, and only the top Activity is recreated with its Bundle; the ones below are recreated as the user navigates back. Handle it by saving ids and inputs to saved state and reloading the rest.

blocks.title: How does a ViewModel survive rotation?
blocks.text: Each ComponentActivity owns a ViewModelStore. On a configuration change the Activity hands the store to the system through onRetainNonConfigurationInstance, and the new instance receives the same store, so the same ViewModel objects are returned. When the Activity finishes for real, the store is cleared and onCleared is called.

blocks.title: Activity A starts Activity B. List the callbacks in order.
blocks.text: A.onPause, B.onCreate, B.onStart, B.onResume, A.onStop (and A.onSaveInstanceState). Pressing Back: B.onPause, A.onRestart, A.onStart, A.onResume, B.onStop, B.onDestroy.

blocks.title: What changed about the Back button in Android 12?
blocks.text: For a root launcher Activity, Back no longer finishes it. The system moves the task to the background instead, so the Activity is stopped, not destroyed, and returning is a warm start. Other Activities still finish on Back.

blocks.title: What is the difference between onSaveInstanceState and onRetainNonConfigurationInstance or ViewModel?
blocks.text: onSaveInstanceState serialises small data into a Bundle held by the system process, so it survives process death but is limited in size and type. ViewModel keeps live objects in memory, so it can hold anything but only survives configuration changes.

blocks.title: How do lifecycle-aware components work?
blocks.text: ComponentActivity implements LifecycleOwner and exposes a Lifecycle that dispatches events (ON_CREATE, ON_START and so on) to registered LifecycleObservers. Libraries observe it instead of asking you to call start and stop: LiveData only delivers while at least STARTED, and repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) cancels flow collection in onStop and restarts it in onStart.

quiz.q: The user rotates the phone. Which sequence runs?
options: onPause, onStop, onSaveInstanceState, onDestroy, onCreate, onStart, onRestoreInstanceState, onResume
quiz.why: An unhandled configuration change tears the Activity down fully and builds a new instance with the saved Bundle.

quiz.q: The system kills your backgrounded process for memory. What is called?
quiz.why: The process is simply killed. onStop and onSaveInstanceState already ran when the app went to the background.

quiz.q: Which survives rotation but not process death?
quiz.why: The ViewModel is retained in memory across configuration changes. Memory is gone when the process dies.

quiz.q: On API 28 and later, when is onSaveInstanceState called?
quiz.why: Since Android 9 it is called after onStop. Before that it was called before onStop, with no guarantee relative to onPause.

quiz.q: Activity A starts opaque Activity B. When is A.onStop called?
quiz.why: A pauses first, B is created, started and resumed, and only then is A stopped. A slow A.onPause delays B.

quiz.q: Is onSaveInstanceState called when the user presses Back and the Activity finishes?
quiz.why: A finishing Activity is not coming back, so there is nothing to restore.

modules.title: Fragment Lifecycle
modules.summary: Fragment and view lifecycles, transactions, back stack, leaks.

lessons.title: Fragment lifecycle: two lifecycles in one class

blocks.text: A Fragment is a reusable piece of screen that lives inside an Activity. One Activity can show one fragment at a time and swap them, or several side by side on a tablet.
A Fragment has the same states as an Activity (created, started, resumed) and extra callbacks for joining and leaving its Activity.

The surprising part: the Fragment object and its views have different lifetimes. When you navigate away and the fragment goes onto the back stack, its views are destroyed but the Fragment object is kept. When you come back, the views are built again.
Why it matters

Fragments were added so one Activity could hold several independent screen parts, first for tablets. Today the common design is a single Activity that hosts fragments (or composables) as screens, because swapping a fragment is cheaper and more controllable than starting an Activity. Most View-based codebases you will work in are built this way.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: An actor and a stage set. The actor (Fragment object) stays in the building between scenes. The set (the views) is torn down when the scene ends and rebuilt when it returns. An actor still holding a prop from the old set is holding rubbish, and is stopping it being thrown away.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: UIKit

A Fragment is a child UIViewController. onViewCreated is viewDidLoad. The difference: UIKit keeps the view of a controller that is further down a navigation stack; Android destroys the fragment's view and recreates it on return.
UIKit

Fragment arguments (a Bundle) replace custom initialisers. The system recreates fragments with the no-argument constructor after rotation or process death, so data passed to a constructor would be lost.
SwiftUI
No direct equivalent. The need fragments serve, swappable screen units inside one host, is met by NavigationStack destinations, as it is by Navigation Compose on Android.
Flutter
A Fragment is closest to a Route with its State object, except Flutter keeps the widget state of routes below the top one alive, where Android destroys the fragment view.

blocks.text: A fragment is added and shown

items: onAttach: the fragment is tied to its Activity
onCreate: the fragment object exists. Read arguments here. There are no views yet
onCreateView: inflate the layout
onViewCreated: views exist. Set up binding, adapters and observers
onStart: visible
onResume: interactive

blocks.text: Both versions bind in onViewCreated, observe with the view lifecycle, and clear the binding in onDestroyView. Those three lines prevent the most common fragment bugs.
Walkthrough
Passing the layout id lets the base class inflate it, so you do not need to override onCreateView.
Nullable on purpose: the binding is valid only while the view exists.

blocks.code: private val viewModel: ProductsViewModel by viewModels()
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: Scoped to this fragment. It survives rotation and stays alive while the fragment is on the back stack.
Tied to the view. It is cancelled in onDestroyView, so nothing tries to update views that no longer exist.
Removes the current fragment from the container and adds the new one.
Records the transaction so Back reverses it. Without this, Back would leave the Activity.
Releases the whole view tree while the fragment waits on the back stack.
Arguments are saved and restored by the system. Use them for every input a fragment needs.
With getViewLifecycleOwner the observer is removed when the view is destroyed. With this, a second observer would be added every time the view is recreated.
What happens when it runs

items: Full order going up: onAttach, onCreate, onCreateView, onViewCreated, onViewStateRestored, onStart, onResume.
Full order going down: onPause, onStop, onSaveInstanceState, onDestroyView, onDestroy, onDetach.
Going onto the back stack stops at onDestroyView. Coming back resumes from onCreateView.
There is no runnable sample for this lesson: fragment callbacks only exist inside an Android app. Put a Log.d in each callback of the code above and reproduce the first flowchart on a device.

blocks.text: Memory

items: A fragment on the back stack that still references its binding, an adapter or a view keeps the entire view hierarchy in memory. This is the classic fragment leak, and LeakCanary reports it as "Fragment#mView" or a leaked binding field.
Observers registered with the fragment itself as owner survive view destruction. After two visits to the screen you have two observers updating one set of views.
The ViewModel of a back-stack fragment stays in memory. Large lists held there are still held.
After process death FragmentManager recreates every fragment in the back stack state with the no-argument constructor and the saved arguments, before your Activity onCreate finishes.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: FragmentManager.enableDebugLogging(true) prints every state move of every fragment to Logcat under the FragmentManager tag.
adb shell dumpsys activity <your.package> lists the fragments in each Activity with their state and back stack.
"Fragment already added" and overlapping screens almost always mean the fragment was added again after a restore.
"Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState" means a transaction ran from an asynchronous callback after the Activity was stopped.
LeakCanary names the leaking field. If the path ends in a binding or adapter inside a fragment, the fix is in onDestroyView.

blocks.text: In production

items: Single-Activity apps: one Activity hosts a NavHostFragment and every screen is a fragment or a composable destination.

Migration to Compose usually happens inside fragments first: onCreateView returns a ComposeView, with ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed so the composition follows the fragment view.
DialogFragment and BottomSheetDialogFragment are fragments, so dialogs survive rotation and can own a ViewModel.
Tablet and foldable layouts place a list fragment and a detail fragment side by side and share one ViewModel between them.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Keeping the binding in a lateinit var and never clearing it.
Use a nullable backing field and set it to null in onDestroyView.
observe(this, ...) or lifecycleScope.launch for UI work.
Use viewLifecycleOwner for anything that touches views.
A fragment constructor with parameters.
The system needs a public no-argument constructor. Pass data through arguments, or use a FragmentFactory for dependencies.
Adding the fragment in Activity.onCreate every time.
After rotation FragmentManager has already restored it, so you get two. Add it only when savedInstanceState is null.
Calling commit() after onSaveInstanceState.
It throws IllegalStateException because the change could not be saved. Commit while the Activity is at least started, and treat commitAllowingStateLoss as a last resort.
A fragment calling methods on another fragment directly.
Share a ViewModel scoped to the Activity or navigation graph, or use setFragmentResult.
Using requireContext() or requireActivity() from a background callback.
The fragment may be detached by then and it throws. Check isAdded, or better, scope the work so it is cancelled.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add Log.d to every callback of both fragments. Open the detail, press Back, rotate. Write down the order and compare with the flowchart.
Remove the _binding = null line and navigate back and forth with LeakCanary installed. Read the leak trace.
Change observe(getViewLifecycleOwner(), ...) to observe(this, ...) in the Java version, navigate away and back three times, and count the render calls.
Return a result from the detail fragment to the list using setFragmentResult and setFragmentResultListener.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Describe the Fragment lifecycle and how it differs from the Activity lifecycle.
blocks.text: onAttach, onCreate, onCreateView, onViewCreated, onStart, onResume going up; onPause, onStop, onDestroyView, onDestroy, onDetach going down. The additions are attach and detach, and a separate view lifecycle: onCreateView to onDestroyView can repeat several times within one onCreate to onDestroy span.

blocks.title: What happens to a fragment across a configuration change and across process death?
blocks.text: In both cases the instance is destroyed. FragmentManager saves its state (class name, arguments, saved instance state, back stack) and recreates it through the no-argument constructor. On a configuration change the ViewModel is retained; after process death it is not, and only arguments, saved state and SavedStateHandle come back.

blocks.title: add versus replace, and what does addToBackStack actually store?
blocks.text: add puts a fragment in the container and leaves existing ones in place and resumed. replace removes the existing ones first. addToBackStack records the transaction, not the fragment, so Back reverses exactly what the transaction did: for a replace, it removes the new fragment and re-adds the old, recreating its view.

blocks.title: commit, commitNow, commitAllowingStateLoss?
blocks.text: commit schedules the transaction on the main thread. commitNow runs it at once and cannot be used with addToBackStack. commitAllowingStateLoss permits a commit after state was saved, accepting that the change is lost if the process is killed. Reaching for it usually signals a lifecycle bug elsewhere.

blocks.title: How do fragments share data?
blocks.text: A ViewModel scoped to the Activity (by activityViewModels()) or to a navigation graph (by navGraphViewModels) for ongoing shared state. The Fragment Result API for a one-time result. Arguments for inputs. Never a direct reference from one fragment to another.

blocks.title: Fragments or Compose destinations for a new app?
blocks.text: Compose with Navigation Compose for new code: no view lifecycle split, no binding leaks, less boilerplate. Fragments remain necessary in existing View-based apps, for libraries that expose fragments, and as hosts during an incremental migration.

quiz.q: A fragment is replaced with addToBackStack. Which is the last callback it receives?
quiz.why: The view is destroyed, the fragment instance is kept for the back stack.

quiz.q: Which owner should UI observers in a fragment use?
quiz.why: The view lifecycle ends at onDestroyView, exactly when the views stop existing.

quiz.q: Why must fragment inputs go in arguments?
options: The system recreates fragments with a no-argument constructor
Constructors are not allowed in Kotlin
quiz.why: After rotation or process death only the arguments Bundle is restored.

quiz.q: Where do you set the view binding to null?
quiz.why: That is the end of the view's life. Later callbacks may never come while the fragment sits on the back stack.

quiz.q: After rotation, who recreates the fragment?
quiz.why: FragmentManager restores its state, which is why adding it again creates a duplicate.

modules.title: Android Views and XML
modules.summary: Views, XML layouts, ConstraintLayout, view binding, units and themes.

blocks.text: In the classic Android toolkit, everything on screen is a View: a piece of text, a button, an image. A ViewGroup is a View that contains and positions other Views.

You describe a screen in an XML layout file. Each tag is a View, and attributes set its size, position and appearance. The system reads the file and builds the real objects. That step is called inflating.
In code you get hold of those objects and change them: set text, react to clicks, show or hide. View binding generates a class that gives you each view by name.
Why it matters

Separating layout from code lets the same screen have different layouts for phones, tablets, landscape and languages without changing code. Compose is the modern toolkit, but the View system is what most existing apps are built with, what many libraries expose, and what you will read and maintain for years.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A stage and props. The XML file is the stage plan: where each prop stands. Inflation is the crew building the set from the plan. Your code is the director who, during the play, tells a named prop to change.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: UIKit
View is UIView and ViewGroup is a container view. An XML layout is a storyboard or xib; inflating is loading the nib. View binding replaces IBOutlets, generated for you and never left dangling.
UIKit
ConstraintLayout is Auto Layout: positions expressed as constraints between views. LinearLayout is UIStackView. FrameLayout is a plain container view.
iOS
dp is the iOS point: a density-independent unit. sp is like a point that also scales with the user's font size setting, the role Dynamic Type plays.
SwiftUI
The View system is imperative: you mutate objects. Compose is the SwiftUI counterpart. match_parent and wrap_content roughly correspond to "fill" and "hug" sizing.
Flutter
An XML layout is a widget tree written as data and changed by mutation, not by rebuilding. ConstraintLayout has no common Flutter equivalent; LinearLayout is Row or Column.

blocks.text: A layout pass

items: Something changes: text is set, or a view calls requestLayout()
Measure: each parent gives each child a width and height constraint, and the child reports the size it wants
Layout: each parent places each child at a position
Draw: each view paints itself into the canvas
The frame is handed to the system compositor

blocks.text: Both use view binding. The generated class ItemProductBinding has one field per view that has an android:id.
The layout both files inflate
Strings, plurals, dimensions and a theme
How a parent turns layout_width into a constraint, compiled and run
A model of the rule in ViewGroup.getChildMeasureSpec, without padding and margins.
Walkthrough
As wide as the parent allows. wrap_content means just big enough for the content.
Gives the view a name. The plus sign creates the id if it does not exist yet.
In ConstraintLayout, 0dp means "match the constraints": stretch between the start and end constraints.
This view's start edge is attached to the end edge of the image. Start and end flip automatically for right-to-left languages.
A question mark reads a value from the current theme, so the same layout follows light, dark and brand themes.
48dp is the minimum touch target size recommended for accessibility.
Builds the view tree from the XML and returns typed references to every view with an id.
Formats a string resource with an argument. The format can differ per language.
Picks the right plural form for the language and the number.
GONE removes the view from layout. INVISIBLE hides it but keeps its space.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output of the measure model: 16dp is 16, 32 and 48 pixels at densities 1, 2 and 3. A fixed child size is always EXACTLY that size. match_parent takes the parent's mode and size. wrap_content becomes AT_MOST the parent's size.
This is why wrap_content inside a ScrollView behaves differently: a ScrollView measures its child with UNSPECIFIED height, the "be as tall as you like" rows at the bottom of the output.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Every View is a heavyweight object, typically well over a hundred fields. Deep or wide trees cost memory and make every measure and layout pass slower.
A View holds its Context, normally the Activity. Any long-lived reference to a single View keeps the entire Activity alive.
Inflation reads XML and creates objects by reflection. It is one of the slower things an app does, which is why lists reuse row views.
A bitmap in an ImageView is held at its decoded size: width times height times four bytes. Load images at the size they are shown, with a library such as Coil or Glide.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Layout Inspector shows the live view tree, each view's attributes and where each attribute value came from.
Developer options → Show layout bounds draws the edges and margins of every view on the device.
Developer options → Debug GPU overdraw colours areas that are painted several times per frame.
The layout editor's "Component Tree" warnings catch missing constraints, which make a view jump to the top-left corner at runtime.
Lint flags hard-coded text, missing contentDescription, nested weights and obsolete layout parameters. Run it from Analyze → Inspect Code.

blocks.text: In production

items: Design systems are implemented as styles and theme attributes, so a brand change is made in one theme file.
Alternative layouts live in qualified folders such as layout-sw600dp for tablets and are selected automatically.
Existing View screens adopt Compose gradually by placing a ComposeView in the XML, and Compose screens host legacy views with AndroidView.
Custom views extend View or an existing widget, override onMeasure and onDraw, and expose attributes through a declare-styleable entry.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Nesting LinearLayouts several levels deep, especially with layout_weight.
Weights measure children twice, and nesting multiplies it. Flatten the hierarchy with ConstraintLayout.
Using left and right in attributes and paddings.
Use start and end so the layout mirrors correctly for Arabic, Hebrew and Urdu.
Text sizes in dp, or fixed heights on text containers.
Use sp and let height wrap. Otherwise large font settings clip the text.
findViewById with an id that is not in the inflated layout.
It returns null and crashes later. Use view binding, which only offers ids that exist.
Touch targets smaller than 48dp, and images with no contentDescription.
Set a minimum size, and describe meaningful images. Use contentDescription="@null" for decorative ones.
Hard-coded colours such as #FFFFFF in layouts.
Reference theme attributes so dark theme works.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Rebuild item_product.xml with nested LinearLayouts. Count the views in each version with Layout Inspector.
In MeasureModel.kt, add padding to childSpec so the size offered to the child shrinks by the parent's padding. Check with a 1080 parent and 32 of padding.
Switch a device to an RTL language in developer options ("Force RTL layout direction") and note what moves in the product row.
Set the device font size to the largest setting. Which of your texts get clipped, and why?

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Explain how a View is measured, laid out and drawn.
blocks.text: Measure: starting from the root, each parent calls measure on each child with a width and height MeasureSpec, a mode (EXACTLY, AT_MOST or UNSPECIFIED) plus a size, and the child sets its measured size. Layout: each parent calls layout on each child with its final position. Draw: each view draws its background, its content in onDraw, its children, then decorations such as scrollbars. requestLayout schedules measure and layout; invalidate schedules only draw.

blocks.title: ViewBinding, DataBinding or findViewById?
blocks.text: findViewById is an untyped lookup at runtime that can return null. View binding generates a class per layout with a typed, non-null field for each id, at no runtime cost. Data binding also generates bindings but adds an expression language and observable bindings inside the XML, with slower builds and logic hidden in layouts. View binding is the usual choice.

blocks.title: What is the difference between a style and a theme?
blocks.text: A style is a set of attribute values applied to one view, such as a text appearance. A theme is a set of attribute values applied to a whole Context, and views read from it with ?attr. Styles decide how a widget looks; themes supply the values that many styles refer to, which is how light, dark and brand variants work.

blocks.title: How do you support different screen sizes and densities?
blocks.text: Use dp and sp, never px. Use flexible layouts: constraints, match-constraints and wrap. Provide alternative resources by qualifier, for example layout-sw600dp for tablets and drawable densities, or vector drawables. For large-screen behaviour use window size classes to switch between single-pane and two-pane layouts.

blocks.title: How do you make a View-based screen accessible?
blocks.text: Content descriptions for meaningful images and icon buttons, labels linked to inputs, touch targets of at least 48dp, sp for text so it scales, sufficient colour contrast, a sensible focus order, and testing with TalkBack and the Accessibility Scanner.

blocks.title: When would you write a custom View?
blocks.text: When no combination of existing widgets gives the drawing or interaction you need: a chart, a seek control, a signature pad. Extend the closest existing class, measure correctly in onMeasure, draw in onDraw without allocating objects there, handle touch in onTouchEvent, save state in onSaveInstanceState, and expose accessibility information.

quiz.q: What does wrap_content mean?
options: Be just large enough for the content
quiz.why: The view asks for the size its content needs, limited by what the parent offers.

quiz.q: Which unit should text sizes use?
quiz.why: sp scales with screen density and with the user's font size preference.

quiz.q: In ConstraintLayout, what does layout_width="0dp" do?
options: Matches the constraints on both sides
quiz.why: 0dp is "match constraints": the view stretches between its start and end constraints.

quiz.q: What is the difference between GONE and INVISIBLE?
options: GONE takes no space, INVISIBLE keeps its space
quiz.why: A GONE view is skipped in measure and layout.

quiz.q: What does ?attr/colorPrimary refer to?
options: A value looked up in the current theme
quiz.why: Theme attributes let one layout adapt to whichever theme is applied.

modules.title: RecyclerView
modules.summary: Adapter, ViewHolder, recycling, DiffUtil and ListAdapter.

lessons.title: RecyclerView: lists that reuse their rows

blocks.text: A list can have thousands of items but only about ten fit on screen. RecyclerView creates just enough row views to fill the screen, and when a row scrolls off the top it is reused for the item arriving at the bottom.
You supply an Adapter. It answers three questions: how many items are there, how do I create a row view, and how do I fill a row view with item number N.
A ViewHolder is a small object that keeps references to the views inside one row, so they are looked up once and not on every scroll.
Why it matters

Creating a view from XML is slow, and memory is limited. Building one view per item for a long list would freeze the screen and may run out of memory. Reuse makes the cost depend on the screen size, not the list size.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A restaurant with eight tables and a thousand guests through the day. Nobody builds a table per guest. When a party leaves, the table is cleared and laid again for the next one. Laying the table is binding. Building the table is creating a holder.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: UIKit
RecyclerView is UITableView and UICollectionView in one. onCreateViewHolder plus onBindViewHolder is dequeueReusableCell plus configuring the cell. A LayoutManager is a UICollectionViewLayout.
UIKit
ListAdapter with DiffUtil is UITableViewDiffableDataSource: you hand over a new list and it works out the inserts, moves and deletes.
SwiftUI
The Compose counterpart is LazyColumn, as List or LazyVStack is to SwiftUI. Those hide the adapter and holder entirely; you only provide items and a key.
Flutter
ListView.builder is the same idea with less ceremony: build is called for visible indexes only. Flutter recycles elements internally; you never see a ViewHolder.

blocks.text: A row scrolls into view

items: The LayoutManager sees empty space at the bottom
It asks the Recycler for a view for position 42
The Recycler looks in its cache, then in the pool for that view type
Nothing available: the Adapter creates a holder (inflate once)
The Adapter binds item 42 into the holder
The LayoutManager measures and places the row
The row that left the top goes to the cache or pool

blocks.text: Both use ListAdapter, which wraps DiffUtil and runs the comparison off the main thread.
The row layout
Recycling as a model, compiled and run
Eight visible rows over a thousand items. Count the holders created against the rows shown.
Walkthrough
The base class keeps the current list and computes differences when you submit a new one.
One holder per row view. It keeps the binding so views are never looked up again.
Pass the parent so layout params are read, and false because RecyclerView attaches the view itself.
The listener is created once per holder. It asks for the current position when clicked, because the holder is reused for many positions.
A click can arrive while the row is being removed. Then there is no valid position.
Bind sets every field every time. A recycled row still shows the previous item until you overwrite it.

blocks.code: override fun areItemsTheSame(old: ProductRow, new: ProductRow) = old.id == new.id
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: Identity: is this the same row, possibly with changed content?

blocks.code: override fun areContentsTheSame(old: ProductRow, new: ProductRow) = old == new
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: Content: would the row look identical? Data class equals makes this one line.
Java passes the same ItemCallback to the ListAdapter constructor.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output of the model: 208 rows were shown, 8 holders were created, and there were 208 binds. After jumping to position 600 the holder count is still 8.
A real RecyclerView creates a few more than the visible count because it keeps a small cache and prefetches the next row, but the number still depends on the screen, not on the list.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Memory use is proportional to rows on screen plus cache and pool, not to the item count.
The default pool keeps five holders per view type. Screens with many view types or nested horizontal lists may need a larger or a shared RecycledViewPool.
A holder that starts an image load or a coroutine must cancel or replace it on rebind, or a late result appears in the wrong row.
The adapter is referenced by the RecyclerView. In a Fragment, an adapter held in a field keeps the destroyed view alive unless you clear binding.list.adapter or the field in onDestroyView.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Log in onCreateViewHolder and onBindViewHolder. Creates should stop soon after the first screen; binds should match rows scrolled.
A row showing the wrong image or badge is a bind that did not reset every field, or an async load that was not cancelled.
"Inconsistency detected. Invalid view holder adapter position" means the data changed without the matching notify call, usually from mutating the list on another thread.
Jank while scrolling: profile with the CPU profiler and look inside onBindViewHolder and onCreateViewHolder for inflation depth, image decoding or formatting.
Layout Inspector shows how many row views really exist. If it equals the item count, something has disabled recycling.

blocks.text: In production

items: A product list: ListAdapter, stable ids, rows mapped to a display model before submitList, images loaded by Coil or Glide, which cancel on reuse.
Screens with mixed content (banner, carousel, grid, list) use several view types, or ConcatAdapter to join separate adapters.
Paging 3 supplies PagingDataAdapter, which loads more pages as the user nears the end and still uses DiffUtil.
Horizontal carousels inside a vertical list share one RecycledViewPool and save their scroll position per row.
Swipe to delete and drag to reorder are added with ItemTouchHelper.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Setting a field only in some cases: if (row.onSale) badge.isVisible = true.
A recycled row keeps the old state. Always set both branches: badge.isVisible = row.onSale.
Calling notifyDataSetChanged() after every change.
It rebinds everything and disables animations. Use ListAdapter and submitList with a new list.
Mutating the list you already submitted and submitting it again.
ListAdapter sees the same object and does nothing. Submit a new list instance.
Creating a click listener or doing parsing and formatting inside onBindViewHolder.
Create listeners in onCreateViewHolder and prepare display strings before submitting the list.
Capturing position from onBindViewHolder in a listener.
It goes stale after inserts and removals. Read holder.bindingAdapterPosition at click time.
A RecyclerView with height wrap_content inside a ScrollView.
It lays out every item and recycling is lost. Make the RecyclerView the scrolling container and add headers as view types or with ConcatAdapter.
areContentsTheSame that always returns false or compares only the id.
Compare everything the row displays. Otherwise rows flicker, or changes never appear.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: In RecyclerModel.kt, add a second view type for every tenth row, with its own pool. How many holders are created now?
Add a "sale" badge to the row and the adapter. Scroll fast and confirm it never appears on the wrong row.
Replace the adapter with a plain RecyclerView.Adapter and notifyDataSetChanged. Compare the animation and the bind count when one item changes.
Write the same list in Compose with LazyColumn and items(rows, key = { it.id }). List what disappeared.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does RecyclerView recycling work?
blocks.text: The LayoutManager asks the Recycler for a view for a position. The Recycler checks, in order: scrap (views detached during the current layout), the view cache (a few recently scrolled-off holders still bound to their position, reusable without a bind), an optional ViewCacheExtension, and the RecycledViewPool (holders by view type that must be rebound). Only if all miss does the adapter create a new holder.

blocks.title: What does DiffUtil do, and what is ListAdapter?
blocks.text: DiffUtil computes the minimal set of insert, remove, move and change operations between two lists, using areItemsTheSame and areContentsTheSame. ListAdapter wraps AsyncListDiffer: submitList runs the diff on a background thread and dispatches the operations on the main thread, giving correct animations with no manual notify calls.

blocks.title: How do you optimise a janky list?
blocks.text: Measure first with a system trace. Then: flatten the row layout, do no work in bind beyond setting values, precompute display strings, size images to the view and load them asynchronously, call setHasFixedSize when the list size does not change the RecyclerView size, share a view pool between nested lists, and avoid nested scrolling containers.

blocks.title: How do you handle clicks in a row correctly?
blocks.text: Set the listener once in onCreateViewHolder, read bindingAdapterPosition at click time, check it against NO_POSITION, and pass the item to a callback supplied by the screen. The adapter does not navigate or call the ViewModel itself.

blocks.title: How do you build a list with several kinds of rows?
blocks.text: Override getItemViewType to return a type per position, create the matching holder in onCreateViewHolder, and bind accordingly, usually with a sealed class of row models. For independent sections use ConcatAdapter. For grids with full-width headers, use GridLayoutManager with a SpanSizeLookup.

blocks.title: RecyclerView or LazyColumn?
blocks.text: LazyColumn for Compose screens: no adapter, no holders, keys and content types give the same reuse. RecyclerView stays in View-based screens and remains a mature choice for very complex or highly tuned lists. They can be mixed during migration through ComposeView rows or AndroidView.

quiz.q: A list has 5,000 items and 10 fit on screen. Roughly how many row views exist?
quiz.why: Only visible rows plus a small cache and pool are kept.

quiz.q: Which adapter method is expensive and should run rarely?
quiz.why: It inflates a layout. Binding only sets values on existing views.

quiz.q: Why must onBindViewHolder set every field?
options: The holder still shows the previous item's values
quiz.why: Rows are reused, so anything not overwritten is left over from another item.

quiz.q: What does areItemsTheSame compare?
quiz.why: It decides whether two entries are the same logical item.

quiz.q: What happens if you mutate a list and submit the same instance to ListAdapter?
options: Nothing: it sees the same list
quiz.why: ListAdapter returns early when the new list is the current list object.

modules.title: Jetpack Compose
modules.summary: Composables, modifiers, state and hoisting, with a recomposition visualiser.

blocks.text: In Jetpack Compose you describe the screen with Kotlin functions marked @Composable. There is no XML layout file.
Text, Button and Image put something on screen. Column stacks children vertically, Row places them side by side, Box stacks them on top of each other.
A Modifier is a chain of instructions attached to a composable: size, padding, background, click handling.
You never update a view. When data changes, Compose calls your function again with the new data. That is recomposition.
Why it matters
With XML views you build the tree once and then mutate it by hand, and bugs appear when the views and the data drift apart. Compose removes that step: the UI is a function of the data.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: XML views are a whiteboard you keep erasing and correcting. Compose is a printer: change the document and print the page again. The printer is smart enough to reprint only the part that changed.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: SwiftUI
Column is VStack, Row is HStack, Box is ZStack, LazyColumn is List or LazyVStack. A @Composable function plays the role of a View struct with a body.
SwiftUI
Modifiers are an explicit parameter, not chained methods on the view. Order matters in both: padding then background differs from background then padding.
SwiftUI
@Preview is #Preview.
Flutter
A composable is a Widget build method. Flutter wraps widgets (Padding(child: ...)); Compose applies a Modifier chain to one composable, so trees are flatter.
UIKit
The XML View system is the UIKit counterpart: a mutable object tree that you update imperatively.

blocks.text: How ProductRow gets on screen

items: Activity.onCreate calls setContent { ... }
Compose runs the root composable
ProductRow runs and emits a Row with a Column and a Button
Layout measures children against the Row constraints
The frame is drawn

blocks.text: Compose is Kotlin only: it relies on a Kotlin compiler plugin. A Java screen can host Compose through ComposeView, but composables themselves cannot be written in Java.
Walkthrough
Tells the Compose compiler plugin to add the hidden machinery that tracks this function in the UI tree.
Events leave a composable as lambdas. The row does not know what Add does.
Every reusable composable accepts a modifier so the caller controls size and position.
Applied in order, outside in. dp is density-independent pixels, the Android counterpart of iOS points.
The trailing lambda is the button content. Any composable can go inside.
Renders the composable in Android Studio without running the app.
What happens when it runs

items: Composable functions can run often and in any order. Treat them as pure: same inputs, same UI, no side effects.
Composables emit UI and return Unit.
By convention composable names are nouns in PascalCase.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Compose keeps a slot table: a compact record of what each composable emitted and remembered. It is discarded when the composition leaves the screen.
A lambda that captures a ViewModel is fine. A lambda that captures an Activity and is stored outside the composition leaks it.
LazyColumn composes only visible items, like RecyclerView. A Column with verticalScroll composes every child.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Layout Inspector shows the composable tree with recomposition counts for each node.
Preview several configurations at once: stack @Preview annotations for dark theme, font scale and screen sizes.
Modifier.border(1.dp, Color.Red) while developing shows exactly what space a composable takes.

blocks.text: In production

items: Design systems expose their own composables (AppButton, PriceText) built on Material 3, with colours and type coming from MaterialTheme.
Existing apps migrate screen by screen: ComposeView inside a Fragment, or AndroidView to host a legacy View inside Compose.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Hard-coding size and padding inside a reusable composable.
Accept a modifier parameter and apply it to the root element.
Doing work in the composable body: a network call, logging, mutating a variable.
The body may run many times per second. Put side effects in LaunchedEffect or in the ViewModel.
Using Column with a loop for a long list.
Use LazyColumn with items(list, key = { it.id }).
Wrong modifier order, such as clickable after padding, which shrinks the touch area.
Read the chain top to bottom as outside to inside.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add a quantity stepper (minus, count, plus) to ProductRow using a nested Row.
Swap the order of fillMaxWidth and padding and add a background. Sketch what you expect before running.
Build the same row in XML with ConstraintLayout and compare the two files.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does Compose differ from the View system?
blocks.text: Views are stateful objects created once and mutated. Compose is declarative: functions describe the UI for the current state and the runtime works out the changes. There is no findViewById and no view state to keep in sync. Layout is single pass, so deep nesting does not cost what nested XML layouts cost.

blocks.title: What does the @Composable annotation do?
blocks.text: It changes the function type. The compiler plugin adds a Composer parameter and a bit mask of changed parameters, wraps the body in a restart group so it can be re-run on its own, and inserts skip checks when the parameters are unchanged.

blocks.title: Why does every composable take a Modifier parameter?
blocks.text: So the caller, which knows the surrounding layout, decides size, weight, alignment and padding. A component that hard-codes these cannot be reused.

quiz.q: What does a @Composable function return?
options: Unit: it emits UI as a side effect of being called
quiz.why: Composables emit nodes into the composition and return Unit.

quiz.q: Modifier.padding(16.dp).background(Color.Red): where is the red?
quiz.why: Padding is applied first, then the background fills what is left inside it.

quiz.q: Which is the SwiftUI VStack equivalent?
quiz.why: Column lays children out vertically.

blocks.text: State is any value that can change over time and should change what is on screen.
Compose only notices changes to values held in a State object, created with mutableStateOf. Changing an ordinary variable does nothing.
A composable function runs again on every recomposition, so local variables reset. remember keeps a value across recompositions. rememberSaveable also keeps it across rotation and process death.
State hoisting means moving state up to the caller. The child receives the value as a parameter and reports events through a lambda.
Why it matters

A composable that owns its state is hard to test, preview and reuse. Once the state is hoisted, the child is a plain function of its inputs, and one owner (usually a ViewModel) is the single source of truth.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A thermostat display does not decide the temperature. It shows the number it is given and tells the controller when you press a button. The controller owns the number.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: SwiftUI

remember { mutableStateOf(x) } is @State. Passing the value down with an onChange lambda is the usual replacement for @Binding. A ViewModel exposing StateFlow is the ObservableObject or @Observable counterpart.
SwiftUI
rememberSaveable is @SceneStorage. CompositionLocal is @Environment.
SwiftUI
SwiftUI re-evaluates body of the view whose state changed. Compose recomposes the smallest restartable scope that read the state, which can be smaller than a whole composable.
Flutter

remember plus mutableStateOf replaces StatefulWidget with setState. There is no setState call: writing to the state object triggers the update. Hoisting to a ViewModel is the BLoC or ChangeNotifier role.

blocks.text: From tap to new text

items: Button calls onIncrement
The owner writes count = count + 1 to a MutableState
The snapshot system marks every scope that read count as invalid
On the next frame those scopes are re-run
Composables whose inputs did not change are skipped

blocks.text: Kotlin only. The by keyword uses property delegation so you can write count instead of count.value.
Walkthrough
mutableIntStateOf creates observable state without boxing the Int. rememberSaveable stores it in the saved instance state Bundle. by unwraps .value.
The value goes down, the event comes up. CounterScreen is the single owner.
Stateless. It can be previewed and tested with any value.
This is the read that subscribes the surrounding scope to changes of count.
What happens when it runs

items: First composition: count is 0 and the state object is stored in the slot table.
Tap: the lambda writes 1.
Recomposition: CounterScreen and Counter re-run. remember returns the existing state object instead of creating a new one.
Try the three switches in the visualiser below to see what recomposes and what is skipped.

blocks.text: Memory

items: remember stores the value in the composition. It is dropped when the composable leaves the screen, for example an item scrolled out of a LazyColumn or a branch of an if that turned false.
rememberSaveable writes to the saved state Bundle, so it has the same limits: small, Parcelable or primitive values, or a custom Saver.
State that must survive navigation or be shared belongs in a ViewModel, read with collectAsStateWithLifecycle().

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Layout Inspector → Show Recomposition Counts. A number that climbs while nothing visible changes marks a wasted recomposition.
Compose compiler reports (the reportsDestination option) list every composable as skippable or not, and every class as stable or unstable.
If a value resets unexpectedly, check for a missing remember or for the composable leaving and re-entering the composition.

blocks.text: In production

items: A screen-level composable collects the ViewModel state and passes plain data down: val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle().
TextField state: keep the text in the ViewModel or rememberSaveable and pass value plus onValueChange. This is hoisting in its most common form.
Lists pass a stable key and immutable item models so unchanged rows are skipped.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: var count = mutableStateOf(0) without remember.
A new state object is created on every recomposition, so the value resets to 0. Wrap it in remember.
Using a mutable collection as state: remember { mutableListOf<Item>() } and calling add.
Compose cannot see the mutation. Use mutableStateListOf, or hold an immutable List in state and assign a new list.
Passing the whole ViewModel into child composables.
Pass the values and lambdas the child needs. It stays previewable and skippable.
Reading rapidly changing state high in the tree.
Read state as low as possible, or pass a lambda () -> T so only the reader recomposes.
Writing to state during composition.
This can loop forever. Write state in event handlers or effects only.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: In the visualiser, turn off remember and tap +. Explain the result in your own words.
Add a Reset button to Counter. Which function gains a parameter, and which one owns the logic?
Move count into a ViewModel with MutableStateFlow and collect it with collectAsStateWithLifecycle.
Replace remember with rememberSaveable in a small app and rotate the device. Then test process death with adb shell am kill.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is recomposition and what triggers it?
blocks.text: Re-running composable functions to update the UI. It is triggered when a State object that was read during composition is written with a different value. Compose re-runs only the restart scopes that read it and skips composables whose parameters are unchanged.

blocks.title: remember versus rememberSaveable versus ViewModel?
blocks.text: remember: survives recomposition only. rememberSaveable: also survives configuration change and process death, limited to Bundle-compatible data. ViewModel: survives configuration change, holds any object, is scoped to a navigation destination or Activity, and needs SavedStateHandle to survive process death.

blocks.title: What is state hoisting and why do it?
blocks.text: Moving state out of a composable to its caller, replacing it with a value parameter and an event lambda. It gives a single source of truth, makes the composable reusable, previewable and testable, and lets the owner intercept or validate changes.

blocks.title: What does stability mean in Compose?
blocks.text: A type is stable if Compose can trust that equals is consistent and that it will be notified when a public property changes. Primitives, String, function types and classes with only val properties of stable types are stable. Interfaces such as List are treated as unstable because the implementation might be mutable.

blocks.title: What is derivedStateOf for?
blocks.text: When a value is computed from state that changes more often than the result does. Example: showButton = listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0. Without it, every scroll frame recomposes the reader; with it, only a change in the Boolean does.

blocks.title: How do side effects fit with recomposition?
blocks.text: Composable bodies must be free of side effects because they can run many times, be skipped or be abandoned. Effects go in effect handlers: LaunchedEffect(key) runs a coroutine tied to the composition and restarts when the key changes; DisposableEffect pairs setup with cleanup; SideEffect runs after every successful recomposition.

quiz.q: What happens with val count = mutableStateOf(0) (no remember) when the composable recomposes?
options: A new state starting at 0 is created
quiz.why: The function body runs again and creates a fresh state object.

quiz.q: What does remember not survive?
quiz.why: Rotation recreates the Activity and its composition. rememberSaveable or a ViewModel is needed.

quiz.q: Which describes state hoisting?
options: Storing state in a global variable
Moving state to the caller and passing value plus callback down
quiz.why: The composable becomes stateless and the caller becomes the single source of truth.

quiz.q: A composable receives the same stable parameters as last time. What does Compose do?
quiz.why: Skippable composables with unchanged inputs are not re-run.

modules.title: Navigation
modules.summary: Back stack, type-safe routes, popUpTo and deep links.

lessons.title: Navigation: back stack, routes and deep links

blocks.text: Navigation is moving between screens and getting back again. Android keeps the screens you came through in a back stack. Going forward pushes a screen on top. Back removes the top one.
The Navigation library gives you a NavController that owns the back stack, and a navigation graph that lists every screen (destination) and what it needs.
A deep link is a URL that opens the app directly on a particular screen, for example a product page from a notification or a web link.
Why it matters

Done by hand, navigation is fragment transactions and Intents scattered through the code, with arguments passed as untyped bundles and the back stack easy to corrupt. A navigation graph puts the whole map in one place, makes arguments typed, and makes Back, Up and deep links behave consistently.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A stack of plates. You add a plate on top when you go somewhere new and take the top one off when you go back. Sometimes you need to take several off at once: after paying, you do not want the checkout plates still sitting under the receipt.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: SwiftUI
NavHost with type-safe routes is NavigationStack with a path and navigationDestination(for:). navController.navigate(ProductDetail(42)) is path.append(...). popBackStack is path.removeLast.
UIKit

NavController is UINavigationController: push and pop. popUpTo is popToViewController. Android has a system Back gesture and button that every screen must handle; iOS has only the in-app back affordance and edge swipe.
iOS
App Links are Universal Links: both verify domain ownership with a file on the website (assetlinks.json and apple-app-site-association). Custom URL schemes work the same way on both.
Flutter

Navigation Compose with typed routes is go_router with typed routes: a declarative route table, path parameters, redirects and deep links. popUpTo corresponds to go() replacing the stack, where push() only adds.

blocks.text: navigate(ProductDetail(42))

items: The route object is serialised into arguments
NavController finds the matching destination in the graph
NavOptions are applied: popUpTo, launchSingleTop
A new NavBackStackEntry is pushed
NavHost shows the new destination and moves the old one out of RESUMED
The screen reads its arguments with toRoute() or from SavedStateHandle

blocks.text: Kotlin shows Navigation Compose with type-safe routes. Java cannot use Compose, so it shows the Navigation Component with fragments and an XML graph. The NavController concepts are identical.
A back stack model, compiled and run
Thirty lines that implement navigate, popUpTo, inclusive and singleTop. NavController does this for you, plus state saving and lifecycles.
Walkthrough
The route is a type. Its properties are the arguments, checked by the compiler.
Declares the graph. The start destination is the bottom of the back stack.
The screen gets a lambda. Only this file knows about NavController.
Reads the typed arguments back from the back stack entry.
Generates the URL pattern from the route type, so /product/42 fills id = 42. The manifest still needs a matching intent filter.
Removes Cart and everything above it before pushing the confirmation.
Prevents two copies if the callback fires twice, for example on a double tap.
Navigates along an action defined in the XML graph, with arguments in a Bundle.
The same popUpTo with inclusive, through NavOptions.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output of the back stack model: after navigating, home > products > product/42. singleTop leaves it unchanged. After the order, cart and checkout are gone: home > products > product/42 > order/9001. After logout the stack is just login, and Back is no longer handled by the app, so the Activity would finish.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Every entry on the back stack keeps its ViewModels alive. A stack that only grows, because screens navigate forward where they should pop, is a slow leak the user feels as a long walk back.
In Navigation Compose, a destination that is not on top has its composition removed. rememberSaveable state is saved and restored; plain remember state is lost.
The back stack and each entry's saved state survive process death. Arguments must therefore be small and serialisable: pass an id, not an object.
Navigation arguments are copied into the destination ViewModel's SavedStateHandle, so the ViewModel can load its data without the UI passing anything in.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Log the stack on every change: navController.addOnDestinationChangedListener { _, destination, arguments -> Log.d("Nav", "$destination $arguments") }.
Test a deep link from the terminal: adb shell am start -W -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "https://shop.example.com/product/42" <your.package>.
Check App Links verification: adb shell pm get-app-links <your.package>. A domain that is not "verified" opens the browser.
"Navigation destination ... cannot be found" means the route or id is not in the graph that this NavController is using, often a nested graph mix-up.
adb shell dumpsys activity activities shows the task and Activity back stack, which is separate from the NavController stack inside one Activity.

blocks.text: In production

items: The graph is split into nested graphs per feature (auth, shop, checkout), each exposed by its feature module as an extension function on NavGraphBuilder.
A bottom navigation bar keeps a separate back stack per tab using saveState and restoreState.
Push notifications carry a deep link URL. The PendingIntent is built with a TaskStackBuilder so Back from the opened screen lands on the app home.
Auth is conditional navigation: the start destination checks login state and navigates to the auth graph with popUpTo, so logged-out users never see a protected screen.

Predictive back (Android 13 and later) animates a preview of the previous screen during the back gesture. It requires handling Back through OnBackPressedDispatcher or BackHandler, not by overriding onBackPressed.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Passing whole objects as navigation arguments.
Pass an id and load the object from the repository. Large arguments risk TransactionTooLargeException and go stale.
Passing NavController into screen composables or ViewModels.
Pass lambdas such as onProductClick. The screen stays previewable and the ViewModel stays free of Android types.
Calling navigate() from the body of a composable.
It runs on every recomposition. Navigate from an event callback, or from a LaunchedEffect keyed on the state that triggers it.
Navigating to login or home without popUpTo.
Back then returns to a screen that should be unreachable. Clear the finished flow.
A double tap pushing the same screen twice.
Use launchSingleTop, or ignore clicks unless the current entry is RESUMED.
Declaring a deep link in the graph and not in the manifest, or the reverse.
Both are needed: the manifest lets the system start the Activity, the graph maps the URL to a destination.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: In BackStack.kt, add a bottom-bar style switchTab(route) that keeps only home under the new tab. Print the stack.
Add an Orders destination that takes an optional status filter with a default value.
blocks.text: Hint: @Serializable data class Orders(val status: String? = null)

blocks.title: Add a nested checkout graph with Cart, Address and Payment, and share one ViewModel across the three screens.
Run the adb deep link command against a sample app and press Back. Where do you land, and why?

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does the back stack work, and what is the difference between Back and Up?
blocks.text: The back stack is the history of destinations in a task. Back pops the top entry and, at the start destination, leaves the app. Up navigates to the logical parent inside the app and never leaves it. They differ when the app was entered through a deep link: Back may return to the app that sent you, Up goes to the parent screen.

blocks.title: How do you pass data between destinations?
blocks.text: Forward: small arguments in the route, an id or a filter. Shared ongoing state: a ViewModel scoped to a nested navigation graph. Backward: a result written to the previous entry's SavedStateHandle and observed there. Never a mutable singleton and never large objects in arguments.

blocks.title: How do deep links work end to end?
blocks.text: The manifest declares an intent filter with the scheme, host and path so the system can route the URL to your Activity. For https links, android:autoVerify plus a Digital Asset Links file on the domain makes it a verified App Link. Inside the app the navigation graph maps the URL pattern to a destination and extracts arguments. For links that start a new task, Navigation builds a synthetic back stack from the graph hierarchy.

blocks.title: How do you scope a ViewModel to several screens?
blocks.text: Put the screens in a nested graph and obtain the ViewModel from the graph's back stack entry: in Compose, viewModel(navController.getBackStackEntry(CheckoutGraph)); with fragments, by navGraphViewModels(R.id.checkout_graph). It lives until the graph is popped.

blocks.title: How do you structure navigation in a multi-module app?
blocks.text: Each feature module exposes its destinations as an extension on NavGraphBuilder and its route types, and takes navigation callbacks as lambdas. The app module assembles the NavHost and wires the lambdas. Features never import each other; cross-feature navigation goes through the app module or through deep link URIs.

blocks.title: How do you handle the system Back button in Compose and in Views?
blocks.text: Compose: BackHandler(enabled) { } intercepts Back while enabled. Views: register an OnBackPressedCallback on onBackPressedDispatcher with a lifecycle owner. Overriding onBackPressed is deprecated and incompatible with predictive back. Keep the callback enabled only while you really need to intercept, for example with unsaved changes.

quiz.q: What does popUpTo(Cart) { inclusive = true } remove?
options: Everything above Cart, and Cart itself
Everything above Cart, but not Cart
quiz.why: popUpTo pops entries above the target; inclusive also removes the target.

quiz.q: What should you pass as a navigation argument for a product screen?
quiz.why: Arguments are saved with the back stack, so they must be small. The screen loads the rest.

quiz.q: What does launchSingleTop prevent?
options: A second copy of the destination already on top
quiz.why: If the destination is already at the top, no new entry is pushed.

quiz.q: What makes an https link open your app without a chooser on Android 12 and later?
options: A verified App Link: intent filter with autoVerify plus assetlinks.json on the site
quiz.why: Verification proves that the app and the domain belong to the same owner.

quiz.q: What happens to a screen's ViewModel when its back stack entry is popped?
options: It moves to the next screen
quiz.why: Each NavBackStackEntry owns a ViewModelStore that is cleared when the entry is removed.

modules.title: ViewModel
modules.summary: Scope, lifetime, SavedStateHandle and sharing between screens.

lessons.title: ViewModel: scope, lifetime and saved state

blocks.text: A ViewModel is an object that holds the data for a screen and is kept alive while the screen is rebuilt. Rotate the phone and the Activity is a new object, but it gets the same ViewModel back.
A ViewModel belongs to an owner: an Activity, a Fragment, or a navigation destination. It lives until that owner is finished for good, and then onCleared() is called once.
A ViewModel lives in memory only. If the system kills the process, it is gone. SavedStateHandle is a small map inside the ViewModel that the system does save and restore.
Why it matters

Activities and Fragments are recreated on every configuration change. Without somewhere stable to keep things, each rotation would lose loaded data and restart network calls. ViewModel is that stable place, provided by the framework so you do not build your own retained object.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A hotel cloakroom. You (the Activity) may leave and come back as a different person on the next shift, but you hand in the same ticket and get the same coat. When you check out of the hotel, the cloakroom clears your peg. If the hotel burns down, the coat is gone, but the note you left in the safe (saved state) survives.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: SwiftUI
A ViewModel is what @StateObject gives you: an object that outlives view rebuilds and is owned by one place in the tree. viewModel() in a composable is like declaring @StateObject at the screen root.
UIKit
iOS has no direct counterpart because view controllers are not recreated on rotation. A UIKit view model lives exactly as long as its controller; the Android class exists to bridge recreation.
SwiftUI
SavedStateHandle is close to @SceneStorage: small values the system keeps for you across termination.
Flutter
Flutter state already survives rotation because the Activity is not recreated. A ViewModel plays the role of a Cubit or ChangeNotifier provided above the route.

blocks.text: by viewModels() on a fresh screen and after rotation

items: The screen asks its ViewModelStore for the ViewModel under a key
First time: nothing there, so the factory creates one and the store keeps it
Rotation: the old Activity is destroyed, the store is retained
The new Activity asks again and receives the same object
The user leaves the screen for good: the store is cleared and onCleared() runs
viewModelScope is cancelled, stopping any coroutine still running

blocks.text: Kotlin exposes saved state as a StateFlow and uses viewModelScope. Java exposes it as LiveData and manages its own executor.
A model of the ViewModelStore, compiled and run
Forty lines that reproduce the three situations: rotation, process death and leaving the screen.
Walkthrough
A StateFlow backed by saved state. It starts with the restored value if there is one, else the default.
Writes to the handle. The StateFlow above emits, and the value is included the next time state is saved.
A coroutine scope on the main dispatcher that is cancelled in onCleared.
finally also runs on cancellation, so the flag is never left stuck at true.
A factory is needed whenever the constructor has parameters. Hilt generates this for you.
CreationExtras gives the factory access to the Application without the ViewModel ever holding a Context.
The Java counterpart: LiveData that is saved and restored.
Without viewModelScope, Java code stops its own background work in onCleared.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output of the model: after rotation it is the same ViewModel with memory=3 and saved=3. After process death it is a different ViewModel with memory=0 and saved=3. On Back, onCleared() runs once.
That one table is the whole lesson: the in-memory field follows the ViewModel, the saved value follows the system.

blocks.text: Memory

items: A ViewModel is held by its store, and the store by the retained state of its owner. Anything the ViewModel references lives equally long.
Never reference a View, Activity, Fragment or their lifecycles from a ViewModel. After rotation those objects are dead and the ViewModel keeps them from being collected.
A ViewModel scoped to the Activity lives for the whole Activity. Per-screen data placed there is never released while the app is open.
SavedStateHandle is written into the instance state Bundle, which shares the Binder transaction limit. Keep it to ids and short text.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Log in init and onCleared. Two init logs for one screen visit means the ViewModel is being created outside the store or under different keys.
If data reloads on every rotation, the load is in the UI layer or the ViewModel is obtained from a different owner each time.
To check process-death handling: background the app, run adb shell am kill <package>, return. Fields reset, SavedStateHandle values remain.
Layout Inspector and the debugger both show which ViewModel instance a screen holds; compare identity hash codes across a rotation.

blocks.text: In production

items: One ViewModel per screen, created by Hilt with @HiltViewModel, receiving repositories and a SavedStateHandle that Navigation has filled with the route arguments.
Multi-step flows share one ViewModel scoped to the flow's nested navigation graph, so pressing Back out of the flow discards its state.
Form screens keep every field the user typed in SavedStateHandle and everything derived in normal StateFlows.
Unit tests construct the ViewModel directly with SavedStateHandle(mapOf("id" to 42)) and fake repositories.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Creating a ViewModel with its constructor: val vm = CheckoutViewModel(...).
It is then an ordinary object that dies with the Activity. Always obtain it through by viewModels, viewModel() or ViewModelProvider.
Assuming the ViewModel survives the app being killed in the background.
It does not. Put what must survive in SavedStateHandle or storage, and test with adb shell am kill.
Scoping everything to the Activity "to share it".
Scope to the destination or the flow's navigation graph, so state is cleared when the flow ends.
Passing a Context into the ViewModel to read a string or start a screen.
Expose state or an event and let the UI resolve resources and navigate.
Starting work in init that needs arguments not yet known.
Read arguments from SavedStateHandle, which is filled before init runs, or start the work from an explicit call.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: In ViewModelStoreModel.kt, add a second Screen that uses the key "other". Show that two keys give two ViewModels in one store.
Add a search query to CheckoutViewModel that survives process death, and a results list that does not. Explain the choice.
Write a unit test that creates the ViewModel with a SavedStateHandle containing an address and asserts the StateFlow value.
Move a per-screen ViewModel to activity scope in a sample app, open and close the screen, and observe with logs that onCleared no longer runs.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How is a ViewModel created and where is it stored?
blocks.text: ViewModelProvider asks the owner's ViewModelStore for a ViewModel under a key derived from the class name. If none exists, it calls the Factory, passing CreationExtras (which carry the SavedStateRegistryOwner, default arguments and the Application), stores the result and returns it. Every later request with the same owner and key returns that instance.

blocks.title: How does SavedStateHandle work?
blocks.text: It is a key-value map handed to the ViewModel. It registers a saved state provider with the owner's SavedStateRegistry. When the system saves instance state, the handle's contents are written into the Bundle; on recreation they are read back before the ViewModel is constructed. Navigation also places a destination's arguments in it.

blocks.title: ViewModel versus onSaveInstanceState versus persistent storage?
blocks.text: ViewModel: in-memory, survives configuration change, any object, lost on process death. Saved instance state (and SavedStateHandle, rememberSaveable): small serialisable values, survives process death, discarded when the user finishes the screen. Persistent storage: survives everything, for data the user owns.

blocks.title: How do you share data between two screens?
blocks.text: Pass an id as a navigation argument when the second screen can load what it needs. For state both screens edit, scope one ViewModel to their common owner, ideally a nested navigation graph. For app-wide data, use a repository both ViewModels observe.

blocks.title: Should a ViewModel expose suspend functions?
blocks.text: Generally no. The UI should call a plain function and the ViewModel should launch in viewModelScope, so the work survives rotation and is cancelled with the ViewModel. A suspend function called from the UI runs in the UI's scope and is cancelled when the screen is recreated.

blocks.title: What is the difference between ViewModel and AndroidViewModel?
blocks.text: AndroidViewModel receives the Application, for cases that truly need a Context that outlives screens. It makes unit testing harder and invites using Context where a repository should be injected, so prefer plain ViewModel with dependencies passed in.

quiz.q: When is onCleared() called?
options: When the owner is finished for good
When the app goes to the background
quiz.why: It runs once, when the ViewModelStore is cleared because the screen will not come back.

quiz.q: What survives process death?
quiz.why: The process memory is gone. Only state the system saved is restored.

quiz.q: Why can a ViewModel not hold an Activity?
options: It outlives the Activity object and would leak it
quiz.why: After rotation the old Activity should be collected, and a ViewModel reference prevents that.

quiz.q: Two fragments call by activityViewModels<CartViewModel>(). How many instances exist?
quiz.why: Both ask the same Activity store under the same key.

quiz.q: What does viewModelScope do when the ViewModel is cleared?
quiz.why: The scope is cancelled as part of clearing the ViewModel.

modules.title: MVVM
modules.summary: ViewModel, UiState and one-way data flow, with a runnable model.

lessons.title: MVVM: ViewModel, UiState and one-way data flow

blocks.text: MVVM splits a screen into three parts. The View draws what it is told and reports what the user did. The ViewModel holds the state of the screen and decides what happens next. The Model is everything behind it: repositories, the network, the database.
Data moves in one direction. State flows from the ViewModel down to the View. Events flow from the View up to the ViewModel. The View never changes state itself.
The ViewModel has no reference to the View. It only exposes an observable value, and whoever is watching redraws.
Why it matters

Activities and Fragments are destroyed on rotation and are hard to unit test. Logic left in them is lost, repeated and untested. Moving state and logic into a ViewModel gives it a longer life than the screen object and lets you test it on the JVM with no device.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A restaurant. The waiter (View) takes your order and brings plates. The kitchen (ViewModel) decides what gets cooked and when. The suppliers (Model) provide ingredients. The waiter never cooks, and the kitchen never walks to your table: it puts plates on the pass and whoever is on shift picks them up.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: SwiftUI
A ViewModel exposing StateFlow<UiState> is an ObservableObject with @Published, or an @Observable class. collectAsStateWithLifecycle() plays the role of @StateObject plus automatic observation.
UIKit
Same pattern as MVVM with Combine or closures binding a view controller to a view model. The Android difference is that the framework itself keeps the ViewModel alive across recreation of the screen.
Swift
viewModelScope is close to storing a Task and cancelling it in deinit, except cancellation is automatic and tied to the screen being gone for good, not to rotation.
Flutter
A ViewModel with one UiState is a Cubit. Add explicit event classes and a reducer and you have BLoC, which Android calls MVI.

blocks.text: First load of the products screen

items: The screen is created and asks for its ViewModel
ViewModel init sets state to Loading and launches load()
The View collects the state and shows a spinner
The repository returns the products
ViewModel sets state to Content(items)
StateFlow emits and the View shows the list

blocks.text: The Java version uses LiveData and an executor because Java has no coroutines or StateFlow collection. The shape is the same: private mutable state, public read-only state, events as methods.
The same pattern with no Android classes, compiled and run
These strip MVVM down to its idea so it can run on a plain JVM. The Kotlin file uses a real StateFlow. The Java file uses a ten-line stand-in for LiveData.
Walkthrough
The writable state is private. Only the ViewModel can change it.
The View gets a read-only type. It cannot cast its way back to the mutable one.
Work started here survives rotation and is cancelled when the screen is finished for good.
Reads the current value and writes a new one atomically, so two quick events cannot overwrite each other.
Converts the flow into Compose state and stops collecting when the app goes to the background.
The stateless screen receives plain data and a lambda. It can be previewed and tested without a ViewModel.
postValue is safe from a background thread and delivers on the main thread. setValue must be called on the main thread.
Java has no viewModelScope, so you stop background work yourself.
What happens when it runs

items: The trace below steps through the runnable model. The output lines are the real output of that file.
Notice that the ViewModel never calls the View. It writes a value, and the collector reacts.

blocks.text: Memory

items: The ViewModel outlives the Activity object across rotation. If it held a View, Activity or Fragment, that object could never be collected: a leak of the whole screen.
A collector that keeps running in the background wastes work and battery. Collect with repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) or collectAsStateWithLifecycle so it stops below STARTED.
ViewModel state is lost on process death. Put ids and user input in SavedStateHandle and reload the rest.
UiState objects should be immutable. Each change allocates a new one, which is cheap and makes change detection a simple equals check.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Log every state transition in one place: add .onEach { Log.d("ProductsVM", "state=$it") } to the flow while developing.
