If the screen does not update, check three things in order: was a new object assigned (not a mutated one), is the collector active, is equals returning true for the old and new state.
Unit test the ViewModel with runTest and a fake repository. A bug that reproduces in a JVM test is found in seconds.
Layout Inspector shows whether Compose received the new state. If it did and nothing changed on screen, the bug is in the composable, not the ViewModel.

blocks.text: In production

items: One ViewModel per screen (navigation destination), injected by Hilt with its repositories.
UiState is a data class or sealed interface that contains everything the screen needs to draw, already formatted where formatting is not locale work.
User actions are methods named for intent: onAddToCartClicked(productId), onQueryChanged(text), onRetry().
Flows from the data layer are converted with stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial) so upstream work stops shortly after the screen goes away but survives rotation.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Passing a Context, View or Fragment into the ViewModel.
Pass data in and expose state out. For strings, expose a resource id or let the View map an enum to text.
Exposing MutableStateFlow or MutableLiveData publicly.
Expose StateFlow or LiveData and keep the mutable one private.
Several separate flags: isLoading, items, error, each observed separately.
One UiState object, or a sealed type, so the screen can never show a spinner and an error together by accident.
Loading data in the Activity or composable so every rotation loads again.
Load in the ViewModel. The new screen instance observes the result that is already there.
Using StateFlow for a one-off event such as navigation, then seeing it fire again after rotation.
Model the event as state that the View marks as handled, or send it through a Channel collected with lifecycle awareness.
A ViewModel of a thousand lines.
Move reusable logic into use cases or plain classes that the ViewModel calls.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add pull-to-refresh to the model: a refreshing flag inside Content, set while a reload runs, without ever showing the full-screen Loading state again.
Write a unit test for ProductsViewModel with FakeProductRepository(fail = true). Assert the state is Error.
blocks.text: Hint: runTest { val vm = ...; advanceUntilIdle(); assertTrue(vm.state.value is ProductsUiState.Error) }

blocks.title: Add onAddToCartClicked(id) that shows a one-time "Added" message. Decide how the message is cleared and why.
Convert the Java ViewModel to Kotlin with StateFlow. List every line that disappears.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What goes in a ViewModel and what must stay out?
blocks.text: In: screen state, the logic that turns user events and data into new state, and coroutines for that work. Out: anything tied to the UI toolkit (View, Activity, Fragment, Context for UI, resources lookups that depend on configuration), and data access details, which belong in repositories.

blocks.title: How do you handle one-off events such as navigation or a snackbar?
blocks.text: Three workable approaches. Fold it into state (for example userMessage: String?) and have the View call onMessageShown() to clear it; this is what Google recommends and it survives rotation. Or use a Channel exposed as a Flow, collected with repeatOnLifecycle, which delivers each event once. Avoid SharedFlow with replay 0 for must-deliver events: an emission while nobody collects is dropped.

blocks.title: LiveData or StateFlow?
blocks.text: StateFlow for Kotlin code: it works in every layer, has the full Flow operator set, and is easy to test. It is not lifecycle-aware by itself, so the UI must collect with repeatOnLifecycle or collectAsStateWithLifecycle. LiveData is lifecycle-aware out of the box and is still the practical choice in Java screens.

blocks.title: How do you test a ViewModel?
blocks.text: Construct it with fake repositories. Use runTest, replace Dispatchers.Main with a test dispatcher through a rule, trigger an event, advance the scheduler, and assert on state.value or on the sequence of emissions collected with a tool such as Turbine.

blocks.title: What problems does MVVM not solve?
blocks.text: It says nothing about navigation, about where business rules shared by several screens live, or about how to structure a very complex screen. Those are answered by a navigation layer, by a domain layer with use cases, and by splitting state holders or moving to MVI-style reducers.

quiz.q: Which reference must a ViewModel never hold?
quiz.why: The ViewModel outlives the Activity across rotation, so holding one leaks it.

quiz.q: Why expose StateFlow instead of MutableStateFlow?
options: So only the ViewModel can change state
quiz.why: A single writer keeps the data flow one-way and the state predictable.

quiz.q: What happens to viewModelScope work when the phone rotates?
quiz.why: The ViewModel survives the configuration change. The scope is cancelled only in onCleared.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of a single UiState object?
quiz.why: One value describes the whole screen, so the View cannot observe half-updated state.

quiz.q: Where should a composable collect ViewModel state?
options: Once, at the screen-level route, then pass plain data down
quiz.why: The children stay stateless, previewable and skippable.

modules.title: MVI
modules.summary: Actions, a pure reducer, one state, side effects and one-off effects.

lessons.title: MVI: actions, a reducer and one state

blocks.text: MVI stands for Model, View, Intent. Here "intent" means something the user intends to do, such as "add milk". It has nothing to do with the Android Intent class. This lesson calls them actions to avoid the clash.
The whole screen is described by one immutable state object. The only way to change it is to send an action.
A reducer is a function that takes the current state and an action and returns the next state. It does nothing else: no network, no database, no clock.
Work that touches the outside world, such as placing an order, is a side effect. It runs outside the reducer and reports back by sending another action.
Why it matters

As a screen grows, state changed from many methods in many orders becomes hard to follow. With one state, one entry point and a pure reducer, every change is a line in a log: this state, plus this action, gave that state. Bugs can be replayed, and the reducer can be tested with no mocks at all.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A bank ledger. Nobody edits the balance directly. Every change is a written transaction, and the balance is what you get by applying the transactions in order. If the balance looks wrong you read the ledger.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
This is The Composable Architecture in miniature: State, Action, a Reducer, and Effects that feed actions back. It is also Redux, which is where the reducer idea comes from.
SwiftUI
A sealed action type with an exhaustive when is a Swift enum with associated values and a switch.
Flutter
MVI is BLoC: events in, states out. A Cubit, with methods and no event classes, corresponds to plain MVVM.
UIKit
Compared with a view controller mutating its own properties from many callbacks, the state can only move through one function.

blocks.text: The user taps Checkout

items: The View sends the Checkout action
The reducer returns the state with loading = true
The View shows a spinner
The store starts the side effect: place the order
The order call finishes and the store dispatches CheckoutSucceeded or CheckoutFailed
The reducer returns the next state: an empty cart, or the error
The store sends a one-off effect to show a message

blocks.text: Both files are compiled and run. The Java file shows only the reducer, which needs nothing but the language. The Kotlin file adds the store, the side effect and one-off effects, using coroutines.
The same store inside an Android ViewModel with a Compose screen
Walkthrough

blocks.code: data class CartState(val items: Map<String, Int> = emptyMap(), val loading: Boolean = false, val error: String? = null)
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: Everything the screen needs, in one immutable value.
Every way the state can change is listed here. Some come from the user, some from finished side effects.

blocks.code: fun reduce(state: CartState, action: CartAction): CartState = when (action) { ... }
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: Exhaustive: adding an action without handling it stops the build.
Never mutate. Return a new state with the changed fields.
update is atomic, so two actions dispatched at the same moment are applied one after the other.
The side effect is started here, outside the reducer, and reports back with dispatch.
A Channel delivers each effect to one collector once, and buffers it if the collector is briefly away.
Java has no data class or copy, so immutability is enforced by hand.
With plain interfaces Java cannot prove every action is handled. Sealed interfaces in newer Java versions can.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output of MviCart.kt, in order: the empty state; milk=1; milk=2; milk=2 and bread=1; bread removed; loading=true; loading=false with error "Payment declined" and the effect "Try another card"; loading=true again; the empty cart and the effect "Order placed".
Read it as a ledger. Each state line is the previous state plus one action. The first checkout failed and the second succeeded because the fake order function was written that way.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Each action allocates a new state object. Unchanged fields are shared, not copied, so this is cheap, but very large lists inside state should be immutable persistent collections or kept in a repository.
StateFlow keeps only the latest state. If you want a history for debugging you must record it yourself.
A Channel holds undelivered effects until collected. Effects are lost on process death, which is correct for a snackbar and wrong for anything that must happen.
The store lives in a ViewModel, so the usual rule applies: no View, Activity or Context inside state, actions or effects.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Log in dispatch: the action, then the resulting state. That one line gives a complete history of the screen.
Reproduce a bug by replaying the logged actions against the reducer in a unit test.
If the UI does not update, compare old and new state with equals. Equal states are not emitted.
If an effect is missed, check that it is collected in a LaunchedEffect or with repeatOnLifecycle, and that it is not sent before the collector exists on a SharedFlow with no replay.

blocks.text: In production

items: Checkout, onboarding and multi-step forms, where many inputs and server responses interact, are the usual MVI screens.
Libraries such as Orbit and MVIKotlin package this pattern. Many teams write the thirty lines themselves.
Analytics can be attached in one place by observing actions.
Reducer tests are plain function calls: assertEquals(expectedState, reduce(startState, action)). They need no coroutines, no fakes and no Android.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Calling the network or reading the clock inside the reducer.
The reducer must be pure. Move the work to a side effect and pass its result in as an action.
Putting one-off events such as "navigate" into state as a Boolean.
It fires again on every recomposition or rotation. Send it as an effect, or model it as state that the View explicitly consumes.
Mutating a list inside state: state.items.add(x).
StateFlow sees the same object and emits nothing. Build a new collection.
One enormous state and reducer for a whole feature.
Split by screen, or compose small reducers, each owning part of the state.
An action per trivial setter, hundreds of lines of boilerplate.
Use MVI where transitions are the hard part. Simple screens do not need it.
Launching a side effect for every Checkout action while one is already running.
Let the reducer ignore the action when loading is true, or cancel the previous job.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add a Clear action to MviCart.kt. Note the compile error you get before the reducer handles it.
Make the reducer ignore Checkout when the cart is empty or when loading is already true. Run the script again.
Write three unit tests for reduce with no coroutine code at all.
Record every action in a list and add a function that rebuilds the state by folding them through the reducer.
blocks.text: Hint: actions.fold(CartState(), ::reduce)
Interview questions

blocks.title: Compare MVVM and MVI.
blocks.text: Both keep state in a ViewModel and push it one way to the UI. MVVM lets the ViewModel expose several methods and, if you allow it, several observable values. MVI restricts it to one immutable state, one entry point taking an action, and a pure reducer producing the next state, with side effects kept apart. MVI gives traceability and trivially testable transitions; MVVM gives less ceremony.

blocks.title: How do you handle side effects in MVI?
blocks.text: Outside the reducer. The store reacts to certain actions by launching work in viewModelScope and dispatches a result action when it completes. One-off UI effects are sent through a Channel. The reducer stays a pure function of state and action.

blocks.title: Why must state be immutable?
blocks.text: So that every change is a new object: StateFlow and Compose detect changes by comparison, an old state can be kept for logging or undo, and no other code can change what the UI is drawing from underneath it. Mutating in place produces no emission and no recomposition.

blocks.title: How do you test an MVI screen?
blocks.text: Reducer: plain unit tests of input and output. Store: in runTest with a fake side-effect function, dispatch actions and assert the sequence of states and effects, for example with Turbine. UI: render the stateless screen with a fixed state and assert what is shown and which action a click sends.

blocks.title: What goes wrong with a single state object on a large screen?
blocks.text: Every change emits a new state, and in Compose anything reading the whole object recomposes. Mitigate by passing each child only the fields it needs, keeping item models stable, deriving sub-states with map and distinctUntilChanged, and splitting independent parts of the screen into their own stores.

blocks.title: State or effect: how do you decide?
blocks.text: If the UI should still show it after rotation or coming back from the background, it is state: loading, errors displayed inline, form contents. If it should happen exactly once and never again, it is an effect: navigation, a toast, haptics. When losing it would be a bug, such as "payment done, go to receipt", model it as state the UI acknowledges.

quiz.q: What may a reducer do?
options: Return a new state from the old state and an action
quiz.why: A reducer is a pure function. Everything else is a side effect.

quiz.q: In MVI, what is an "intent"?
options: Something the user wants to do, expressed as an action
quiz.why: The name predates Android's Intent and is unrelated to it.

quiz.q: Where should "show a snackbar" go?
quiz.why: It must happen once. State is re-read whenever the UI recomposes or is recreated.

quiz.q: How does a finished network call change the state?
options: It writes to the state directly
It dispatches a result action that the reducer handles
quiz.why: Every change goes through the reducer, including results of side effects.

quiz.q: What is the main cost of MVI?
options: More types and boilerplate per screen
quiz.why: Actions, state, effects and a reducer are more code than a few ViewModel methods.

modules.title: Clean Architecture
modules.summary: Layers, use cases, repository interfaces and the dependency rule.

lessons.title: Clean Architecture: layers, use cases and the dependency rule

blocks.text: Clean Architecture splits an app into layers by what the code is about. The UI layer shows things. The domain layer holds the business rules. The data layer fetches and stores.
There is one rule about who may know whom: the domain knows nothing about the other two. UI and data both depend on the domain, never the other way round.

A use case is a small class for one business action, such as "get the products this customer can afford". A repository is an interface the domain declares for getting data; the data layer implements it.
Why it matters

Frameworks, screens, APIs and databases change often. Business rules change for different reasons and more slowly. If the rules depend on Retrofit or Room or Compose, every library change threatens them and they cannot be tested without those libraries. Pointing every dependency at the rules keeps them stable and testable on a plain JVM.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A restaurant kitchen. The recipes (domain) do not mention which supplier delivers the flour or what the dining room looks like. Suppliers (data) and waiters (UI) both work to the recipes. You can change supplier or redecorate without rewriting a recipe.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
The same idea as Clean Swift, VIPER's Interactor layer, or a Swift package named Domain with no UIKit import. A use case is an Interactor. The repository interface is a protocol owned by the domain.
Swift
Gradle modules enforce the rule the way Swift Package targets do: the domain module simply does not list the data module as a dependency, so the import cannot compile.
Flutter
Identical to the common Flutter layout of presentation, domain and data folders with repositories and use cases. BLoC sits where the ViewModel sits.
iOS
Mapping DTOs to domain models is the same discipline as not passing Codable response structs into views.

blocks.text: The products screen loads

items: The ViewModel calls getAffordableProducts(budget)
The use case calls repository.products() on the interface
The implementation in the data layer calls the API
DTOs are mapped to domain Products; broken rows are dropped
The use case applies the rule: in stock, within budget, sorted by price
The ViewModel maps Products to display strings in its UiState

blocks.text: Both files are compiled and run. All layers sit in one file so you can read them top to bottom; in a project each section is its own Gradle module or package.
Walkthrough

blocks.code: interface ProductRepository { suspend fun products(): List<Product> }
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: Declared in the domain. It speaks only domain types, so the domain needs nothing from the data layer.
One class, one business action, with its dependency passed in.
operator invoke lets callers write getAffordableProducts(budget) as if it were a function.
The rule lives here once. No screen re-implements it.

blocks.code: class DefaultProductRepository(private val api: FakeProductApi) : ProductRepository
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: The data layer implements the domain's interface. This is the dependency pointing inward.
The mapper is the border control. Nullable, oddly named server fields stop here and never reach the rest of the app.
The composition root: the single place that knows all layers. In an app, Hilt does this.
A test replaces the whole data layer with four lines, because the use case only knows the interface.
The same mapping guard in Java: bad server rows are dropped at the boundary.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output of the Kotlin file: with a budget of Rs 100, only Milk. With Rs 1000, Milk then Ghee, cheapest first. Bread is out of stock and the row with missing fields was dropped by the mapper. The last line is the use case running against a fake repository.
The Java file prints the same two results.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Use cases are stateless and cheap. Create them unscoped; do not make them singletons.
Repositories often hold caches and are singletons. Because they live as long as the app, they must not reference anything from the UI layer.
Mapping between DTO, entity, domain and UI models allocates objects. For ordinary screens the cost is negligible; for very large lists, map lazily or page.
More layers mean more classes. Each has a cost in build time and in what a reader must hold in their head.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: A wrong value on screen: check each border in turn. Log the DTO, the domain model, then the UiState. The layer where it first goes wrong owns the bug.
Enforce the rule with the build: a domain module with no Android plugin and no dependency on data makes a forbidden import a compile error.
Tools such as Konsist or a custom lint rule can assert "nothing in domain imports retrofit2 or androidx".
A use case that is hard to unit test is telling you it depends on something concrete. Find the constructor parameter that is not an interface or a plain value.

blocks.text: In production

items: Large apps split by feature first and by layer inside each feature: feature-cart has ui, domain and data packages, and shared models live in a core module.
The domain layer is where code is shared with iOS in Kotlin Multiplatform projects, precisely because it has no platform imports.
Use cases commonly inject a dispatcher and switch to it, so they are main-safe for every caller.
Offline-first repositories expose Flows from the database and a refresh function; use cases combine several of those flows into what a screen needs.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: A use case for every repository method, each one line that forwards the call.
Call the repository from the ViewModel. Add a use case when there is a rule, reuse or combination.
Domain models carrying @SerializedName, @Entity or Parcelable.
Those are data and UI concerns. Keep separate DTO or entity classes and map.
The repository interface placed in the data layer.
Then the domain depends on data. The interface belongs to the domain; only the implementation is in data.
Passing Context, Flow<PagingData> or other Android types through the domain.
Keep the domain pure Kotlin so it tests and reuses anywhere, including Kotlin Multiplatform.
Business rules in mappers or in the ViewModel.
If the business would name it, it is a use case or a method on a domain model.
Applying the full three-layer template to a two-screen app.
Start with UI and data. Introduce a domain layer when rules start repeating.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add a rule to CleanLayers.kt: free delivery if the total of affordable products exceeds Rs 500. Decide where it goes and why.
Replace FakeProductApi with a FakeProductDao and write a repository that reads the database first. Which layers changed?
Write a unit test for the use case with a fake repository that returns one out-of-stock and one in-stock product.
Take one ViewModel from your own experience and list every line in it that is really a business rule.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Explain the dependency rule and dependency inversion.
blocks.text: Source code dependencies point inward, toward the business rules. The domain declares interfaces for what it needs, such as a repository. Outer layers implement them. At runtime the call still flows from domain to data, but at compile time data depends on domain. That inversion means the rules never import a framework.

blocks.title: What is a use case and when do you create one?
blocks.text: A class that represents one business action, takes its collaborators by constructor, and exposes a single operator invoke. Create one when there is real logic, when logic is shared by several ViewModels, or when several repositories are combined. Do not create one that merely forwards a call.

blocks.title: Why separate DTOs, entities and domain models?
blocks.text: Each changes for a different reason: the DTO when the API changes, the entity when the schema changes, the domain model when the business changes, the UI model when the screen changes. Separate types stop a backend rename from touching every screen and let each be shaped for its job, for example non-null domain fields from nullable JSON.

blocks.title: What are the downsides of Clean Architecture?
blocks.text: More files, more mapping, more indirection to follow when reading, and slower onboarding. On small apps or simple CRUD screens it costs more than it returns. Misapplied, it produces layers of pass-through classes.

blocks.title: How does Google's recommended architecture relate to it?
blocks.text: It recommends a UI layer and a data layer with unidirectional data flow, and an optional domain layer for complex or reused logic. It is the same idea with the domain layer made a choice, not a requirement, and it places the repository in the data layer as the single source of truth.

blocks.title: How would you structure modules for a large app?
blocks.text: By feature, with a small set of core modules. Each feature module owns its UI and, if large, its own domain and data. Core modules hold shared models, the network and database setup, the design system and common utilities. Features do not depend on each other; the app module assembles them and wires navigation and DI.

quiz.q: Which layer may the domain depend on?
quiz.why: The dependency rule: everything points toward the domain, and the domain points at nothing.

quiz.q: Where is the repository interface declared?
quiz.why: The domain states what it needs. The data layer supplies an implementation.

quiz.q: What is the job of a mapper from DTO to domain model?
options: Keeping server shapes out of the rest of the app
quiz.why: It isolates the app from API naming, nullability and changes.

quiz.q: When is a use case not worth adding?
options: When it holds a business rule
When it only forwards one repository call
quiz.why: A pass-through adds indirection with no benefit.

quiz.q: How do you make the dependency rule impossible to break?
options: Separate Gradle modules with one-way dependencies
quiz.why: If the domain module does not depend on the data module, the import cannot compile.

modules.title: Dependency Injection
modules.summary: Constructor injection by hand, then Hilt modules and scopes.

lessons.title: Dependency injection: by hand, then with Hilt

blocks.text: A dependency is any object another object needs in order to work. A ViewModel needs a repository. A repository needs an API client.
Dependency injection means an object does not create what it needs. It receives it, usually through its constructor.
Something still has to create everything and pass it along. You can write that by hand in one place, called a container. Hilt is a library that generates that container for you from annotations.
Why it matters

A class that builds its own collaborators cannot be tested with a fake, cannot share an instance with another class, and hides what it depends on. Passing dependencies in makes them visible, replaceable and shareable. On Android there is an extra problem: you do not construct Activities and Fragments, the system does, so you need a way to get dependencies into them.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A chef who grows the vegetables, raises the cattle and forges the knives cannot be given different ingredients. A chef who is handed ingredients can cook with whatever arrives, including the cheap test batch. The kitchen manager who orders the ingredients is the container.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
Constructor injection is initializer injection, the same idea. iOS teams usually do it by hand or with a small container such as Factory or Swinject. Hilt has no first-party iOS equivalent.
SwiftUI
@Environment and @EnvironmentObject pass dependencies down a view tree. CompositionLocal is the Compose counterpart. Neither replaces a container for non-UI objects.
Swift
Hilt checks the whole graph at compile time: a missing dependency is a build error. Swinject resolves at runtime, so the same mistake is a crash.
Flutter
get_it is a service locator, the pattern Hilt replaces. Riverpod providers are closer to a scoped dependency graph. injectable adds code generation on top of get_it.

blocks.text: How Hilt builds a ProductsViewModel

items: The screen asks for ProductsViewModel
Hilt reads its @Inject constructor: it needs a ProductRepository
A @Binds rule says ProductRepository is DefaultProductRepository
DefaultProductRepository needs a ProductApi
A @Provides function builds ProductApi from an OkHttpClient
Both are @Singleton, so existing instances are reused
The ViewModel is constructed and returned

blocks.text: Hilt works in both languages with the same annotations. The differences are syntax only: lateinit var in Kotlin, a non-private field in Java.
The same idea by hand, compiled and run
Read this first. AppContainer is what Hilt generates for you. Both files print the same four lines.
Walkthrough
Constructor injection. The repository depends on the interface and has no idea which implementation it gets.

blocks.code: val cartRepository: CartRepository by lazy { CartRepository(analytics) }
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: A hand-made singleton: created on first use, then the same instance every time.
A factory function: a new object per call. This is "unscoped".
Triggers code generation and creates the application-level container.
Says which container a module belongs to, and therefore how long its objects can live.
Maps an interface to an implementation with no function body. Cheaper than @Provides.

blocks.code: class DefaultProductRepository @Inject constructor(private val api: ProductApi)
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: @Inject on a constructor tells Hilt how to build the class and what it needs.
Required on each Activity and Fragment that injects. Hilt generates a base class that performs the injection.
Field injection. It exists only because Android, not you, calls the Activity constructor.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output of both runnable files: analytics: add_to_cart:milk, same ViewModel: false, screen B badge: 1, test recorded: [add_to_cart:bread].
Two different ViewModels saw the same badge count because the container gave both the one repository. The test container swapped analytics for a fake and nothing else changed.

blocks.text: Memory

items: A @Singleton lives until the process dies. It must not hold an Activity, Fragment or View. If it needs a Context, inject @ApplicationContext.
Hilt enforces direction: an Activity-scoped object cannot be injected into a singleton. The build fails, which is the point.
An unscoped binding creates a new object at every injection site. That is usually what you want for stateless classes.
Hilt generates code at build time and uses no reflection at runtime, so it adds build time, not startup time.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Hilt errors are build errors. Read the last "error:" line first: it names the missing type and the chain that asked for it, in "is injected at ... is requested at ..." form.
"MissingBinding" means no @Inject constructor, @Binds or @Provides exists for that type in a component visible from the requester.
"Scoped bindings may not reference bindings with a narrower scope" means something long-lived is asking for something short-lived.
To see what was generated, open the Hilt_MainActivity and DaggerShopApp_HiltComponents classes under build/generated.

blocks.text: In production

items: Modules are grouped by layer or feature: NetworkModule, DatabaseModule, one small module per feature for its repository binding.
Coroutine dispatchers are injected with qualifiers (@IoDispatcher) so tests can substitute a test dispatcher.
In instrumented tests, @TestInstallIn replaces a production module with a fake one for the whole test run.
In multi-module apps each feature module declares its own bindings and the app module depends on all of them, so the graph is assembled without features knowing each other.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Marking everything @Singleton.
Scope only what holds shared state or is expensive. Unneeded singletons are memory that is never released.
Forgetting @AndroidEntryPoint on the hosting Activity when a Fragment has it.
Every Android class in the chain must be an entry point: Fragment and its Activity.
Reading an @Inject field before super.onCreate().
Fields are set during super.onCreate (onAttach for Fragments). Use them after that call.
Creating a dependency with new inside a class "just this once".
That instance bypasses the graph: it is not shared, not scoped and not replaceable in tests.
Passing the container itself around and calling get<T>() from anywhere.
That is a service locator. Dependencies become invisible again. Inject the specific types.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: In ManualDi.kt, add a PriceFormatter that the ViewModel needs. Count how many places you had to change. Then imagine twenty ViewModels.
Make cartViewModel() return the same instance each time. What is the name for that in Hilt terms, and when would it be wrong?
Write the Hilt module that provides a Room AppDatabase and its CartDao.
blocks.text: Hint: Two @Provides functions: one @Singleton for the database taking @ApplicationContext, one unscoped returning db.cartDao()

blocks.title: Define @IoDispatcher as a qualifier and provide Dispatchers.IO with it.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Dependency injection versus service locator?
blocks.text: With injection, dependencies are pushed into a class through its constructor, so they are visible in its signature and the class knows nothing about the container. With a locator, the class pulls dependencies from a global registry, hiding them and coupling every class to the registry. Injection is easier to test and to reason about; a locator is easier to bolt onto existing code.

blocks.title: How does Hilt relate to Dagger?
blocks.text: Hilt is built on Dagger. Dagger is a general compile-time DI framework where you define components and their relationships yourself. Hilt predefines the Android component hierarchy and scopes, generates the components, and adds entry points for Activities, Fragments, ViewModels, Services and WorkManager. You write modules and @Inject; Hilt writes the rest.

blocks.title: @Binds versus @Provides?
blocks.text: @Binds is an abstract function mapping an interface to an implementation that Hilt already knows how to construct; it generates no extra factory code. @Provides is a concrete function whose body constructs the object, needed for third-party types, builders or any creation logic.

blocks.title: How do you inject a value known only at runtime, such as a product id?
blocks.text: For ViewModels, read it from SavedStateHandle, which Hilt provides and Navigation fills with the route arguments. For other classes use assisted injection: mark the runtime parameter @Assisted, the constructor @AssistedInject, and declare an @AssistedFactory interface that Hilt implements.

blocks.title: How does DI help testing?
blocks.text: Because a class receives its collaborators, a unit test constructs it directly with fakes, no framework needed. For instrumented tests Hilt can replace whole modules with @TestInstallIn or bind test values with @BindValue, so the app runs against a fake server or in-memory database.

blocks.title: What are the costs of Hilt?
blocks.text: Build time from annotation processing (KSP reduces it), generated code that is hard to read, a learning curve for error messages, and a rigid component hierarchy that can be awkward for features with unusual lifetimes. For a very small app, a hand-written container is a legitimate choice.

quiz.q: What is constructor injection?
quiz.why: The class declares what it needs and someone else supplies it.

quiz.q: When do you need @Provides instead of @Inject constructor?
options: For types you cannot annotate, such as a Retrofit instance
quiz.why: Library classes and objects made by builders need a function that constructs them.

quiz.q: A @Singleton class asks for an @ActivityScoped object. What happens?
quiz.why: A longer-lived component cannot depend on a shorter-lived one. Hilt rejects it at compile time.

quiz.q: Why is field injection used in Activities?
options: Android constructs Activities, so you cannot pass constructor arguments
quiz.why: The framework calls the no-argument constructor, so dependencies must be set afterwards.

quiz.q: What does an unscoped binding give you?
options: A new instance each time it is injected
quiz.why: Without a scope annotation Hilt creates a fresh object for each request.

modules.title: Networking
modules.summary: Retrofit and OkHttp: requests, errors, retry.

lessons.title: Retrofit and OkHttp: calling an API

blocks.text: Your app talks to a server over HTTP. It sends a request (a method such as GET or POST, a URL, headers, sometimes a body) and receives a response (a status code, headers, a body, usually JSON).
OkHttp is the library that does the actual networking: connections, TLS, timeouts, caching, retries of the connection.
Retrofit sits on top. You describe each endpoint as a function in an interface, and Retrofit writes the code that builds the request and turns the JSON response into your Kotlin or Java objects.
Why it matters

Writing HTTP by hand means repeating URL building, JSON parsing, threading and error handling for every call. Retrofit turns an endpoint into one line and makes the API a typed interface that can be replaced by a fake in tests.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Retrofit is the order form and OkHttp is the courier. You fill in a form (which product, which page). The courier works out the route, carries it, deals with traffic and brings back a parcel. A converter unpacks the parcel into something you can use.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift

OkHttp is URLSession. Retrofit has no first-party iOS equivalent; it is closest to Moya or a hand-written API client. kotlinx.serialization is Codable: @Serializable is Codable conformance and @SerialName is a CodingKey.
Swift

A suspend API function is try await session.data(for:). On both platforms an HTTP 404 is not a thrown transport error by default, but Retrofit suspend functions do throw HttpException for non-2xx when the return type is the body.
iOS
An OkHttp Interceptor covers what you would do with a URLProtocol subclass or a request adapter. Certificate pinning is CertificatePinner here and a URLSessionDelegate challenge there.
Flutter
OkHttp plus Retrofit is dio plus retrofit.dart, which copied the annotation style. Interceptors work the same way.

blocks.text: A successful call, top to bottom and back

items: ViewModel calls repository.products(1) in viewModelScope
Retrofit builds GET /v1/products?page=1 from the annotations
Interceptors add the Authorization header and log the request
OkHttp sends it on a background thread; the coroutine is suspended, the main thread is free
The server answers 200 with JSON
The converter parses the JSON into List<ProductDto>
The repository maps DTOs to domain models and returns Success
The ViewModel sets state to Content and the UI redraws

blocks.text: Java uses Call<T> with enqueue and a callback. Kotlin uses suspend functions. Both run the request on OkHttp threads, never on the main thread.
Error mapping and retry with backoff, compiled and run
This runs without Retrofit: a small HttpException class stands in for retrofit2.HttpException. The mapping and retry logic is what you would ship.
Walkthrough
A relative path, resolved against baseUrl. Do not start it with a slash unless you mean to replace the whole base path.
A null query parameter is left out of the URL entirely.
Maps the server field name to a Kotlin property name.
An interceptor receives the request, may change it, passes it on and may inspect or change the response on the way back.
Without this, a new field added by the backend crashes every installed version of the app.
The server replied with an error status. The body may hold a machine-readable error you can parse.
No usable reply arrived. This is the "check your connection" case.
Starts the call asynchronously. execute() would block the calling thread.
With Call<T>, a 404 or 500 still arrives in onResponse. You must check the status yourself.
A cancelled call also lands in onFailure. Do not show an error for a call you cancelled.
What happens when it runs

items: The runnable model below prints, for five calls: an immediate success, a success after two retries, a 404 returned at once, a 503 retried and then reported, and a network error retried and then reported.
A suspend Retrofit function is main-safe: it suspends the caller and resumes it with the result, so you may call it from viewModelScope without withContext.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Create one OkHttpClient and one Retrofit instance and share them. Each OkHttpClient owns a connection pool and thread pool; creating one per request leaks threads and loses connection reuse.
A Java Callback implemented as an anonymous class holds its enclosing Activity until the call completes. Cancel the call in onDestroy or move it into a ViewModel.
A coroutine call is cancelled automatically when its scope is cancelled, and Retrofit cancels the underlying OkHttp call.
Large response bodies are streamed. Converting a huge body to a String (for example with body logging in release) can exhaust memory. Use Level.BASIC or NONE outside debug builds.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: App Inspection → Network Inspector in Android Studio shows every OkHttp request with headers, body and timing.

For a call that works in Postman and fails in the app, compare the exact URL and headers from the log line with the Postman request. Most often it is a missing header or a doubled or missing path segment.

java.net.UnknownHostException means DNS or no internet. SocketTimeoutException means the server was reached but slow. SSLHandshakeException means a certificate problem, often a proxy or wrong device clock.
Android blocks plain http:// traffic by default (cleartext is disabled from API 28). Use https, or a network security config for local debugging only.
Check the manifest for <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />. Without it every call fails.

blocks.text: In production

items: One Retrofit instance per base URL, provided as a singleton by dependency injection, with interceptors for auth, common headers and metrics.
A sealed result type returned from repositories, so ViewModels handle success and each failure kind with an exhaustive when.
Paged list endpoints are wrapped by Paging 3, which requests pages as the user scrolls.
Search requests are debounced and use flatMapLatest so a slow old response never overwrites a newer one.
Timeouts are chosen per use: short for search-as-you-type, longer for uploads.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: catch (e: Exception) around a suspend call.
It swallows CancellationException. Catch HttpException, IOException and SerializationException, or rethrow cancellation first.
HttpLoggingInterceptor at Level.BODY in release builds.
It writes tokens and personal data to Logcat and buffers whole bodies. Enable it for debug builds only.
A baseUrl without a trailing slash, or endpoint paths that start with a slash.
baseUrl must end with /. Keep endpoint paths relative so the base path is preserved.
Using the DTO class everywhere in the app.
Map DTOs to domain models in the repository. A backend rename then touches one file.
Refreshing an expired token inside an Interceptor with no lock.
Use an Authenticator, synchronise the refresh, and check whether another request already refreshed.
Retrying a POST blindly.
Retry only idempotent requests, or send an idempotency key the server understands.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add an endpoint that deletes a cart item by id. Which annotation and return type do you use?
blocks.text: Hint: @DELETE("v1/cart/items/{id}") suspend fun remove(@Path("id") id: Int)

blocks.title: Extend safeApiCall so 429 (too many requests) is retried like a 5xx. Run it and check the output.
Write a HeaderInterceptor that adds X-App-Version and X-Platform: android to every request.
Write a fake ProductApi that returns two products and use it to unit test ProductRepository with no network.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does Retrofit turn an interface into working code?
blocks.text: At create() it builds a java.lang.reflect.Proxy for the interface. On the first call to each method it parses the annotations into a request factory and picks a call adapter and a converter, then caches that. Each call builds an OkHttp Request, executes it and converts the body.

blocks.title: How do you model network errors for the rest of the app?
blocks.text: Catch at the repository boundary and convert to a sealed type with cases the UI can act on: success, HTTP error with code and parsed error body, network unavailable, and unexpected. ViewModels then use an exhaustive when instead of try and catch in every screen.

blocks.title: How does OkHttp caching work?
blocks.text: Give the client a Cache directory and size. OkHttp then honours HTTP cache headers from the server (Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified), serving fresh responses from disk and making conditional requests for stale ones. Only GET responses are cached. A network interceptor can rewrite headers when the server does not send them.

blocks.title: How would you implement pagination?
blocks.text: The endpoint takes a page number or cursor and returns items plus the next cursor. On Android use Paging 3: a PagingSource loads pages from the network, or a RemoteMediator writes pages to Room and the UI pages from the database. The UI collects PagingData and LazyColumn or RecyclerView requests more as the user scrolls.

blocks.title: How do you upload a file?
blocks.text: Annotate the function with @Multipart and pass @Part MultipartBody.Part built from a RequestBody that streams from the file or content URI. For large uploads that must finish in the background, run it in WorkManager with a foreground notification and report progress from a counting RequestBody.

blocks.title: What timeouts does OkHttp have?
blocks.text: connectTimeout for establishing the connection, readTimeout between bytes read, writeTimeout between bytes written, each 10 seconds by default, and callTimeout for the whole call, off by default. A slow server that keeps trickling bytes never hits readTimeout, which is why callTimeout matters for user-facing calls.

quiz.q: A suspend Retrofit function returning the body type receives HTTP 500. What happens?
quiz.why: Non-2xx responses throw HttpException when the return type is the body itself.

quiz.q: Where do you add an Authorization header to every request?
quiz.why: An interceptor sees every request once, in one place.

quiz.q: With Java Call<T>.enqueue, where does a 404 arrive?
quiz.why: onFailure is only for calls that got no response.

quiz.q: Which exception means the device could not reach the server at all?
quiz.why: IOException and its subclasses cover offline, timeout and TLS failures.

quiz.q: Why share one OkHttpClient?
quiz.why: The client owns the connection pool and dispatcher.

modules.title: Room Database
modules.summary: Entities, DAOs, Flow queries, migrations, offline-first.

lessons.title: Room: a local database you can observe

blocks.text: Every Android device ships with SQLite, a small SQL database stored in a file inside your app.
Room is a library that sits on top of SQLite. You describe a table as a class (an Entity), write the queries in an interface (a DAO), and Room generates the code that runs them.
A query can return a Flow. Room then re-runs the query and emits a new result every time the table changes, so the screen updates by itself.
Why it matters

Raw SQLite code is strings and cursors: a typo in a column name is found at runtime by a user. Room checks every query against your schema when the app is compiled, removes the cursor boilerplate, keeps queries off the main thread, and gives you observable results, which is the base of an offline-first app.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A shared notice board. Screens do not ask each other for news. Anyone who has an update pins it to the board, and everyone watching the board sees it at once. The database is the board.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: iOS
Room is closest to GRDB or a thin layer over SQLite, not to Core Data. There is no object graph, no managed object context and no faulting. Rows are plain immutable objects.
SwiftUI
A DAO method returning Flow<List<T>> does the job of a SwiftData @Query or an NSFetchedResultsController: results that update when the store changes.
Swift
Core Data lightweight migration is automatic for simple changes. Room requires an explicit Migration, or an AutoMigration declaration backed by exported schema files.
Flutter
Room is what drift is to Flutter: typed queries generated at build time, with streams of results. sqflite corresponds to using SQLite directly.

blocks.text: A write that updates a screen nobody told

items: The basket screen collects dao.observeAll()
Room runs the query on a background thread and emits the rows
Another screen calls dao.upsert(item)
Room commits the write and marks cart_items as changed
The invalidation tracker re-runs every active query that reads cart_items
The Flow emits the new list and the basket screen redraws

blocks.text: Java DAOs return LiveData and use blocking methods that you must call from a background executor. Kotlin DAOs use suspend functions and Flow.
Single source of truth, compiled and run
A MutableStateFlow stands in for the Room table so the file runs on a plain JVM. The repository shape is what you would write against a real DAO.
Walkthrough
This class is a table. Each property is a column.
Uniquely identifies a row. Upsert uses it to decide between insert and update.
Not suspend. It returns at once with a Flow that runs the query when collected and again after every change to the table.
Checked at compile time. A wrong column name fails the build, not the user.
Insert, or update when the primary key already exists. suspend makes Room run it off the main thread.
Observers see either the old rows or the new rows, never the empty table in between.
Raise the version on every schema change. Exported schema files let you test migrations and use AutoMigration.

blocks.code: db.execSQL("ALTER TABLE cart_items ADD COLUMN updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0")
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: A migration is plain SQL. The new column must match the Entity exactly, including NOT NULL and the default.
The Java counterpart of a Flow query. Room loads it on a background thread and delivers on the main thread.
Blocking. Called on the main thread, Room throws IllegalStateException unless you opted in with allowMainThreadQueries(), which you should not.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output of the runnable model: ui: (empty), refresh ok=true, ui: Milk x2, Bread x1, ui: Milk x2, Bread x2, refresh ok=false.
Read the last line carefully. The refresh failed and nothing was printed for the UI, because the cached rows are still correct and still on screen.

blocks.text: Memory

items: Build one database instance per process. Each instance has its own connection pool and invalidation tracker; two instances on one file do not see each other's changes.
A query result is fully loaded into memory as objects. For large tables select only the columns you need, add LIMIT, or page with Paging 3.
A Flow query holds a database observer while it is collected. Collect with lifecycle awareness so it is released in the background.
An index speeds up reads on a column and slows down every write to the table. Add one for columns used in WHERE, ORDER BY or joins, after measuring.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: App Inspection → Database Inspector shows tables live, lets you run SQL, and can re-run a DAO query from the gutter icon.
When a Flow does not re-emit, check that the write went through the same database instance and the same table that the query reads.
"Room cannot verify the data integrity" means the schema changed without a version increase. During development, uninstall the app; before release, write the migration.
Prefix a slow query with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN in the inspector. "SCAN TABLE" on a large table means an index is missing.
Pull the file for offline inspection: adb exec-out run-as <package> cat databases/app.db > app.db (debuggable builds only).

blocks.text: In production

items: The basket badge in an e-commerce app is observeCount() collected in a top-level ViewModel. Any screen that changes the cart updates the badge with no extra code.
Product lists use Paging 3 with a RemoteMediator: the network fills Room page by page and the UI pages from Room.
Writes made offline go into a pending-operations table and are sent by WorkManager when the network returns.
Sensitive data is kept out of the database, or the database is encrypted with SQLCipher using a key from the Android Keystore.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: Changing an Entity and forgetting to raise the version or add a Migration.
Raise the version, add a Migration or AutoMigration, and test it with MigrationTestHelper against the exported schema.
Shipping fallbackToDestructiveMigration() to production.
It silently deletes user data on upgrade. Use it only for a pure cache that can be refetched.
Marking a DAO method that returns Flow as suspend.
A Flow-returning query is a normal function. Collecting it is what suspends.
Many inserts in a loop with no transaction.
Each insert commits separately, which is slow and notifies observers every time. Insert a list, or wrap the loop in withTransaction.
Exposing Entity classes to the UI layer.
Map to domain or UI models in the repository so a schema change does not ripple through every screen.
Showing the network response directly and also saving it.
Now there are two sources of truth that drift apart. Save, and let the UI read only from the database.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: Add a column note: String with default empty text. Write MIGRATION_2_3 and raise the version.
blocks.text: Hint: ALTER TABLE cart_items ADD COLUMN note TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT ''

blocks.title: Write a DAO query that returns the three most recently updated items as a Flow.
In SingleSourceOfTruth.kt, make addOne fail to sync and roll the quantity back. Where does that logic belong?
Add an orders table with a foreign key to a users table. Write a query that returns each user with their order count.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does Room know to re-emit a Flow?
blocks.text: Room creates triggers that record which tables were modified in a tracking table. After a transaction commits, the InvalidationTracker checks that record and notifies observers of the affected tables, and each active Flow re-runs its query. The granularity is the table, not the row, so a query re-runs even if its own result did not change.

blocks.title: How do you write and test a migration?
blocks.text: Raise the version, write a Migration with the SQL that turns the old schema into the new one, register it with addMigrations, and export schemas to a folder under version control. In an instrumented test, MigrationTestHelper creates the database at the old version, inserts rows, runs the migration and validates the result against the exported schema.

blocks.title: Room, DataStore or SharedPreferences?
blocks.text: Room for structured, queryable or relational data and lists. DataStore for a small set of settings or flags, with transactional writes and a Flow API. SharedPreferences is the legacy key-value store: synchronous reads, apply() failures are silent, and it can cause ANRs; use DataStore for new code.

blocks.title: How do you model relationships?
blocks.text: Store foreign keys, declared with @ForeignKey and indexed. To read a parent with its children use a data class with @Embedded for the parent and @Relation for the children, queried inside a @Transaction. Many-to-many needs a junction table. Room does not lazy-load: you ask explicitly for what you need.

blocks.title: What is a TypeConverter and when is it the wrong tool?
blocks.text: A pair of functions that convert a type SQLite cannot store, such as Instant or an enum, to one it can. It is the wrong tool for lists of objects serialised to JSON in one column: you cannot query or index inside it. Use a child table.

blocks.title: How do you keep the local database in sync with the server?
blocks.text: Reads: fetch, then write to the database in one transaction; the UI observes the database. Writes: apply locally first for instant feedback, record a pending operation, send it with WorkManager under a network constraint, and reconcile with the server response. Decide the conflict rule in advance: last write wins, server wins, or merge by field.

quiz.q: What does a DAO function returning Flow<List<T>> do when the table changes?
quiz.why: Room re-runs the whole query and emits the full new result.

quiz.q: You add a column and do not change the database version. What happens for existing users?
options: Crash at open: the schema hash does not match
quiz.why: Room detects that the stored schema differs from the compiled one and throws IllegalStateException.

quiz.q: What does @Transaction guarantee for replaceAll?
options: Observers never see the half-finished state
It runs on the main thread
quiz.why: All statements commit together, and invalidation happens once after the commit.

quiz.q: In an offline-first app, where does the UI read from?
quiz.why: A single source of truth: network results are written to the database and observed from there.

quiz.q: When does Room verify your SQL?
quiz.why: The annotation processor checks every @Query against the entities.

modules.title: DataStore
modules.summary: Preferences DataStore, transactions, defaults and what not to store.

blocks.text: DataStore saves small pieces of data: a theme choice, whether onboarding was seen, the last selected city. It is for settings, not for lists of things.
You read it as a Flow, so the screen updates by itself when a value changes. You write it with a suspend function, so it never blocks the main thread.
There are two kinds. Preferences DataStore stores keys and values, like a small dictionary. Proto DataStore stores one typed object that you define.
It replaces SharedPreferences, the older tool for the same job.
Why it matters

SharedPreferences reads the whole file synchronously the first time it is used, often on the main thread; its apply() can block the main thread later and hides write failures; and it gives no way to observe one value safely. DataStore was built on coroutines and Flow to remove those problems: asynchronous by design, each write a transaction, errors reported.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A notebook kept at the front desk. To change a line you hand the clerk a note saying "change this", and the clerk rewrites the page as a whole, one request at a time, so two people can never half-overwrite each other. Anyone can ask to be told whenever the page changes.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: iOS
Preferences DataStore covers what UserDefaults does. UserDefaults is synchronous and observed through KVO or @AppStorage; DataStore is asynchronous and observed through a Flow.
SwiftUI
@AppStorage("dark_theme") is the closest experience: a stored setting that drives the UI. On Android you collect a Flow<Boolean> with collectAsStateWithLifecycle.
iOS
Neither UserDefaults nor DataStore is for secrets. Tokens belong in the Keychain on iOS and, on Android, in storage encrypted with a Keystore key.
Flutter
shared_preferences on Android is backed by SharedPreferences or DataStore depending on the API used. The model is the same key-value store without the Flow.

blocks.text: setDarkTheme(true)

items: The UI calls the suspend function from a coroutine
edit { } waits its turn: writes run one at a time
The current preferences are read into a mutable copy
Your block changes the copy
The whole file is written to a temporary file, then swapped in atomically
data emits the new snapshot and every collector receives it

blocks.text: DataStore is built on coroutines. Java uses it through the RxJava wrapper, so reads are a Flowable and writes return a Single. The two are not equivalent in style, only in what is stored.
DataStore's two promises as a model, compiled and run
A StateFlow of immutable snapshots and a Mutex around writes. It keeps data in memory only; the real DataStore also writes the file atomically.
Walkthrough

blocks.code: private val Context.dataStore: DataStore<Preferences> by preferencesDataStore(name = "settings")
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: A property delegate at the top level of a file. It guarantees one instance per process for this file name.
A typed key. The type parameter stops you reading a Boolean as an Int.

blocks.code: .catch { error -> if (error is IOException) emit(emptyPreferences()) else throw error }
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: A corrupt or unreadable file should fall back to defaults, not crash the app. Other errors are bugs and are rethrown.
A key that was never written is absent. The default is applied here, in code.
A suspend function. The block receives a mutable copy, and the write is committed when the block returns.
Read and write inside one edit block are a single transaction, so concurrent increments are not lost.
Java builds the store explicitly. Create it once and share it.
The Java write: convert to mutable, change, and return it wrapped in a Single.
What happens when it runs

items: Real output of the model: dark theme false, then true. Writing a different key, launch_count, produced no dark theme line, because distinctUntilChanged filtered it. After 100 concurrent increments on several threads the count is 101, starting from 1: none was lost. Finally dark theme false again.
Without the lock around read-modify-write, that 101 would be a smaller, changing number.

blocks.text: Memory

items: DataStore keeps the whole file content in memory and rewrites the whole file on every edit. That is why it suits a handful of settings and not thousands of entries.
Create exactly one DataStore per file per process. A second instance on the same file throws IllegalStateException.
There is no synchronous read. Code that needs a value before the first frame must either show a default first or keep the splash screen until the first emission.
Preferences DataStore is not multi-process safe by default. A multi-process variant exists for apps that need it.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: The file is at /data/data/<package>/files/datastore/<name>.preferences_pb. Pull it with adb exec-out run-as <package> cat files/datastore/settings.preferences_pb on a debuggable build.
"There are multiple DataStores active for the same file" means two instances were created. Find the second creation site.
If a setting appears to reset, check for a catch that emits empty preferences and hides a real read error. Log inside it.
To observe values while developing, collect data in a debug-only coroutine and log each snapshot.

blocks.text: In production

items: Theme, language override, notification toggles, onboarding-completed flags and the last selected delivery address id are typical contents.
A SettingsRepository wraps DataStore and exposes typed Flows and suspend setters, so no other class knows about keys.
Feature flag values fetched from a server are cached in DataStore so the next start uses the last known values.
Proto DataStore is chosen when settings form one object with enums and nested fields, giving compile-time types and schema evolution through protocol buffers.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: runBlocking { dataStore.data.first() } on the main thread to get a value synchronously.
It blocks the UI on disk I/O, the very problem DataStore removes. Collect the Flow and render a default until it emits.
Storing a list of objects as a JSON string in one preference.
That is a database. Use Room, or Proto DataStore for one structured settings object.
Storing an auth token in plain DataStore.
The file is private to the app but not encrypted. Encrypt with a key from the Android Keystore.
Creating the DataStore inside an Activity or a function, so several instances exist.
Declare the delegate once at file top level, or provide a singleton through dependency injection.
Reading a value, then writing based on it in a separate edit.
Another write can land in between. Do the read and the write inside the same edit block.
Forgetting to migrate existing SharedPreferences.
Pass SharedPreferencesMigration when creating the DataStore so existing users keep their settings.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: In DataStoreModel.kt, remove the Mutex and run it several times. Record the launch_count values you get.
Add a "language" string setting to SettingsStore with a default of "system".
Write the code that keeps the splash screen visible until the theme setting has been read once.
blocks.text: Hint: splashScreen.setKeepOnScreenCondition { !themeLoaded }

blocks.title: Write a SharedPreferences to DataStore migration for a key named "dark_mode".

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Why was DataStore introduced when SharedPreferences existed?
blocks.text: SharedPreferences has a synchronous API that does disk I/O, loads the whole file on first access, can block the main thread on apply() during lifecycle transitions, reports parse errors as runtime exceptions, has no transactional read-modify-write, and its change listener is easy to leak. DataStore is asynchronous through coroutines and Flow, makes every write a transaction, surfaces I/O errors in the flow, and is safe to call from the main thread.

blocks.title: Preferences DataStore versus Proto DataStore?
blocks.text: Preferences: untyped storage accessed with typed keys, no schema, quickest to adopt, defaults handled in code. Proto: one message type defined in a .proto file, generated classes, compile-time field types, defaults and schema evolution from protocol buffers, at the cost of build setup. Choose Proto when settings have structure or must stay consistent as a group.

blocks.title: How does DataStore guarantee consistency?
blocks.text: All writes go through a single actor-like queue so they run one at a time. Each edit reads the current value, applies your transform, writes the complete new value to a scratch file and renames it over the original, which is atomic on the file system. Readers always see a complete snapshot, old or new.

blocks.title: How do you get a setting synchronously at startup, for example the theme?
blocks.text: You do not read synchronously. Options: keep the system splash screen on with setKeepOnScreenCondition until the first emission; render with a neutral default and update; or, for the day and night theme specifically, let AppCompatDelegate persist the night mode itself. Blocking with runBlocking on the main thread reintroduces the problem DataStore solves.

blocks.title: How do you migrate from SharedPreferences?
blocks.text: Pass SharedPreferencesMigration(context, "old_prefs_name") in the produceMigrations parameter of the delegate. On first access DataStore copies the keys across and deletes the old file. After that, remove every remaining use of the old preferences so two sources of truth do not coexist.

blocks.title: Where do you store sensitive values?
blocks.text: Not in plain DataStore or SharedPreferences. Encrypt the value with a key generated in the Android Keystore, which keeps key material in secure hardware where available, and store only the ciphertext. Prefer short-lived tokens so a leak has limited value.

quiz.q: What is DataStore for?
quiz.why: It loads and rewrites the whole file, so it suits a small amount of data.

quiz.q: How do you read a value from DataStore?
quiz.why: data is a Flow that emits the current snapshot and every later change.

quiz.q: Why put a read and its dependent write in one edit block?
options: So the pair is one transaction and no update is lost
It is required by the compiler
quiz.why: Edits run one at a time, each seeing the result of the previous one.

quiz.q: What happens if you create two DataStore instances for the same file?
quiz.why: DataStore detects it and throws, because two writers would corrupt the file.

quiz.q: Which is a real weakness of SharedPreferences that DataStore fixes?
options: Synchronous disk I/O that can block the main thread
quiz.why: The first read and pending apply() writes can block the main thread and cause ANRs.

modules.title: Flow and StateFlow
modules.summary: Cold and hot flows, operators, debounced search, lifecycle-aware collection.

blocks.text: A suspend function returns one value, later. A Flow returns many values, over time.
A plain Flow is cold: it is a recipe. Nothing happens until someone collects it, and each collector gets its own run from the start.

StateFlow and SharedFlow are hot: they exist whether or not anyone is collecting, and all collectors share the same values. StateFlow always holds one current value. SharedFlow is a broadcast with no current value.
Operators such as map, filter, debounce and flatMapLatest transform a flow into another flow.
Why it matters

Screens show things that change: a cart count, search results as you type, a download percentage, rows in a database. Flow gives every layer one way to say "this value changes over time", with cancellation and threading handled by coroutines.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A cold Flow is a film on demand: each viewer presses play and watches from the beginning. A StateFlow is a scoreboard: look at any moment and you see the current score. A SharedFlow is a live radio broadcast: tune in late and you missed what was said.
If you know iOS or Flutter

rows: Swift
A cold Flow is an AsyncSequence built with AsyncStream. collect is for await. Cancellation follows the task in both.
Swift
In Combine terms: StateFlow is CurrentValueSubject, SharedFlow is PassthroughSubject, flatMapLatest is switchToLatest, debounce is debounce, stateIn is roughly share plus a stored latest value.
SwiftUI
collectAsStateWithLifecycle is what @Published with ObservableObject, or Observation, does for you: a changing value drives a redraw.
Flutter
A cold Flow is a single-subscription Stream from an async* function. A broadcast StreamController is a SharedFlow. BehaviorSubject from rxdart is a StateFlow.

blocks.text: What collect does to a cold flow

items: collect is called on the last operator
Each operator collects the one above it, up to the source
The flow { } block starts running
emit(value) passes the value down through each operator to your collect lambda
emit suspends until the collector has finished with the value
When the block ends, collect returns

blocks.text: Java has no Flow. The closest tools are LiveData with Transformations.switchMap and a hand-written debounce. They are not equivalent: switchMap stops listening to the old result but does not cancel the request behind it, and LiveData has no backpressure or threading operators.
Cold flow, StateFlow, SharedFlow and search, compiled and run
Four small experiments. Read the output under the code against each numbered section.
Walkthrough
Not a suspend function. Calling it only creates the recipe. The block runs when collected.
Each operator returns a new cold flow. Nothing has executed yet.
A terminal operator. It suspends until the flow completes.
A hot flow that needs an initial value and always has a current one, readable with .value.

blocks.code: cartCount.value = 2   // equal to the current value
blocks.caption: Kotlin

blocks.text: StateFlow compares with equals and skips equal values. This is why state objects should be immutable.
Default replay is 0: a value emitted with no collector is gone.
Holds a value and emits it only if no newer one arrives within the window.
Switches to a new inner flow for each value and cancels the previous inner flow.
Runs the pipeline once in the ViewModel scope and shares the latest value. It stops 5 seconds after the last collector leaves, so rotation does not restart it.
Each new query swaps the observed LiveData. The request for the old query keeps running unless the repository cancels it.
What happens when it runs

items: Section 1: "producer started" is printed twice, once per collector. That is what cold means.
Section 2: the late collector first sees 2, the current value, then 3. Setting 2 again produced nothing.
Section 3: the first event was emitted before anyone collected and never appears.
Section 4: only "mil" is searched after the fast typing. The search for "milk" starts and is cancelled, so its results never print.

blocks.text: Memory

items: A cold flow holds nothing between collections. A hot flow lives as long as its scope; one created in GlobalScope or a singleton never ends.
A collector that keeps running in the background keeps the upstream work alive: database observers, location updates, sockets. Collect with repeatOnLifecycle or collectAsStateWithLifecycle.
emit suspends until the collector is ready. That is backpressure: a slow collector slows the producer. buffer(), conflate() and collectLatest change that trade-off.
flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) changes the thread of everything above it in the chain, never of the collector.

blocks.text: Debugging

items: Put .onEach { Log.d("Search", "after debounce: $it") } between operators to see where values stop.
If a pipeline never runs, look for the missing terminal operator: nothing happens without collect, launchIn or stateIn.
If work runs twice, a cold flow is being collected twice. Share it with stateIn or shareIn.
Test with runTest and the Turbine library: flow.test { assertEquals(x, awaitItem()) }. Virtual time makes debounce tests instant.

blocks.text: In production

items: ViewModels combine several repository flows into one UiState: combine(cartFlow, userFlow, promoFlow) { ... }.stateIn(...).
Room and DataStore already return flows, so the cart badge, theme setting and login state update everywhere with no manual refresh.
Listener-based SDKs (location, connectivity, Firebase) are wrapped once in callbackFlow with awaitClose to unregister the listener.
A download or upload reports progress as Flow<Int>, with conflate() so a slow UI skips to the latest percentage.

blocks.text: Common mistakes

rows: lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect { } } in a Fragment or Activity.
It keeps collecting while the app is in the background. Wrap the collect in repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED).
A function that returns a new stateIn or shareIn flow on every call.
Each call starts a new upstream. Create the shared flow once as a property.
Mutating a list held in a StateFlow and assigning the same list back.
equals says nothing changed, so nothing is emitted. Assign a new list: state.update { it + item }.
Calling withContext inside flow { } to emit from another dispatcher.
It throws an IllegalStateException about flow invariants. Use flowOn, or channelFlow when you need to emit from several coroutines.
Using SharedFlow with replay 0 for navigation events.
An emission during rotation, with no collector, is lost. Use state that the UI acknowledges, or a Channel.
try and catch around collect to handle upstream errors.
It also catches errors thrown by your own collector code. Use the catch operator, which sees only upstream errors.

blocks.text: Exercises

blocks.title: In Flows.kt, replace flatMapLatest with flatMapMerge and run it. Explain the extra output.
Change MutableSharedFlow<String>() to replay = 1. What does the late listener print now?
Write a countdown: fun countdown(from: Int): Flow<Int> that emits once per second and completes at zero.
Combine two StateFlows, items and query, into a filtered list flow.
blocks.text: Hint: combine(items, query) { list, q -> list.filter { it.contains(q, ignoreCase = true) } }

blocks.title: Wrap a callback API in callbackFlow. What happens if you forget awaitClose?

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is the difference between a cold and a hot flow, and how do you convert one to the other?
blocks.text: A cold flow runs its producer per collector and only while collected. A hot flow is active independently and shares emissions. stateIn and shareIn turn a cold flow into a hot one by collecting it once in a given scope.

blocks.title: StateFlow versus SharedFlow?
blocks.text: StateFlow: one current value, required initial value, new collectors get the latest, equal values are skipped, .value is readable synchronously. SharedFlow: configurable replay and buffer, no initial value, emits every value including duplicates. StateFlow is a SharedFlow with replay 1, drop-oldest overflow and distinctness.

blocks.title: How does backpressure work in Flow?
blocks.text: By suspension. emit does not return until the downstream has processed the value, so a slow collector naturally slows the producer. buffer() lets the producer run ahead into a channel, conflate() keeps only the latest, and collectLatest cancels the handler for the previous value when a new one arrives.

blocks.title: Why is flowOn needed, and why can you not use withContext inside a flow builder?
blocks.text: Flow preserves context: values must be emitted in the context of the collector, so that a collector on the main thread always receives on the main thread. withContext around emit breaks that and is rejected at runtime. flowOn runs the upstream in another context and hands values over through a channel.

blocks.title: How do you combine several flows?
blocks.text: combine emits whenever any input emits, using the latest of each: right for UI state built from several sources. zip pairs values one to one. merge interleaves flows of the same type. flatMapLatest, flatMapConcat and flatMapMerge map each value to a flow and differ in whether the previous one is cancelled, awaited or run in parallel.

blocks.title: How do you convert a callback API into a Flow?
blocks.text: callbackFlow { val listener = ...; api.register(listener); awaitClose { api.unregister(listener) } }, sending values with trySend. awaitClose keeps the flow open and is where the listener is removed when the collector cancels. Without it the builder throws, because the flow would complete at once and leak the listener.

blocks.title: How do you test a Flow?
blocks.text: In runTest, collect to a list with toList() for finite flows, or use Turbine for step-by-step assertions on hot or infinite flows. Inject test dispatchers so delay and debounce run on virtual time. For StateFlow built with WhileSubscribed, the test must be collecting or the upstream never starts.

quiz.q: A cold flow is collected by two collectors. How many times does its producer block run?
quiz.why: Each collection starts the block from the beginning.

quiz.q: What does a new StateFlow collector receive first?
quiz.why: StateFlow replays its one current value to each new collector.

quiz.q: What does flatMapLatest do when a new value arrives?
options: Cancels the previous inner flow and starts a new one
quiz.why: Only the flow for the latest value stays active.

quiz.q: Which operator changes the thread the upstream runs on?
quiz.why: flowOn affects the operators above it and leaves the collector on its own context.

quiz.q: Setting a MutableStateFlow to a value equal to its current one does what?
quiz.why: StateFlow skips values that are equal to the current one.

questions.q: Is Java pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?
questions.a: Always pass-by-value. For primitives the value is copied. For objects the reference is copied, so the method can mutate the object but cannot make the caller point at a different one.

points.title: Follow-up
