items: Show a method that tries to swap two Integer arguments and explain why it fails.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Relate this to defensive copies: returning an internal List from a getter leaks mutability because the caller gets a copy of the reference.

questions.q: What is the difference between == and equals()?
questions.a: == compares primitive values or object addresses. equals() compares content as defined by the class. Strings, boxed numbers and data holders must be compared with equals().

points.title: Follow-up
items: Why does Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b print true while 128 prints false?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The Integer cache covers -128 to 127 by default, so autoboxed values in that range share one object. Never rely on it.

questions.q: What is autoboxing and why can it hurt on Android?
questions.a: The compiler converts between int and Integer automatically. Each boxing can allocate an object, which adds garbage collection pressure in loops and collections. Android provides SparseIntArray and similar classes to avoid it.

questions.q: What is short-circuit evaluation?
questions.a: && does not evaluate its right side when the left is false, and || does not when the left is true. This makes checks such as list != null && !list.isEmpty() safe. & and | on booleans always evaluate both sides.

questions.q: Difference between while and do-while?
questions.a: while checks the condition before each turn, so the body may run zero times. do-while checks after, so the body runs at least once.

questions.q: Can a switch use strings? What are its limits?
questions.a: Yes, since Java 7, along with integral types, enums and their wrappers. Classic switch compares with equals for strings, throws NullPointerException on null, and cannot switch on long, float or arbitrary objects. Newer Java versions add arrow cases, switch expressions and pattern matching.

questions.q: Why are Strings immutable in Java?
questions.a: So they can be shared safely between threads and pooled, so their hash code can be cached (making them good map keys), and for security, since a file path or class name cannot change after it was checked.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What is the string pool and what does intern() do?

questions.q: String, StringBuilder, StringBuffer?
questions.a: String is immutable. StringBuilder is mutable and not synchronised: the normal choice. StringBuffer is the older, synchronised version, rarely needed.

questions.q: How do arrays differ from ArrayList?
questions.a: An array has a fixed length, can hold primitives directly and has no methods beyond length. ArrayList grows, holds only objects (so numbers are boxed) and offers add, remove, contains and so on. ArrayList is backed by an array that it replaces with a larger one when full.

questions.q: What is the difference between a static nested class and an inner class?
questions.a: An inner (non-static) class holds an implicit reference to its enclosing instance and can use its fields. A static nested class does not. On Android, an inner class Handler, Runnable or AsyncTask that outlives its Activity leaks the Activity through that hidden reference.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How would you fix a leaking inner Handler?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Static nested class plus WeakReference was the classic fix. Today the answer is lifecycle-aware scopes: lifecycleScope or viewModelScope cancel the work instead of merely weakening the reference.

questions.q: What happens, in order, when you call new?
questions.a: Memory is allocated and zeroed, field initialisers and instance initialiser blocks run in source order, then the constructor body runs. If there is a superclass, its constructor runs first.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What goes wrong if a superclass constructor calls an overridable method?

questions.q: Explain the four access levels in Java.
questions.a: private: same class. No modifier (package-private): same package. protected: same package plus subclasses. public: everywhere. Prefer the narrowest level that works.

questions.q: Abstract class or interface: how do you choose?
questions.a: Use an interface for a capability that unrelated classes can share. Use an abstract class when subclasses share state or a partly implemented algorithm. Since Java 8 interfaces can carry default methods but still cannot hold instance state.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What is the diamond problem and how does Java resolve it for default methods?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: If two interfaces supply the same default method the class must override it and can call A.super.method(). Class methods always win over interface defaults.

questions.q: What is the difference between overloading and overriding?
questions.a: Overloading: same name, different parameter list, chosen at compile time. Overriding: a subclass replaces an inherited method with the same signature, chosen at runtime.

questions.q: Why is composition often preferred over inheritance?
questions.a: Inheritance couples the subclass to the internals of its parent and fixes the relationship at compile time. Composition lets you swap collaborators, test them separately and avoid fragile base classes.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: On Android this is why logic moved out of BaseActivity classes into ViewModels, delegates and lifecycle observers.

questions.q: Checked versus unchecked exceptions: when do you use each?
questions.a: Checked for conditions a correct program must expect and can recover from, such as a missing file or a failed network call. Unchecked for programming errors, such as a null argument or an illegal state. Many modern codebases prefer unchecked throughout to avoid signatures cluttered with throws, which is also what Kotlin chose.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Checked exceptions do not compose with lambdas and streams, which is a practical reason for the shift.

questions.q: What can a Java enum do beyond listing constants?
questions.a: Hold fields and constructors, define methods, give each constant its own method body, implement interfaces, and be used in switch, EnumSet and EnumMap. Because each constant is a guaranteed single instance, an enum is also the simplest thread-safe singleton.

questions.q: What are the annotation retention policies?
questions.a: SOURCE: discarded by the compiler, used by lint and code generators (@Override). CLASS: kept in the class file but not visible to reflection, the default. RUNTIME: available through reflection while the program runs, used by frameworks.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How does an annotation processor differ from reflection?

questions.q: How does HashMap work internally?
questions.a: It keeps an array of buckets. The hashCode of the key picks a bucket; equals finds the exact entry inside it. Collisions are chained in a linked list that becomes a balanced tree once a bucket holds 8 or more entries and the table has at least 64 buckets. When the load factor (0.75 by default) is exceeded the table doubles and entries are redistributed.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What happens if two unequal keys return the same hashCode? What if equal keys return different hashCodes?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Equal objects with different hash codes break the contract: lookups miss. That is why data classes and records generate both together.

questions.q: ArrayList or LinkedList?
questions.a: ArrayList for almost everything: index access is constant time and iteration is cache friendly. LinkedList only wins for frequent inserts or removals at the ends, and ArrayDeque usually beats it there too.

questions.q: What are wildcards ? extends T and ? super T for?
questions.a: They make generic APIs flexible. A producer of values is declared with extends (you can read T out). A consumer is declared with super (you can put T in). The mnemonic is PECS: producer extends, consumer super.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Kotlin expresses the same idea at the declaration with out and in, which removes most wildcards from call sites.

questions.q: Explain PECS.
questions.a: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. If a parameter only produces values for you to read, declare it ? extends T so more specific collections are accepted. If it only consumes values you write, declare it ? super T so more general collections are accepted. If you do both, use plain T.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Kotlin moves this to the declaration: interface Source<out T> and Sink<in T>, so call sites need no wildcards.

questions.q: What are the consequences of type erasure?
questions.a: No runtime check of type arguments, no generic array creation, no instanceof with a parameterised type, overloads that differ only in type argument clash, and reflection-based libraries need a type token to know the full type.

questions.q: Why are arrays covariant and generics invariant?
questions.a: Arrays were made covariant in Java 1.0 so methods such as sort(Object[]) could exist before generics, at the price of a runtime check on every store. Generics came later and chose compile-time safety, since erasure makes a runtime check impossible.

questions.q: How is a lambda different from an anonymous inner class?
questions.a: A lambda can only implement a functional interface, has no this of its own (this refers to the enclosing object), and is compiled with invokedynamic, so no extra class file is created per lambda. An anonymous class can implement any interface or extend a class and has its own this and state.

questions.q: map versus flatMap?
questions.a: map turns each element into one result. flatMap turns each element into a stream of results and flattens them into one stream, for example orders into all their line items. Optional has both with the same meaning.

questions.q: When should you not use parallel streams?
questions.a: When the work is small, when the source splits poorly (LinkedList, I/O), when operations have side effects or depend on order, and inside servers, because parallel streams share the common ForkJoinPool with everything else in the process and one slow task starves the rest.

questions.q: What is Optional for, and what is it not for?
questions.a: It is a return type that makes "no result" explicit and offers map, filter and orElse to handle it. It is not a general replacement for null: it should not be used for fields, parameters or collections, and it is not serialisable.

questions.q: How does garbage collection work in the JVM?
questions.a: It is tracing and generational. From the GC roots it marks every reachable object; the rest is garbage. New objects go to the young generation, which is collected often by copying the few survivors; long-lived objects are promoted to the old generation, collected less often. Modern collectors such as G1 and ZGC do most work concurrently to keep pauses short.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What are GC roots?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Roots include thread stacks, static fields, JNI references and monitors. On Android an Activity leak is always "a root still reaches it", and the fix is to cut that reference.

questions.q: Explain class loading.
questions.a: A class is loaded the first time it is needed. Loaders form a parent chain: bootstrap, platform, application. A loader asks its parent first, so core classes cannot be replaced. After loading, the class is verified, its static fields get default values, and its static initialisers run once, thread-safely.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: That one-time, thread-safe initialisation is what makes the "holder" idiom and enum singletons safe without locks.

questions.q: What is the difference between stack and heap memory?
questions.a: Each thread has its own stack of frames for method calls; it holds parameters, local primitives and references, and is reclaimed when methods return. The heap is shared, holds all objects, and is reclaimed by the collector. StackOverflowError means too many frames; OutOfMemoryError means the heap (or another memory area) is exhausted.

questions.q: What is the JIT compiler?
questions.a: The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode and counts how often methods and loops run. Hot code is compiled to optimised machine code while the program runs, using what it observed, such as which implementation a call really uses. This is why Java code speeds up after warm-up.

questions.q: What is the difference between synchronized, volatile and AtomicInteger?
questions.a: synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility for a block of code. volatile gives visibility for a single field, nothing more. Atomic classes give lock-free atomic updates of a single value using compare-and-swap.

points.title: Follow-up
items: When would you choose a ReentrantLock over synchronized?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: ReentrantLock adds tryLock with timeout, interruptible waits, fairness and multiple Conditions. On hot paths, prefer confining state to one thread over sharing and locking it.

questions.q: What causes an ANR and how do you investigate one?
questions.a: The main thread did not respond in time: about 5 seconds for an input event, with shorter limits for BroadcastReceivers and Service start. Pull the ANR trace from Play Console or /data/anr, find the main thread stack and see what it is blocked on: disk or network I/O, a lock held by another thread, a long loop or a binder call.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Many ANRs are lock contention where main waits on a monitor held by a background thread doing I/O. The fix is to stop sharing that lock, not to make the I/O faster.

questions.q: Explain Handler, Looper and MessageQueue.
questions.a: A Looper runs a loop on one thread, pulling Messages and Runnables from its MessageQueue. A Handler posts work to that queue. The main thread has a Looper created by the system, which is how other threads hand work back to the UI.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How do Kotlin coroutines on Dispatchers.Main relate to this?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Dispatchers.Main is a Handler on the main Looper. Dispatchers.Main.immediate skips the post when already on the main thread.

questions.q: What is a thread pool and how do you size one?
questions.a: A set of reusable threads fed from a queue. CPU-bound work wants about as many threads as cores. I/O-bound work can use more, because threads spend their time waiting. Unbounded pools risk memory exhaustion.

questions.q: synchronized versus ReentrantLock?
questions.a: Both give mutual exclusion and are reentrant. synchronized is simpler and released automatically. ReentrantLock adds tryLock with timeout, interruptible waiting, optional fairness and several Condition objects, at the cost of having to unlock in finally.

questions.q: What is a deadlock and how do you prevent one?
questions.a: Two or more threads each hold a lock the other needs, so none can proceed. Prevent it by acquiring locks in one global order, holding as few locks as possible for as short as possible, using tryLock with a timeout, and never calling outside code while holding a lock.

questions.q: How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety?
questions.a: Reads are lock-free. Writes lock only the bucket being changed, using compare-and-swap for empty buckets and a small synchronized section otherwise, so threads working on different buckets do not block each other. Iterators are weakly consistent and never throw ConcurrentModificationException.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: It protects its own structure, not your invariants across keys. A rule involving two keys still needs your own lock or a single compute call.

questions.q: What does the Java Memory Model guarantee?
questions.a: It defines happens-before relationships. If action A happens-before B, B sees A's effects. Such edges come from locks, volatile, thread start and join, and final fields after construction. Without one, visibility and ordering between threads are not guaranteed, even if the code looks sequential.

questions.q: What happens when a server receives an HTTP request?
questions.a: The connection is accepted, the request line, headers and body are parsed, and the request is dispatched to a worker thread. Routing picks a handler by method and path. The handler authenticates, validates, runs business logic, usually talks to a database, and builds a response with a status code, headers and a serialised body, which is written back before the thread returns to the pool.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What changes with a non-blocking server such as Netty?

questions.q: How do you design REST endpoints for a product catalogue?
questions.a: Nouns for resources and HTTP methods for actions: GET /products (list, with paging and filters as query parameters), GET /products/{id}, POST /products (201 with a Location header), PUT or PATCH /products/{id}, DELETE /products/{id}. Consistent error bodies, correct status codes, and versioning in the path or a header.

questions.q: What makes an operation idempotent, and why does a mobile client care?
questions.a: Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are meant to be; POST is not. Mobile networks drop responses, so the client retries: a retried non-idempotent "place order" can create two orders. The fix is an idempotency key the server remembers.

questions.q: Thread-per-request versus event loop?
questions.a: Thread-per-request is simple to write and debug, since code blocks naturally, but each waiting request holds a thread. An event loop handles many connections on few threads and never blocks, which scales for I/O-heavy loads but needs asynchronous code. Virtual threads in Java 21 aim to give the simple style with the scalable cost.

questions.q: As a mobile developer, what do you want from a backend API?
questions.a: Stable contracts with versioning, correct status codes and machine-readable errors, pagination, fields that are never removed without notice, tolerance for old app versions, idempotent writes, small payloads, and clear nullability. Old clients stay in use for years, so the server must not break them.

questions.q: PUT versus PATCH versus POST?
questions.a: POST creates a resource under a collection or triggers an action, and is not idempotent. PUT replaces the resource at a known address with the body sent, and is idempotent. PATCH applies a partial change. Use PUT when the client sends the full state, PATCH when it sends only what changed.

questions.q: How do you version an API?
questions.a: Avoid needing to: only make additive changes, and have clients ignore unknown fields. For breaking changes, put a version in the path (/v2/products) or a header, run both versions until old clients are gone, and measure usage of the old one before removing it.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Mobile makes this slow: you need a minimum-supported-version check and a forced-upgrade path before a version can ever be retired.

questions.q: How do you paginate a large collection?
questions.a: Offset and limit is simple but slow on deep pages and unstable when rows are inserted. Cursor pagination returns an opaque token for "after this item", based on an indexed sort key, and stays fast and stable. Always cap the page size.

questions.q: What makes a good error response?
questions.a: The right status code, a stable machine-readable code, a human-readable message, field-level details for validation failures, and a request id for support. No stack traces or internal names. The same structure on every endpoint.

questions.q: What does Spring's dependency injection container do?
questions.a: At startup it finds classes marked as components, works out the dependency graph from their constructors, creates each object once in the right order, and passes dependencies in. It can also wrap objects in proxies to add behaviour such as transactions, security checks and caching.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Those proxies explain a classic surprise: calling a @Transactional method from another method of the same class bypasses the proxy, so no transaction starts.

questions.q: Constructor injection versus field injection?
questions.a: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit and final, allows creating the object without the framework, and fails at startup if something is missing. Field injection hides dependencies, needs reflection, and permits half-built objects. Constructor injection is the recommended style.

questions.q: What is a bean scope?
questions.a: How long the container keeps an instance. Singleton, the default, is one per application. Prototype is a new one per injection. Request and session scopes are one per HTTP request or session. Most beans are stateless singletons.

questions.q: How is a backend service layer like an Android architecture?
questions.a: Controller corresponds to the UI layer and ViewModel, service to the domain layer and use cases, repository to the data layer. Both point dependencies at the rules and inject implementations. The main difference is concurrency: a server shares each object among many request threads.

questions.q: Explain ACID.
questions.a: Atomicity: a transaction's changes all happen or none do. Consistency: constraints hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other's unfinished work, to a degree set by the isolation level. Durability: once committed, changes survive a crash.

questions.q: What are the isolation levels and the problems they prevent?
questions.a: Read uncommitted allows dirty reads. Read committed prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads. Repeatable read keeps rows you have read stable but may allow phantom rows. Serializable behaves as if transactions ran one at a time. Higher levels cost more locking or more retries.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Even at read committed, a read-then-write sequence can lose an update. Fix it with an atomic conditional UPDATE, SELECT FOR UPDATE, or optimistic locking, not by raising isolation everywhere.

questions.q: Optimistic versus pessimistic locking?
questions.a: Pessimistic: lock the row when you read it (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) so nobody else can change it until you commit. Optimistic: read a version number, and make the update conditional on the version being unchanged; if zero rows update, someone else got there first and you retry or report a conflict. Optimistic suits rare conflicts; pessimistic suits frequent ones.

questions.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
questions.a: Loading a list with one query and then issuing one more query per item for a related object, which turns one request into hundreds of round trips. It usually comes from lazy loading in an object mapper. Fix with a join fetch, a batch size, or a dedicated query.

questions.q: JDBC, JPA or something in between?
questions.a: JDBC gives full control and full boilerplate. JPA with Hibernate maps objects to tables, tracks changes and writes SQL for you, which is productive for ordinary operations and opaque when performance matters. JdbcTemplate and jOOQ sit between: you write the SQL, they remove the plumbing. Many teams use JPA by default and SQL for the hard queries.

questions.q: Sessions versus tokens?
questions.a: A session keeps state on the server and gives the client an opaque id, usually in a cookie: easy to revoke, needs shared session storage across servers. A signed token carries the state itself: no server lookup and easy to scale, but hard to revoke before it expires and larger on every request. Browsers often use sessions; mobile apps and service-to-service calls usually use tokens.

questions.q: How does a JWT work, and what are its risks?
questions.a: It is three base64url parts: a header naming the algorithm, a payload of claims such as subject and expiry, and a signature over the first two. The server verifies the signature and expiry and then trusts the claims. Risks: the payload is readable, tokens cannot be revoked without extra state, algorithm confusion if the server trusts the header, and long lifetimes turning a leak into lasting access.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: With asymmetric signing (RS256 or ES256) only the identity provider holds the private key; services verify with the public key, so a compromised service cannot mint tokens.

questions.q: How should passwords be stored?
questions.a: With a password hashing function designed to be slow and salted per user: Argon2id is the current preference, bcrypt and scrypt are established, PBKDF2 is acceptable with a high iteration count. Store the algorithm, parameters and salt with the hash so settings can be raised later and old hashes upgraded at next login.

questions.q: Describe the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow with PKCE for a mobile app.
questions.a: The app opens the provider's login page in the system browser with a code challenge derived from a random verifier. The user signs in there, and the provider redirects back to the app with a one-time code. The app exchanges the code plus the original verifier for tokens. PKCE stops another app that intercepts the code from using it, and the app never sees the password.

questions.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization, with an example of a bug in each?
questions.a: Authentication establishes identity; a bug is accepting an expired or unsigned token. Authorization decides permission; a bug is letting any logged-in user fetch /orders/123 without checking that order 123 is theirs. The second kind is more common and harder for tests to notice.

questions.q: Mock, stub, fake, spy: what is the difference?
questions.a: A stub returns canned answers. A mock also records calls so you can verify interactions. A fake is a real but simplified implementation, such as an in-memory repository. A spy wraps a real object and records calls. Prefer fakes and stubs with assertions on results; use interaction verification where the interaction is the behaviour, such as "an email was sent".

questions.q: What makes code testable?
questions.a: Dependencies passed in through the constructor, behind interfaces at the boundaries; no static or global state; time, randomness and I/O treated as dependencies; and small methods that return values. Code that is hard to test is usually telling you about a design problem.

questions.q: Unit test or integration test for a repository?
questions.a: Integration. A repository's job is its interaction with the database, so mocking the database tests nothing. Run it against the same database engine used in production, in a container, with a clean schema per test.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: An in-memory substitute such as H2 can accept SQL that PostgreSQL rejects, and the reverse. Testing on the real engine removes that class of surprise.

questions.q: How do you deal with flaky tests?
questions.a: Treat them as bugs. Typical causes: shared state between tests, dependence on timing or real time, test order, and external services. Reproduce by running the test repeatedly, remove the nondeterminism by injecting it, and do not paper over it with retries.

questions.q: What does code coverage tell you, and what does it not?
questions.a: It tells you which lines ran during tests, so it finds code with no tests at all. It does not tell you whether the assertions were meaningful. High coverage with weak assertions is false comfort; use it to find gaps, not as a target.

questions.q: Liveness versus readiness probes?
questions.a: Liveness asks whether the process should be restarted; it should check only that the process itself can respond. Readiness asks whether the instance should receive traffic; it may check dependencies and warm-up. Failing liveness causes a restart, failing readiness only removes the instance from the load balancer.

questions.q: How do you manage configuration and secrets?
questions.a: Keep configuration out of the artefact and supply it at runtime: environment variables, mounted files or a configuration service. Secrets come from a secret manager with access control and rotation, never from source control or the image. Validate everything at startup and fail fast.

questions.q: How do you deploy without downtime?
questions.a: Run several instances behind a load balancer. Replace them one at a time (rolling), or bring up a full new set and switch (blue-green), or send a small share of traffic to the new version first (canary). All require readiness checks, graceful shutdown, and database changes that both the old and the new version can work with.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Schema changes are the hard part: add first, deploy code that handles both shapes, migrate data, and remove the old column only in a later release.

questions.q: What would you monitor for a service?
questions.a: Request rate, error rate and latency percentiles per endpoint; saturation of threads, connection pool, memory and CPU; garbage collection pauses; and the health of each dependency. Alerts should be on symptoms users feel, such as error rate and latency, not on every internal metric.

questions.q: Maven or Gradle?
questions.a: Both resolve dependencies, compile, test and package. Maven is declarative XML with a fixed lifecycle: predictable and uniform. Gradle uses a Kotlin or Groovy build script: more flexible and faster with caching, which is why Android uses it. Backend teams use either; what matters is a reproducible build with pinned versions.

questions.q: What does @SpringBootApplication do?
questions.a: It combines three annotations. @Configuration marks the class as a source of bean definitions. @EnableAutoConfiguration configures what it finds on the classpath: with spring-web present it sets up an embedded server and JSON conversion, with a JDBC driver and JPA present it sets up a connection pool and Hibernate. @ComponentScan finds annotated classes in this package and below.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How would you find out why something was or was not auto-configured?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Run with --debug to print the conditions report. Auto-configuration backs off whenever you define your own bean of the same type, which is the intended way to customise it.

questions.q: Constructor injection versus field injection?
questions.a: With constructor injection the dependencies are parameters: they can be final, the object is never half-built, and a test can create the class with new and pass in fakes. Field injection hides dependencies, needs reflection to set them, and makes it easy for a class to collect too many. Constructor injection is the recommended form; with a single constructor no annotation is needed.

questions.q: How does @Transactional work, and when does it silently not work?
questions.a: Spring wraps the bean in a proxy. A call through the proxy begins a transaction, runs the method, and commits, or rolls back on an unchecked exception. It does nothing when the call does not pass through the proxy: a method calling another method of the same object, or a private method. By default checked exceptions do not cause a rollback.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Keep transactions short and free of remote calls: a transaction holds a pooled connection for its whole length, so a slow HTTP call inside one can exhaust the pool.

questions.q: Why should a controller not return JPA entities?
questions.a: It ties the API to the table: renaming a column changes the JSON, and new columns leak out without a decision. Lazy relations can trigger queries during serialisation or fail outside a transaction. Accepting entities as request bodies lets a client set fields it should not. Map to request and response records at the boundary.

questions.q: What happens between an HTTP request arriving and your controller method running?
questions.a: The embedded server accepts the connection and takes a thread from its pool. The request passes through filters (security, logging), then the DispatcherServlet finds the handler method whose mapping matches the path and method. Argument resolvers build the parameters: path variables are converted, the body is read by Jackson, and @Valid arguments are validated. Then the method is called, and its return value is written back as JSON. Exceptions at any step go to the exception handlers.

questions.q: How would you move this service from H2 to PostgreSQL safely?
questions.a: Add a migration tool and make the current schema the first migration. Run the same engine in tests as in production, for example with Testcontainers, because H2 does not behave identically. Supply the connection settings from the environment, keep ddl-auto on validate, and size the connection pool against the database's connection limit multiplied by the number of instances.

questions.q: How does Kotlin null safety work, and where can a NullPointerException still occur?
questions.a: Nullability is part of the type. The compiler rejects dereferencing a nullable type without a check. NPEs can still come from !!, from Java code returning null through a platform type, from lateinit accessed too early, and from using this in a constructor before fields are initialised.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What is a platform type and how do you make interop safe?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Annotate the Java side with @Nullable and @NonNull so Kotlin sees real types, and declare explicit types at the boundary. The compiler also inserts null checks on parameters of public functions, so a bad Java caller fails fast at the entry point.

questions.q: What is the difference between lateinit and by lazy?
questions.a: lateinit is for a non-null var that is assigned later, for example by dependency injection or in onCreate. by lazy is for a val computed on first access and cached. lazy is thread-safe by default; lateinit has no synchronisation.

questions.q: val versus const val?
questions.a: val is assigned at runtime and read through a getter. const val is a compile-time constant of a primitive or String type, declared at top level or in an object, and inlined at use sites.

questions.q: How does when differ from Java switch?
questions.a: It is an expression, has no fall-through, accepts any type as subject, and its branches can be values, ranges (in 1..10), type checks (is String) or arbitrary conditions when used without a subject. Used as an expression it must be exhaustive, which the compiler verifies for enums and sealed types.

questions.q: Does Kotlin have primitive types?
questions.a: Not in the language: Int and Double are classes with methods. The compiler represents them as JVM primitives wherever possible and boxes them only when needed, such as for nullable types (Int?) and generic arguments (List<Int>). IntArray and friends give primitive arrays.

questions.q: What is a smart cast and when does it not work?
questions.a: After a check such as is String or != null, the compiler treats the value as that type without an explicit cast. It only works when the value cannot change between the check and the use: local val or var not captured in a lambda that modifies it, and val properties without a custom getter in the same module. For a var property, copy it to a local val first.

questions.q: What do inline, noinline and crossinline do?
questions.a: inline copies the function body and its lambda arguments into the call site, removing the lambda allocation and allowing non-local return. noinline opts one lambda parameter out so it can be stored or passed on. crossinline keeps a lambda inlined but forbids non-local return, which is needed when the lambda is invoked from another execution context.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What is a reified type parameter and why does it need inline?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Because the body is copied into the call site, the real type argument is known there, so T::class and is T work despite erasure. That is how inline fun <reified T> Gson.fromJson(json) avoids passing a Class object.

questions.q: How do Kotlin lambdas interoperate with Java interfaces?
questions.a: A Java interface with one abstract method accepts a Kotlin lambda through SAM conversion. For Kotlin interfaces you must declare fun interface to get the same conversion.

questions.q: How are default arguments exposed to Java?
questions.a: They are not, by default: Java sees one method with all parameters. @JvmOverloads generates overloads that drop trailing defaulted parameters.

questions.q: Sealed class, sealed interface or enum: when do you use each?
questions.a: enum when every case is a constant with the same shape. sealed class or interface when cases carry different data. Prefer sealed interface unless subtypes need shared state or a common constructor, because a class can implement several interfaces.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How would you model one-off events such as navigation or a snackbar next to state?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Keep state in StateFlow. Either model the event as state that the UI acknowledges, or use a Channel collected with lifecycle awareness. SharedFlow with replay 0 drops events when nobody is collecting, such as during rotation.

questions.q: What are the limits of data classes?
questions.a: They cannot be open, abstract, sealed or inner. Only primary constructor properties count for equality. copy is shallow. Arrays as properties compare by reference, so use List.

questions.q: == versus === in Kotlin?
questions.a: == calls equals (structural equality) with null handled for you. === compares references. This is the reverse of Java, where == on objects is reference equality.

questions.q: object, companion object and top-level declarations: how do you choose?
questions.a: Top-level functions and constants for utilities with no natural owner. A companion object for factories and constants that belong to a class or need access to its private constructor. An object for a real singleton that holds state or implements an interface. From Java, top-level members appear on a FileKt class and companion members need @JvmStatic to be static.

questions.q: How does by lazy work and is it thread-safe?
questions.a: It creates a Lazy<T> holder. The default mode, SYNCHRONIZED, uses a lock so the initialiser runs at most once even with several threads. PUBLICATION may run it several times and keep the first result. NONE has no locking and is for single-thread use, such as the Android main thread.

questions.q: What is a property delegate?
questions.a: An object with getValue (and setValue for var) operator functions. Writing val x by delegate makes the compiler route every read and write of x through it. lazy, observable, vetoable, map-backed properties, viewModels and Compose's remember all use this mechanism.

questions.q: Composition by delegation versus inheritance?
questions.a: Inheritance fixes the parent at compile time and exposes you to changes in its internals. Delegating an interface to a held object keeps the two independent, lets the delegate be swapped or faked, and works with final classes, which Kotlin classes are by default.

questions.q: How are extension functions implemented, and what follows from that?
questions.a: As static methods with the receiver as the first parameter. Therefore they are dispatched statically on the declared type, cannot be overridden, cannot access private members, and lose to a member with the same signature.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How does Java call a Kotlin extension?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: As FileNameKt.function(receiver, args). @file:JvmName gives the generated class a friendlier name for mixed codebases.

questions.q: Explain the difference between let, run, with, apply and also.
questions.a: Two axes. Context object: this for run, with and apply; it for let and also. Return value: the object for apply and also; the lambda result for let, run and with. Use apply to configure, also for side effects, let for null checks and transforms, run and with to compute something from an object.

questions.q: When would you not use an extension?
questions.a: When the behaviour needs private state, needs to be polymorphic, or is core to the type and you own the class. Overusing extensions on common types such as String also pollutes autocomplete across the codebase.

questions.q: List versus MutableList, and is List immutable?
questions.a: List exposes only read operations; MutableList adds add, remove and set. List is read-only, not immutable: the same object may be referenced as a MutableList elsewhere and change underneath you, and Java code can always mutate it. For real immutability, copy defensively or use kotlinx.collections.immutable.

questions.q: Collection operations versus Sequence versus Java Stream?
questions.a: Collection operations are eager and build a list per step. Sequences are lazy, processed element by element, and stop early. Java streams are also lazy, add parallelism, and are single-use. In Kotlin code prefer collection functions for small data and sequences for large or short-circuiting pipelines.

questions.q: map, flatMap, fold, reduce?
questions.a: map transforms each element to one result. flatMap transforms each to a collection and flattens. fold combines all elements starting from an initial value, so it works on an empty collection and can return a different type. reduce starts from the first element and throws on an empty collection.

questions.q: Explain declaration-site and use-site variance.
questions.a: Declaration-site: the class states its variance once, interface Source<out T>, and every use benefits. Use-site: variance is stated where the type is used, as with Java wildcards or Kotlin projections such as Array<out Any>. Kotlin supports both; Java has only use-site.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Kotlin's out and in map to ? extends and ? super when called from Java, which is how the two interoperate.

questions.q: What can and cannot be done with reified type parameters?
questions.a: Inside the function you can use T in is and as checks, get T::class, and call other reified functions with it. You cannot create an instance with T(), the function must be inline, it cannot be called from Java, and it cannot be virtual.

questions.q: What is the cost of inline?
questions.a: The body is duplicated at every call site, increasing code size, and a public inline function cannot use non-public declarations. In exchange you avoid a lambda allocation and a call, gain non-local return, and can use reified. The standard library's collection functions are inline for this reason.

questions.q: How do coroutines differ from threads?
questions.a: A thread is an operating system resource with its own stack, scheduled by the kernel. A coroutine is a compiler-generated state machine that runs on threads and gives the thread back whenever it suspends. Many coroutines share few threads, switching is cheap, and cancellation and parent-child structure are built in.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What does the compiler generate for a suspend function?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Continuation-passing style: an extra Continuation parameter, a state machine class holding locals and a label, and a COROUTINE_SUSPENDED return marker. Each suspension point becomes a state.

questions.q: What is structured concurrency?
questions.a: Every coroutine runs in a scope and has a parent. A parent does not complete until its children do, cancelling a parent cancels the children, and a failing child cancels its parent and siblings unless a SupervisorJob is used. Work cannot leak past the scope that started it.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Job versus SupervisorJob?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: viewModelScope uses SupervisorJob with Dispatchers.Main.immediate, so one failed launch does not cancel the others. Inside a single launch, children still follow normal Job rules unless you open a supervisorScope.

questions.q: launch versus async?
questions.a: launch returns a Job and is for work with no result; an uncaught exception goes to the scope handler immediately. async returns Deferred and holds its exception until await, though it still cancels the parent on failure in a regular scope.

questions.q: How does cancellation work, and how can it fail?
questions.a: cancel() marks the Job as cancelling. The coroutine notices at its next suspension point, where a CancellationException is thrown and finally blocks run. It fails to stop if the code never suspends, or catches and swallows CancellationException. Cleanup that must suspend goes in withContext(NonCancellable).

questions.q: Dispatchers.IO versus Dispatchers.Default?
questions.a: Default is sized to the CPU core count, for computation. IO allows many more threads (64 by default, or the core count if larger) because they spend their time blocked. They share one pool, so switching between them often needs no thread hop.

questions.q: Job versus SupervisorJob?
questions.a: With a Job, a failing child cancels the parent, which cancels all other children: all or nothing. With a SupervisorJob, a child's failure is its own and siblings continue. Cancellation of the parent still cancels all children in both. Use coroutineScope when the results only make sense together, supervisorScope when they are independent.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: A SupervisorJob only supervises its direct children. Inside one of them, nested launches follow normal Job rules unless you open another supervisorScope.

questions.q: How do exceptions propagate in coroutines?
questions.a: In launch, an uncaught exception goes up to the parent Job; at the root it is passed to the CoroutineExceptionHandler, or the thread's uncaught handler, which on Android crashes the app. In async, the exception is stored and thrown at await, but in a non-supervisor scope it still cancels the parent. CancellationException is special: it is normal termination and is not propagated as a failure.

questions.q: How do you protect shared mutable state in coroutines?
questions.a: Best: do not share; keep state in one coroutine or confine it to a single-threaded dispatcher. Otherwise use atomic types or MutableStateFlow.update for single values, and Mutex.withLock for compound changes. Avoid thread locks around suspension points.

questions.q: Channel versus Flow?
questions.a: A Channel is a hot communication primitive between coroutines: each value is received by exactly one receiver, and it exists whether or not anyone is listening. A Flow is a cold description that runs per collector. Use a Channel for hand-offs and one-off events, a Flow for streams of data, and SharedFlow or StateFlow to broadcast to several collectors.

questions.q: What is the difference between cancel(), cancelAndJoin() and withTimeout?
questions.a: cancel() requests cancellation and returns immediately. cancelAndJoin() also suspends until the coroutine has actually finished, including its finally blocks. withTimeout runs a block and cancels it by throwing TimeoutCancellationException when time is up; withTimeoutOrNull returns null instead of throwing.

questions.q: What is the difference between a cold and a hot flow, and how do you convert one to the other?
questions.a: A cold flow runs its producer per collector and only while collected. A hot flow is active independently and shares emissions. stateIn and shareIn turn a cold flow into a hot one by collecting it once in a given scope.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Explain the SharingStarted options.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Eagerly starts at once and never stops. Lazily starts on the first collector and never stops. WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis) stops the upstream after the last collector leaves; 5000 ms bridges a rotation without restarting and still frees resources in the background.

questions.q: StateFlow versus SharedFlow?
questions.a: StateFlow: one current value, required initial value, new collectors get the latest, equal values are skipped, .value is readable synchronously. SharedFlow: configurable replay and buffer, no initial value, emits every value including duplicates. StateFlow is a SharedFlow with replay 1, drop-oldest overflow and distinctness.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Because StateFlow conflates, a collector slower than the producer will miss intermediate values. That is correct for state and wrong for events you must count.

questions.q: How does backpressure work in Flow?
questions.a: By suspension. emit does not return until the downstream has processed the value, so a slow collector naturally slows the producer. buffer() lets the producer run ahead into a channel, conflate() keeps only the latest, and collectLatest cancels the handler for the previous value when a new one arrives.

questions.q: Why is flowOn needed, and why can you not use withContext inside a flow builder?
questions.a: Flow preserves context: values must be emitted in the context of the collector, so that a collector on the main thread always receives on the main thread. withContext around emit breaks that and is rejected at runtime. flowOn runs the upstream in another context and hands values over through a channel.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: This is why suspend functions called inside flow { } should be main-safe themselves, as Room and Retrofit are, instead of the flow switching dispatchers.

questions.q: How do you combine several flows?
questions.a: combine emits whenever any input emits, using the latest of each: right for UI state built from several sources. zip pairs values one to one. merge interleaves flows of the same type. flatMapLatest, flatMapConcat and flatMapMerge map each value to a flow and differ in whether the previous one is cancelled, awaited or run in parallel.

questions.q: How do you convert a callback API into a Flow?
questions.a: callbackFlow { val listener = ...; api.register(listener); awaitClose { api.unregister(listener) } }, sending values with trySend. awaitClose keeps the flow open and is where the listener is removed when the collector cancels. Without it the builder throws, because the flow would complete at once and leak the listener.

questions.q: How do you test a Flow?
questions.a: In runTest, collect to a list with toList() for finite flows, or use Turbine for step-by-step assertions on hot or infinite flows. Inject test dispatchers so delay and debounce run on virtual time. For StateFlow built with WhileSubscribed, the test must be collecting or the upstream never starts.

questions.q: Walk through what happens when the user taps an app icon.
questions.a: Launcher calls startActivity, a Binder call to the system server. ActivityTaskManager resolves the Intent, sees no process and asks Zygote to fork one. The new process runs ActivityThread.main, prepares the main Looper and attaches to the system server. The system server then instructs it to bind the Application (ContentProviders are created, then Application.onCreate) and to launch the Activity. The Activity is created, started and resumed, the view tree is attached to a window, and after the first traversal a frame is submitted and shown.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Where does time usually go in a slow cold start?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Often in Application.onCreate and in library initialisers that run as ContentProviders before it, then in inflating a heavy first layout. Measure with a system trace and reportFullyDrawn, not with guesses.

questions.q: What is Binder and why did Android need it?
questions.a: A kernel driver providing fast inter-process calls with one copy of the data and with the caller's identity (UID and PID) attached by the kernel, so services can check permissions reliably. It supports object references across processes, death notifications and a thread pool in each process to serve incoming calls. Android builds system services, Intents, ContentProviders and AIDL on it.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Incoming Binder calls run on Binder threads, not the main thread, so a bound service or a ContentProvider must be thread-safe.

questions.q: Explain Looper, MessageQueue and Handler.
questions.a: A Looper owns a MessageQueue for one thread and loops forever taking messages. A Handler is the object that posts messages or Runnables to a Looper and handles them when they are dequeued. The main thread's Looper is created for you; a HandlerThread gives a background thread one.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What is an IdleHandler? What is a sync barrier?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Frame callbacks are posted as asynchronous messages behind a sync barrier so that drawing is not delayed by ordinary queued work.

questions.q: How does Android decide which process to kill?
questions.a: Each process gets an importance from the components running in it: foreground (resumed Activity, foreground service, executing receiver), visible, service, and cached. The system translates that into an oom_adj score and the low memory killer removes the highest scores first. Among cached processes, least recently used goes first.

questions.q: What is the application sandbox?
questions.a: Each app is installed as a distinct Linux user with a private data directory, runs in its own process, and is confined by SELinux. Access to anything outside, such as the camera, contacts or another app's data, goes through a system service that checks permissions, or through a component the other app explicitly exports.

questions.q: How does ART differ from Dalvik and from a desktop JVM?
questions.a: Dalvik interpreted DEX with a JIT. ART added ahead-of-time compilation, a better garbage collector and profile-guided compilation: it interprets and JIT-compiles first, records hot methods, and compiles them ahead of time when the device is idle. Unlike a desktop JVM it runs DEX, a register-based format designed for small memory, not stack-based class files.

questions.q: What is the manifest for, and what goes wrong without it?
questions.a: It declares the app's components, permissions, hardware requirements and application-level settings so that the system and the store can know them without running the app. Components not declared cannot be started; permissions not declared are denied; intent filters not declared mean other apps and links cannot reach you.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What is manifest merging?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Libraries contribute their own entries, including permissions and auto-initialising ContentProviders you may not want. Review the merged manifest and remove entries with tools:node="remove".

questions.q: Explain Intent filters and how an implicit Intent is resolved.
questions.a: A filter lists actions, categories and data (scheme, host, path, MIME type). An implicit Intent matches when its action is in the filter, every one of its categories is in the filter, and its data matches. startActivity adds CATEGORY_DEFAULT, so an Activity must list DEFAULT to receive implicit Intents. If several match, the system shows a chooser unless a default or a verified App Link applies.

questions.q: What are the different Contexts and how do they differ?
questions.a: Application, Activity and Service are all Contexts. The Activity context is themed and tied to one screen's lifetime; use it for anything visual. The application context lasts for the process and is safe to keep, but it cannot start an Activity without FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK and inflates with the default theme. ContextWrapper lets classes such as ContextThemeWrapper adjust one.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Leaks nearly always come from an Activity context stored somewhere long-lived. If an API you write only needs resources or services, ask for applicationContext yourself inside it.

questions.q: What does android:exported mean and why is it a security topic?
questions.a: An exported component can be started by other apps. Any app can then send it arbitrary Intents. Exported Activities must validate extras and URLs, exported Services and Receivers should require a permission where possible, and ContentProviders should be unexported or protected with read and write permissions.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What is a PendingIntent and why must it be immutable?

questions.q: What is a PendingIntent?
questions.a: A token wrapping an Intent that another app or the system can fire later as if it were your app, with your identity and permissions. Notifications, alarms and widgets use them. Since Android 12 you must declare FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE; immutable is the default choice so the holder cannot alter the Intent.

questions.q: How does the resource system choose a resource?
questions.a: Resources live in folders with qualifiers: language and region, night mode, screen density, smallest width, orientation, API level. At runtime the system removes folders that contradict the device configuration and picks the best remaining match by qualifier precedence. A configuration change invalidates those choices, which is why the Activity is recreated.

questions.q: Walk through the Activity lifecycle.
questions.a: onCreate: build the UI and restore state. onStart: visible. onResume: in the foreground with input focus. onPause: losing focus, may still be visible. onStop: no longer visible. onDestroy: finishing or being recreated. onRestart runs before onStart when returning from the stopped state. The pairs are symmetric: create and destroy, start and stop, resume and pause.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Which callbacks are guaranteed to be called?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Nothing after onStop is guaranteed, and on old releases nothing after onPause was. Design so that losing the process at any point after onStop loses no user data.

questions.q: What happens on a configuration change, and how do you keep state?
questions.a: The Activity is destroyed and recreated so resources can be reloaded for the new configuration. Three tools, by lifetime: ViewModel keeps in-memory objects across the recreation; saved instance state (or SavedStateHandle, or rememberSaveable in Compose) keeps small values across recreation and process death; persistent storage keeps real data across everything.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Why not just set configChanges in the manifest?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: It only covers the changes you list, you must then update resources by hand, and it does nothing for process death. It is appropriate for cases such as video players and games, and Compose apps sometimes opt in because Compose can react to configuration without recreation.

questions.q: What is process death and how do you handle it?
questions.a: While the app is in the background the system may kill its process to reclaim memory. No callback runs. The system keeps the task, the back stack and each Activity's saved state Bundle. When the user returns, a new process starts, Application.onCreate runs, and only the top Activity is recreated with its Bundle; the ones below are recreated as the user navigates back. Handle it by saving ids and inputs to saved state and reloading the rest.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How do you test it?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Singletons, static fields and in-memory caches are all empty after restoration while the UI resumes mid-flow. Screens deep in a flow must not assume an earlier screen populated something in memory. This is the most common cause of crashes that only appear in production.

questions.q: How does a ViewModel survive rotation?
questions.a: Each ComponentActivity owns a ViewModelStore. On a configuration change the Activity hands the store to the system through onRetainNonConfigurationInstance, and the new instance receives the same store, so the same ViewModel objects are returned. When the Activity finishes for real, the store is cleared and onCleared is called.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The store is kept by the ActivityThread in memory, so it cannot survive process death. SavedStateHandle bridges that gap by registering with the SavedStateRegistry, which writes into the instance state Bundle.

questions.q: Activity A starts Activity B. List the callbacks in order.
questions.a: A.onPause, B.onCreate, B.onStart, B.onResume, A.onStop (and A.onSaveInstanceState). Pressing Back: B.onPause, A.onRestart, A.onStart, A.onResume, B.onStop, B.onDestroy.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What changes if B is translucent or a dialog-themed Activity?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: A stays visible, so it gets onPause but not onStop. This is why onPause must be fast: the next Activity cannot resume until it returns.

questions.q: What changed about the Back button in Android 12?
questions.a: For a root launcher Activity, Back no longer finishes it. The system moves the task to the background instead, so the Activity is stopped, not destroyed, and returning is a warm start. Other Activities still finish on Back.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Apps that used onDestroy of the root Activity as an "app closed" signal broke. Predictive back (Android 13+) further requires registering OnBackPressedCallback up front instead of overriding onBackPressed.

questions.q: What is the difference between onSaveInstanceState and onRetainNonConfigurationInstance or ViewModel?
questions.a: onSaveInstanceState serialises small data into a Bundle held by the system process, so it survives process death but is limited in size and type. ViewModel keeps live objects in memory, so it can hold anything but only survives configuration changes.

questions.q: How do lifecycle-aware components work?
questions.a: ComponentActivity implements LifecycleOwner and exposes a Lifecycle that dispatches events (ON_CREATE, ON_START and so on) to registered LifecycleObservers. Libraries observe it instead of asking you to call start and stop: LiveData only delivers while at least STARTED, and repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) cancels flow collection in onStop and restarts it in onStart.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Collecting a Flow with lifecycleScope.launch alone keeps collecting in the background. repeatOnLifecycle or collectAsStateWithLifecycle is the correct pattern.

questions.q: Describe the Fragment lifecycle and how it differs from the Activity lifecycle.
questions.a: onAttach, onCreate, onCreateView, onViewCreated, onStart, onResume going up; onPause, onStop, onDestroyView, onDestroy, onDetach going down. The additions are attach and detach, and a separate view lifecycle: onCreateView to onDestroyView can repeat several times within one onCreate to onDestroy span.

points.title: Follow-up
items: When does the view lifecycle repeat?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: On back-stack navigation with replace, and with detach and attach. That is why Fragment exposes two LifecycleOwners, and why Lint flags observing with the fragment as owner in onViewCreated.

questions.q: What happens to a fragment across a configuration change and across process death?
questions.a: In both cases the instance is destroyed. FragmentManager saves its state (class name, arguments, saved instance state, back stack) and recreates it through the no-argument constructor. On a configuration change the ViewModel is retained; after process death it is not, and only arguments, saved state and SavedStateHandle come back.

questions.q: add versus replace, and what does addToBackStack actually store?
questions.a: add puts a fragment in the container and leaves existing ones in place and resumed. replace removes the existing ones first. addToBackStack records the transaction, not the fragment, so Back reverses exactly what the transaction did: for a replace, it removes the new fragment and re-adds the old, recreating its view.

questions.q: commit, commitNow, commitAllowingStateLoss?
questions.a: commit schedules the transaction on the main thread. commitNow runs it at once and cannot be used with addToBackStack. commitAllowingStateLoss permits a commit after state was saved, accepting that the change is lost if the process is killed. Reaching for it usually signals a lifecycle bug elsewhere.

questions.q: How do fragments share data?
questions.a: A ViewModel scoped to the Activity (by activityViewModels()) or to a navigation graph (by navGraphViewModels) for ongoing shared state. The Fragment Result API for a one-time result. Arguments for inputs. Never a direct reference from one fragment to another.

questions.q: Fragments or Compose destinations for a new app?
questions.a: Compose with Navigation Compose for new code: no view lifecycle split, no binding leaks, less boilerplate. Fragments remain necessary in existing View-based apps, for libraries that expose fragments, and as hosts during an incremental migration.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The practical migration path is fragment by fragment: each fragment returns a ComposeView, navigation stays as is, and the navigation graph moves to Compose last.

questions.q: Explain how a View is measured, laid out and drawn.
questions.a: Measure: starting from the root, each parent calls measure on each child with a width and height MeasureSpec, a mode (EXACTLY, AT_MOST or UNSPECIFIED) plus a size, and the child sets its measured size. Layout: each parent calls layout on each child with its final position. Draw: each view draws its background, its content in onDraw, its children, then decorations such as scrollbars. requestLayout schedules measure and layout; invalidate schedules only draw.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Why are nested weights slow?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: A LinearLayout with weights measures children twice. Nest two and the inner children are measured four times, and so on. ConstraintLayout solves the whole level in one or two passes.

questions.q: ViewBinding, DataBinding or findViewById?
questions.a: findViewById is an untyped lookup at runtime that can return null. View binding generates a class per layout with a typed, non-null field for each id, at no runtime cost. Data binding also generates bindings but adds an expression language and observable bindings inside the XML, with slower builds and logic hidden in layouts. View binding is the usual choice.

questions.q: What is the difference between a style and a theme?
questions.a: A style is a set of attribute values applied to one view, such as a text appearance. A theme is a set of attribute values applied to a whole Context, and views read from it with ?attr. Styles decide how a widget looks; themes supply the values that many styles refer to, which is how light, dark and brand variants work.

questions.q: How do you support different screen sizes and densities?
questions.a: Use dp and sp, never px. Use flexible layouts: constraints, match-constraints and wrap. Provide alternative resources by qualifier, for example layout-sw600dp for tablets and drawable densities, or vector drawables. For large-screen behaviour use window size classes to switch between single-pane and two-pane layouts.

questions.q: How do you make a View-based screen accessible?
questions.a: Content descriptions for meaningful images and icon buttons, labels linked to inputs, touch targets of at least 48dp, sp for text so it scales, sufficient colour contrast, a sensible focus order, and testing with TalkBack and the Accessibility Scanner.

questions.q: When would you write a custom View?
questions.a: When no combination of existing widgets gives the drawing or interaction you need: a chart, a seek control, a signature pad. Extend the closest existing class, measure correctly in onMeasure, draw in onDraw without allocating objects there, handle touch in onTouchEvent, save state in onSaveInstanceState, and expose accessibility information.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Allocation inside onDraw causes garbage collection during animation. Create Paint, Path and Rect objects once as fields.

questions.q: How does RecyclerView recycling work?
questions.a: The LayoutManager asks the Recycler for a view for a position. The Recycler checks, in order: scrap (views detached during the current layout), the view cache (a few recently scrolled-off holders still bound to their position, reusable without a bind), an optional ViewCacheExtension, and the RecycledViewPool (holders by view type that must be rebound). Only if all miss does the adapter create a new holder.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What is the difference between the cache and the pool?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Cache hits skip onBindViewHolder, which makes small back-and-forth scrolling free. Pool hits need a bind. The cache size is 2 by default plus prefetch; raising it trades memory for fewer binds.

questions.q: What does DiffUtil do, and what is ListAdapter?
questions.a: DiffUtil computes the minimal set of insert, remove, move and change operations between two lists, using areItemsTheSame and areContentsTheSame. ListAdapter wraps AsyncListDiffer: submitList runs the diff on a background thread and dispatches the operations on the main thread, giving correct animations with no manual notify calls.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The diff is O(N) in space and around O(N + D²) in time where D is the number of edits, so it is fast for typical changes and slow for full reshuffles of very long lists. Use getChangePayload to rebind only the part of a row that changed.

questions.q: How do you optimise a janky list?
questions.a: Measure first with a system trace. Then: flatten the row layout, do no work in bind beyond setting values, precompute display strings, size images to the view and load them asynchronously, call setHasFixedSize when the list size does not change the RecyclerView size, share a view pool between nested lists, and avoid nested scrolling containers.

questions.q: How do you handle clicks in a row correctly?
questions.a: Set the listener once in onCreateViewHolder, read bindingAdapterPosition at click time, check it against NO_POSITION, and pass the item to a callback supplied by the screen. The adapter does not navigate or call the ViewModel itself.

questions.q: How do you build a list with several kinds of rows?
questions.a: Override getItemViewType to return a type per position, create the matching holder in onCreateViewHolder, and bind accordingly, usually with a sealed class of row models. For independent sections use ConcatAdapter. For grids with full-width headers, use GridLayoutManager with a SpanSizeLookup.

questions.q: RecyclerView or LazyColumn?
questions.a: LazyColumn for Compose screens: no adapter, no holders, keys and content types give the same reuse. RecyclerView stays in View-based screens and remains a mature choice for very complex or highly tuned lists. They can be mixed during migration through ComposeView rows or AndroidView.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: In LazyColumn the equivalents of recycling mistakes are missing keys, unstable item models that defeat skipping, and heavy work in the item composable.

questions.q: How does Compose differ from the View system?
questions.a: Views are stateful objects created once and mutated. Compose is declarative: functions describe the UI for the current state and the runtime works out the changes. There is no findViewById and no view state to keep in sync. Layout is single pass, so deep nesting does not cost what nested XML layouts cost.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What are the three phases and why do they matter for performance?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Composition, layout, draw. Deferring a state read to layout or draw (lambda-based modifiers such as offset { } and drawBehind { }) avoids recomposition for values that change every frame.

questions.q: What does the @Composable annotation do?
questions.a: It changes the function type. The compiler plugin adds a Composer parameter and a bit mask of changed parameters, wraps the body in a restart group so it can be re-run on its own, and inserts skip checks when the parameters are unchanged.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: That is why a composable can only be called from another composable: the hidden Composer must be passed down, the same constraint suspend functions have with Continuation.

questions.q: Why does every composable take a Modifier parameter?
questions.a: So the caller, which knows the surrounding layout, decides size, weight, alignment and padding. A component that hard-codes these cannot be reused.

questions.q: What is recomposition and what triggers it?
questions.a: Re-running composable functions to update the UI. It is triggered when a State object that was read during composition is written with a different value. Compose re-runs only the restart scopes that read it and skips composables whose parameters are unchanged.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What makes a composable skippable?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: All parameters must be comparable as unchanged. With strong skipping mode, the default since the Kotlin 2.0.20 Compose compiler, stable parameters are compared with equals and unstable ones by instance identity, and lambdas are remembered automatically. Before that, a single unstable parameter such as a List made the composable non-skippable.

questions.q: remember versus rememberSaveable versus ViewModel?
questions.a: remember: survives recomposition only. rememberSaveable: also survives configuration change and process death, limited to Bundle-compatible data. ViewModel: survives configuration change, holds any object, is scoped to a navigation destination or Activity, and needs SavedStateHandle to survive process death.

questions.q: What is state hoisting and why do it?
questions.a: Moving state out of a composable to its caller, replacing it with a value parameter and an event lambda. It gives a single source of truth, makes the composable reusable, previewable and testable, and lets the owner intercept or validate changes.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How far up should state go?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: To the lowest common ancestor of everything that reads or writes it. UI element state such as scroll position can stay in the composable; screen and business state goes to a state holder or ViewModel.

questions.q: What does stability mean in Compose?
questions.a: A type is stable if Compose can trust that equals is consistent and that it will be notified when a public property changes. Primitives, String, function types and classes with only val properties of stable types are stable. Interfaces such as List are treated as unstable because the implementation might be mutable.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Options: kotlinx.collections.immutable types, @Immutable or @Stable annotations as a promise to the compiler, or a stability configuration file for classes from other modules.

questions.q: What is derivedStateOf for?
questions.a: When a value is computed from state that changes more often than the result does. Example: showButton = listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0. Without it, every scroll frame recomposes the reader; with it, only a change in the Boolean does.

questions.q: How do side effects fit with recomposition?
questions.a: Composable bodies must be free of side effects because they can run many times, be skipped or be abandoned. Effects go in effect handlers: LaunchedEffect(key) runs a coroutine tied to the composition and restarts when the key changes; DisposableEffect pairs setup with cleanup; SideEffect runs after every successful recomposition.

questions.q: How does the back stack work, and what is the difference between Back and Up?
questions.a: The back stack is the history of destinations in a task. Back pops the top entry and, at the start destination, leaves the app. Up navigates to the logical parent inside the app and never leaves it. They differ when the app was entered through a deep link: Back may return to the app that sent you, Up goes to the parent screen.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How do tasks and launch modes affect this?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Activities have their own task back stack managed by the system (launchMode, taskAffinity, Intent flags). A single-Activity app with a NavController mostly sidesteps those rules, which is a strong argument for that design.

questions.q: How do you pass data between destinations?
questions.a: Forward: small arguments in the route, an id or a filter. Shared ongoing state: a ViewModel scoped to a nested navigation graph. Backward: a result written to the previous entry's SavedStateHandle and observed there. Never a mutable singleton and never large objects in arguments.

questions.q: How do deep links work end to end?
questions.a: The manifest declares an intent filter with the scheme, host and path so the system can route the URL to your Activity. For https links, android:autoVerify plus a Digital Asset Links file on the domain makes it a verified App Link. Inside the app the navigation graph maps the URL pattern to a destination and extracts arguments. For links that start a new task, Navigation builds a synthetic back stack from the graph hierarchy.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Deep links are an attack surface: any app can fire them. Treat arguments as untrusted input, and never let a deep link bypass the auth check or perform a state-changing action without confirmation.

questions.q: How do you scope a ViewModel to several screens?
questions.a: Put the screens in a nested graph and obtain the ViewModel from the graph's back stack entry: in Compose, viewModel(navController.getBackStackEntry(CheckoutGraph)); with fragments, by navGraphViewModels(R.id.checkout_graph). It lives until the graph is popped.

questions.q: How do you structure navigation in a multi-module app?
questions.a: Each feature module exposes its destinations as an extension on NavGraphBuilder and its route types, and takes navigation callbacks as lambdas. The app module assembles the NavHost and wires the lambdas. Features never import each other; cross-feature navigation goes through the app module or through deep link URIs.

questions.q: How do you handle the system Back button in Compose and in Views?
questions.a: Compose: BackHandler(enabled) { } intercepts Back while enabled. Views: register an OnBackPressedCallback on onBackPressedDispatcher with a lifecycle owner. Overriding onBackPressed is deprecated and incompatible with predictive back. Keep the callback enabled only while you really need to intercept, for example with unsaved changes.

questions.q: How is a ViewModel created and where is it stored?
questions.a: ViewModelProvider asks the owner's ViewModelStore for a ViewModel under a key derived from the class name. If none exists, it calls the Factory, passing CreationExtras (which carry the SavedStateRegistryOwner, default arguments and the Application), stores the result and returns it. Every later request with the same owner and key returns that instance.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What are CreationExtras for?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
