items: They made factories stateless: the factory no longer needs to be constructed with the owner, so one static factory can serve any owner and receive what it needs per call.

questions.q: How does SavedStateHandle work?
questions.a: It is a key-value map handed to the ViewModel. It registers a saved state provider with the owner's SavedStateRegistry. When the system saves instance state, the handle's contents are written into the Bundle; on recreation they are read back before the ViewModel is constructed. Navigation also places a destination's arguments in it.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Because it uses the instance state mechanism, it is saved only when the Activity is stopped, not when finishing, and it shares the Bundle size limit. It is not a persistence layer.

questions.q: ViewModel versus onSaveInstanceState versus persistent storage?
questions.a: ViewModel: in-memory, survives configuration change, any object, lost on process death. Saved instance state (and SavedStateHandle, rememberSaveable): small serialisable values, survives process death, discarded when the user finishes the screen. Persistent storage: survives everything, for data the user owns.

questions.q: How do you share data between two screens?
questions.a: Pass an id as a navigation argument when the second screen can load what it needs. For state both screens edit, scope one ViewModel to their common owner, ideally a nested navigation graph. For app-wide data, use a repository both ViewModels observe.

questions.q: Should a ViewModel expose suspend functions?
questions.a: Generally no. The UI should call a plain function and the ViewModel should launch in viewModelScope, so the work survives rotation and is cancelled with the ViewModel. A suspend function called from the UI runs in the UI's scope and is cancelled when the screen is recreated.

questions.q: What is the difference between ViewModel and AndroidViewModel?
questions.a: AndroidViewModel receives the Application, for cases that truly need a Context that outlives screens. It makes unit testing harder and invites using Context where a repository should be injected, so prefer plain ViewModel with dependencies passed in.

questions.q: What goes in a ViewModel and what must stay out?
questions.a: In: screen state, the logic that turns user events and data into new state, and coroutines for that work. Out: anything tied to the UI toolkit (View, Activity, Fragment, Context for UI, resources lookups that depend on configuration), and data access details, which belong in repositories.

points.title: Follow-up
items: When is AndroidViewModel acceptable?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: A good test: the ViewModel should compile and run in a plain JVM unit test with fakes. If it needs Robolectric, something from the View layer has leaked in.

questions.q: How do you handle one-off events such as navigation or a snackbar?
questions.a: Three workable approaches. Fold it into state (for example userMessage: String?) and have the View call onMessageShown() to clear it; this is what Google recommends and it survives rotation. Or use a Channel exposed as a Flow, collected with repeatOnLifecycle, which delivers each event once. Avoid SharedFlow with replay 0 for must-deliver events: an emission while nobody collects is dropped.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Often the question disappears when you ask "what state change does this event represent?" Navigation after login is a consequence of isLoggedIn becoming true.

questions.q: LiveData or StateFlow?
questions.a: StateFlow for Kotlin code: it works in every layer, has the full Flow operator set, and is easy to test. It is not lifecycle-aware by itself, so the UI must collect with repeatOnLifecycle or collectAsStateWithLifecycle. LiveData is lifecycle-aware out of the box and is still the practical choice in Java screens.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What does SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000) do and why five seconds?

questions.q: How do you test a ViewModel?
questions.a: Construct it with fake repositories. Use runTest, replace Dispatchers.Main with a test dispatcher through a rule, trigger an event, advance the scheduler, and assert on state.value or on the sequence of emissions collected with a tool such as Turbine.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Inject dispatchers instead of hard-coding Dispatchers.IO in classes below the ViewModel, otherwise the test cannot control time.

questions.q: What problems does MVVM not solve?
questions.a: It says nothing about navigation, about where business rules shared by several screens live, or about how to structure a very complex screen. Those are answered by a navigation layer, by a domain layer with use cases, and by splitting state holders or moving to MVI-style reducers.

questions.q: Compare MVVM and MVI.
questions.a: Both keep state in a ViewModel and push it one way to the UI. MVVM lets the ViewModel expose several methods and, if you allow it, several observable values. MVI restricts it to one immutable state, one entry point taking an action, and a pure reducer producing the next state, with side effects kept apart. MVI gives traceability and trivially testable transitions; MVVM gives less ceremony.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Where is the line between them in practice?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: MVVM with a single UiState data class updated through update { } is already unidirectional. Add an action type and a reducer when transitions, not loading, are where the bugs are.

questions.q: How do you handle side effects in MVI?
questions.a: Outside the reducer. The store reacts to certain actions by launching work in viewModelScope and dispatches a result action when it completes. One-off UI effects are sent through a Channel. The reducer stays a pure function of state and action.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Decide the concurrency rule per effect: ignore while running, cancel the previous (search), or queue. Encoding "is running" in state lets the reducer enforce the first.

questions.q: Why must state be immutable?
questions.a: So that every change is a new object: StateFlow and Compose detect changes by comparison, an old state can be kept for logging or undo, and no other code can change what the UI is drawing from underneath it. Mutating in place produces no emission and no recomposition.

questions.q: How do you test an MVI screen?
questions.a: Reducer: plain unit tests of input and output. Store: in runTest with a fake side-effect function, dispatch actions and assert the sequence of states and effects, for example with Turbine. UI: render the stateless screen with a fixed state and assert what is shown and which action a click sends.

questions.q: What goes wrong with a single state object on a large screen?
questions.a: Every change emits a new state, and in Compose anything reading the whole object recomposes. Mitigate by passing each child only the fields it needs, keeping item models stable, deriving sub-states with map and distinctUntilChanged, and splitting independent parts of the screen into their own stores.

questions.q: State or effect: how do you decide?
questions.a: If the UI should still show it after rotation or coming back from the background, it is state: loading, errors displayed inline, form contents. If it should happen exactly once and never again, it is an effect: navigation, a toast, haptics. When losing it would be a bug, such as "payment done, go to receipt", model it as state the UI acknowledges.

questions.q: Explain the dependency rule and dependency inversion.
questions.a: Source code dependencies point inward, toward the business rules. The domain declares interfaces for what it needs, such as a repository. Outer layers implement them. At runtime the call still flows from domain to data, but at compile time data depends on domain. That inversion means the rules never import a framework.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How do you enforce it in a codebase?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: With module boundaries: a pure Kotlin domain module, a data module depending on it, feature modules depending on domain, and only the app module depending on data to wire implementations. Anything else is a convention that erodes.

questions.q: What is a use case and when do you create one?
questions.a: A class that represents one business action, takes its collaborators by constructor, and exposes a single operator invoke. Create one when there is real logic, when logic is shared by several ViewModels, or when several repositories are combined. Do not create one that merely forwards a call.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Use cases should be stateless and main-safe. If one needs state, it is probably a repository or a domain service.

questions.q: Why separate DTOs, entities and domain models?
questions.a: Each changes for a different reason: the DTO when the API changes, the entity when the schema changes, the domain model when the business changes, the UI model when the screen changes. Separate types stop a backend rename from touching every screen and let each be shaped for its job, for example non-null domain fields from nullable JSON.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: It is a trade-off. For a simple read-only model the mapping is pure overhead, and reusing one class across two adjacent layers can be the pragmatic choice.

questions.q: What are the downsides of Clean Architecture?
questions.a: More files, more mapping, more indirection to follow when reading, and slower onboarding. On small apps or simple CRUD screens it costs more than it returns. Misapplied, it produces layers of pass-through classes.

questions.q: How does Google's recommended architecture relate to it?
questions.a: It recommends a UI layer and a data layer with unidirectional data flow, and an optional domain layer for complex or reused logic. It is the same idea with the domain layer made a choice, not a requirement, and it places the repository in the data layer as the single source of truth.

questions.q: How would you structure modules for a large app?
questions.a: By feature, with a small set of core modules. Each feature module owns its UI and, if large, its own domain and data. Core modules hold shared models, the network and database setup, the design system and common utilities. Features do not depend on each other; the app module assembles them and wires navigation and DI.

questions.q: Dependency injection versus service locator?
questions.a: With injection, dependencies are pushed into a class through its constructor, so they are visible in its signature and the class knows nothing about the container. With a locator, the class pulls dependencies from a global registry, hiding them and coupling every class to the registry. Injection is easier to test and to reason about; a locator is easier to bolt onto existing code.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Is Koin a service locator?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Koin can be used either way. Calling by inject() or get() inside a class is location; constructor parameters resolved in a module definition are injection. The pattern, not the library, is what matters.

questions.q: How does Hilt relate to Dagger?
questions.a: Hilt is built on Dagger. Dagger is a general compile-time DI framework where you define components and their relationships yourself. Hilt predefines the Android component hierarchy and scopes, generates the components, and adds entry points for Activities, Fragments, ViewModels, Services and WorkManager. You write modules and @Inject; Hilt writes the rest.

questions.q: @Binds versus @Provides?
questions.a: @Binds is an abstract function mapping an interface to an implementation that Hilt already knows how to construct; it generates no extra factory code. @Provides is a concrete function whose body constructs the object, needed for third-party types, builders or any creation logic.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Prefer @Binds where possible: less generated code, and the implementation keeps its @Inject constructor, so its own dependencies stay declared in one place.

questions.q: How do you inject a value known only at runtime, such as a product id?
questions.a: For ViewModels, read it from SavedStateHandle, which Hilt provides and Navigation fills with the route arguments. For other classes use assisted injection: mark the runtime parameter @Assisted, the constructor @AssistedInject, and declare an @AssistedFactory interface that Hilt implements.

questions.q: How does DI help testing?
questions.a: Because a class receives its collaborators, a unit test constructs it directly with fakes, no framework needed. For instrumented tests Hilt can replace whole modules with @TestInstallIn or bind test values with @BindValue, so the app runs against a fake server or in-memory database.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: If a unit test needs Hilt to construct the class under test, the class has too many dependencies or the test is at the wrong level.

questions.q: What are the costs of Hilt?
questions.a: Build time from annotation processing (KSP reduces it), generated code that is hard to read, a learning curve for error messages, and a rigid component hierarchy that can be awkward for features with unusual lifetimes. For a very small app, a hand-written container is a legitimate choice.

questions.q: How does Retrofit turn an interface into working code?
questions.a: At create() it builds a java.lang.reflect.Proxy for the interface. On the first call to each method it parses the annotations into a request factory and picks a call adapter and a converter, then caches that. Each call builds an OkHttp Request, executes it and converts the body.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How are suspend functions supported?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: A suspend function compiles to a method with an extra Continuation parameter. Retrofit detects that, enqueues the call, resumes the continuation from the callback and cancels the OkHttp call if the coroutine is cancelled. Because of reflection, R8 needs the keep rules that Retrofit ships.

questions.q: How do you model network errors for the rest of the app?
questions.a: Catch at the repository boundary and convert to a sealed type with cases the UI can act on: success, HTTP error with code and parsed error body, network unavailable, and unexpected. ViewModels then use an exhaustive when instead of try and catch in every screen.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Keep cancellation out of that type: CancellationException must propagate. Decide per endpoint which failures are worth retrying.

questions.q: How does OkHttp caching work?
questions.a: Give the client a Cache directory and size. OkHttp then honours HTTP cache headers from the server (Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified), serving fresh responses from disk and making conditional requests for stale ones. Only GET responses are cached. A network interceptor can rewrite headers when the server does not send them.

questions.q: How would you implement pagination?
questions.a: The endpoint takes a page number or cursor and returns items plus the next cursor. On Android use Paging 3: a PagingSource loads pages from the network, or a RemoteMediator writes pages to Room and the UI pages from the database. The UI collects PagingData and LazyColumn or RecyclerView requests more as the user scrolls.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Offset paging or cursor paging: which and why?

questions.q: How do you upload a file?
questions.a: Annotate the function with @Multipart and pass @Part MultipartBody.Part built from a RequestBody that streams from the file or content URI. For large uploads that must finish in the background, run it in WorkManager with a foreground notification and report progress from a counting RequestBody.

questions.q: What timeouts does OkHttp have?
questions.a: connectTimeout for establishing the connection, readTimeout between bytes read, writeTimeout between bytes written, each 10 seconds by default, and callTimeout for the whole call, off by default. A slow server that keeps trickling bytes never hits readTimeout, which is why callTimeout matters for user-facing calls.

questions.q: How does Room know to re-emit a Flow?
questions.a: Room creates triggers that record which tables were modified in a tracking table. After a transaction commits, the InvalidationTracker checks that record and notifies observers of the affected tables, and each active Flow re-runs its query. The granularity is the table, not the row, so a query re-runs even if its own result did not change.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How do you avoid redundant emissions?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Add distinctUntilChanged() downstream. Also remember invalidation is per database instance: a second instance, or another process, needs enableMultiInstanceInvalidation().

questions.q: How do you write and test a migration?
questions.a: Raise the version, write a Migration with the SQL that turns the old schema into the new one, register it with addMigrations, and export schemas to a folder under version control. In an instrumented test, MigrationTestHelper creates the database at the old version, inserts rows, runs the migration and validates the result against the exported schema.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: SQLite ALTER TABLE is limited: for dropping or changing a column on older Android versions you create a new table, copy the data, drop the old table and rename. AutoMigration handles simple cases and needs a spec for renames and deletes.

questions.q: Room, DataStore or SharedPreferences?
questions.a: Room for structured, queryable or relational data and lists. DataStore for a small set of settings or flags, with transactional writes and a Flow API. SharedPreferences is the legacy key-value store: synchronous reads, apply() failures are silent, and it can cause ANRs; use DataStore for new code.

questions.q: How do you model relationships?
questions.a: Store foreign keys, declared with @ForeignKey and indexed. To read a parent with its children use a data class with @Embedded for the parent and @Relation for the children, queried inside a @Transaction. Many-to-many needs a junction table. Room does not lazy-load: you ask explicitly for what you need.

questions.q: What is a TypeConverter and when is it the wrong tool?
questions.a: A pair of functions that convert a type SQLite cannot store, such as Instant or an enum, to one it can. It is the wrong tool for lists of objects serialised to JSON in one column: you cannot query or index inside it. Use a child table.

questions.q: How do you keep the local database in sync with the server?
questions.a: Reads: fetch, then write to the database in one transaction; the UI observes the database. Writes: apply locally first for instant feedback, record a pending operation, send it with WorkManager under a network constraint, and reconcile with the server response. Decide the conflict rule in advance: last write wins, server wins, or merge by field.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Include a version or updatedAt on rows so stale responses do not overwrite newer local edits, and make the sync operations idempotent because WorkManager can run them more than once.

questions.q: Why was DataStore introduced when SharedPreferences existed?
questions.a: SharedPreferences has a synchronous API that does disk I/O, loads the whole file on first access, can block the main thread on apply() during lifecycle transitions, reports parse errors as runtime exceptions, has no transactional read-modify-write, and its change listener is easy to leak. DataStore is asynchronous through coroutines and Flow, makes every write a transaction, surfaces I/O errors in the flow, and is safe to call from the main thread.

points.title: Follow-up
items: Why can apply() cause an ANR?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: apply() queues the disk write, but the framework waits for queued writes to finish when an Activity stops or a Service ends, on the main thread. A slow disk at that moment is an ANR that points at framework code, not yours.

questions.q: Preferences DataStore versus Proto DataStore?
questions.a: Preferences: untyped storage accessed with typed keys, no schema, quickest to adopt, defaults handled in code. Proto: one message type defined in a .proto file, generated classes, compile-time field types, defaults and schema evolution from protocol buffers, at the cost of build setup. Choose Proto when settings have structure or must stay consistent as a group.

questions.q: How does DataStore guarantee consistency?
questions.a: All writes go through a single actor-like queue so they run one at a time. Each edit reads the current value, applies your transform, writes the complete new value to a scratch file and renames it over the original, which is atomic on the file system. Readers always see a complete snapshot, old or new.

questions.q: How do you get a setting synchronously at startup, for example the theme?
questions.a: You do not read synchronously. Options: keep the system splash screen on with setKeepOnScreenCondition until the first emission; render with a neutral default and update; or, for the day and night theme specifically, let AppCompatDelegate persist the night mode itself. Blocking with runBlocking on the main thread reintroduces the problem DataStore solves.

questions.q: How do you migrate from SharedPreferences?
questions.a: Pass SharedPreferencesMigration(context, "old_prefs_name") in the produceMigrations parameter of the delegate. On first access DataStore copies the keys across and deletes the old file. After that, remove every remaining use of the old preferences so two sources of truth do not coexist.

questions.q: Where do you store sensitive values?
questions.a: Not in plain DataStore or SharedPreferences. Encrypt the value with a key generated in the Android Keystore, which keeps key material in secure hardware where available, and store only the ciphertext. Prefer short-lived tokens so a leak has limited value.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The Jetpack security-crypto EncryptedSharedPreferences library has been deprecated, so new code typically pairs DataStore with its own Keystore-backed encryption or a maintained library such as Tink.

questions.q: Why did Android move to Kotlin first?
questions.a: Null safety in the type system, far less boilerplate (data classes, properties, default arguments), coroutines for asynchronous code, extension functions that made KTX possible, and full two-way interop so apps could migrate file by file. Jetpack Compose and most new Jetpack APIs are Kotlin only.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: The cost side: slower builds than Java, annotation processing moved from kapt to KSP, and binary compatibility of public Kotlin APIs needs deliberate care in libraries.

questions.q: How does Kotlin compile for Android?
questions.a: kotlinc produces JVM bytecode (.class) exactly as javac does. D8 then converts all classes to DEX, and R8 shrinks and optimises them. At runtime ART neither knows nor cares which language a class came from.

questions.q: What problems appear in a mixed Java and Kotlin codebase?
questions.a: Platform types that hide nulls, Java callers that bypass Kotlin read-only collections, default arguments invisible to Java, companion members needing @JvmStatic, annotation processors that must see both languages, and build order: Kotlin compiles first and reads Java sources, then javac compiles Java against the Kotlin output.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How would you plan a migration of a 300-file Java module?

questions.q: Does Kotlin have checked exceptions? What are the consequences?
questions.a: No. Every exception is unchecked. Code is shorter, but nothing reminds you that a call can fail. Teams compensate by returning sealed result types from layers such as repositories and by catching at well-defined boundaries.

questions.q: What is the Kotlin equivalent of Java static, and how does it look in bytecode?
questions.a: Top-level declarations compile to static members of a FileNameKt class. Companion object members compile to instance methods on a nested Companion class, unless marked @JvmStatic or const, which produce real statics on the outer class.

questions.q: What are the four Android app components?
questions.a: Activity (a screen), Service (work without UI), BroadcastReceiver (reacts to system or app events) and ContentProvider (shares structured data across apps). Each is declared in the manifest and can be an entry point the system starts directly.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Because any component can be the first thing started, the process may come up without your launcher Activity ever running. Initialisation that everything depends on belongs in Application.onCreate or an on-demand initialiser.

questions.q: What is Context, and which one should you use?
questions.a: Context is the handle to the app environment: resources, system services, files, starting components. Activity context carries the theme and the lifetime of one screen. Application context lives as long as the process. Use the Activity for anything visual (inflating, dialogs) and the application context for anything that outlives a screen.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What goes wrong if a singleton stores an Activity context?

questions.q: What is an Intent? Explicit versus implicit?
questions.a: A message describing an operation. An explicit Intent names the target component and is used inside your app. An implicit Intent names an action and data, and the system resolves it against intent filters, for example opening a URL or sharing text.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: From Android 11, package visibility rules mean you must declare <queries> to resolve other apps. From Android 12, components with intent filters must set android:exported explicitly.

questions.q: How does an app process start?
questions.a: The system asks Zygote, a pre-warmed process with the framework classes loaded, to fork. The new process binds to the system server, creates the Application object and calls its onCreate, then creates the requested component. Forking Zygote is why starts are fast and why framework memory is shared.

questions.q: What is Binder?
questions.a: The kernel-level IPC mechanism of Android. Every call to a system service, such as startActivity or getSystemService, is a Binder transaction to another process. Transactions share a 1 MB buffer per process, which is the origin of TransactionTooLargeException.

questions.q: Why does a Fragment have two lifecycles?
questions.a: The Fragment object and its view have different lifetimes. On the back stack the view is destroyed (onDestroyView) while the Fragment instance survives. That is why view references and bindings must be cleared in onDestroyView, and why UI observers use viewLifecycleOwner, not the Fragment itself.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What leaks if you keep the binding in a field without clearing it?

questions.q: add versus replace in a FragmentTransaction?
questions.a: add places a fragment on top and leaves the existing one resumed underneath. replace removes the existing fragments in the container and adds the new one. With addToBackStack, the replaced fragment has its view destroyed and recreated on return.

questions.q: How should two fragments communicate?
questions.a: Not directly. Share a ViewModel scoped to the Activity or navigation graph, or use the Fragment Result API for one-shot results. Both survive recreation; direct references and target fragments do not.

questions.q: How does RecyclerView recycle views?
questions.a: It creates only enough ViewHolders to fill the screen plus a small cache. As a row scrolls off, its holder goes to a pool and is rebound with new data in onBindViewHolder instead of inflating a new view. Inflation is the expensive part; binding is cheap.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Typical faults: work in onBindViewHolder, missing stable ids or DiffUtil causing full rebinds, nested RecyclerViews without a shared RecycledViewPool, and state left on a recycled holder from its previous item.

questions.q: What does DiffUtil do?
questions.a: It compares the old and new lists and produces the minimal set of insert, remove, move and change operations, so RecyclerView animates and rebinds only what changed. ListAdapter runs the diff on a background thread.

questions.q: ViewBinding versus DataBinding versus findViewById?
questions.a: findViewById is untyped and can return null at runtime. ViewBinding generates a typed class per layout with null safety and no runtime cost. DataBinding adds expressions and observable binding in XML at the price of slower builds and logic in layouts. ViewBinding is the usual choice for View-based screens.

questions.q: What are the measure, layout and draw passes?
questions.a: Measure: each parent asks its children how big they want to be within constraints. Layout: each parent positions its children. Draw: each view renders into the canvas. Nested weights and deep hierarchies cause repeated measure passes, which is the reason for ConstraintLayout and flat hierarchies.

questions.q: Explain MVVM on Android.
questions.a: The View (Activity, Fragment or composable) renders state and forwards user events. The ViewModel holds UI state, exposes it as StateFlow or LiveData, and calls the data layer. The Model is repositories and data sources. The ViewModel has no reference to the View, so it survives rotation and can be unit tested on the JVM.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How do you deliver a one-off event such as a snackbar?

questions.q: MVVM versus MVI?
questions.a: In MVVM a ViewModel may expose several observable properties and several methods. MVI narrows this to one immutable state object, a set of intents, and a reducer that produces the next state. MVI makes state changes traceable and reproducible, at the cost of more boilerplate and care around large state objects.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Most production code is MVVM with a single UiState data class and unidirectional flow, which gets most of the benefit of MVI.

questions.q: What is the dependency rule in Clean Architecture?
questions.a: Source code dependencies point inwards. The domain layer (entities, use cases, repository interfaces) depends on nothing. The data and UI layers depend on the domain. Implementations are supplied from outside through dependency injection.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Know when not to: a use case that only forwards one repository call adds a file and no value. Google's guidance treats the domain layer as optional.

questions.q: Why use a Repository?
questions.a: It gives the rest of the app one API for a kind of data and hides where it comes from: network, database, memory cache. It decides freshness and conflict rules, and it can be replaced with a fake in tests.

questions.q: How would you modularise a large app?
questions.a: By feature, with shared core modules: feature modules depend on core (ui, data, domain, common) and never on each other; the app module wires them. Benefits are parallel and incremental builds, enforced boundaries and ownership. Costs are navigation between features and a more complex dependency graph.

questions.q: What problem does dependency injection solve?
questions.a: A class that creates its own collaborators is welded to them. Receiving them through the constructor makes the dependencies explicit, lets tests pass fakes, and lets one place decide lifetimes such as singleton or per screen.

questions.q: How does Hilt work?
questions.a: Hilt is Dagger with a predefined component hierarchy tied to Android lifecycles: SingletonComponent, ActivityRetainedComponent, ViewModelComponent, ActivityComponent, FragmentComponent. Code is generated at compile time; @AndroidEntryPoint injects framework classes, @HiltViewModel injects ViewModels, and @Module with @Provides or @Binds tells it how to build types it cannot construct.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What is the difference between @Provides and @Binds?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Compile-time generation means errors appear in the build and there is no reflection at runtime, at the cost of build time. Koin resolves at runtime: faster builds, later failures.

questions.q: Service locator versus dependency injection?
questions.a: With a locator the class asks a global registry for what it needs, so dependencies are hidden inside the class. With injection they are passed in and visible in the constructor. Injection is easier to test and reason about.

questions.q: Cold flow versus hot flow?
questions.a: A cold Flow runs its producer block for each collector and does nothing until collected. A hot flow (StateFlow, SharedFlow) is active independent of collectors and shares emissions among them.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How do you turn a cold flow into a hot one?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: stateIn or shareIn with SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000): upstream stops five seconds after the last collector leaves, which survives rotation without restarting and still stops work in the background.

questions.q: StateFlow versus SharedFlow versus LiveData?
questions.a: StateFlow always has a value, replays the latest to new collectors and drops equal consecutive values: use it for state. SharedFlow has configurable replay and no initial value: use it for events. LiveData is lifecycle-aware and main-thread only, with few operators; StateFlow with lifecycle-aware collection replaces it in Kotlin code.

questions.q: What does flatMapLatest do, and where is it used?
questions.a: For each upstream value it starts a new inner flow and cancels the previous one. Search is the standard case: query.debounce(300).distinctUntilChanged().flatMapLatest { api.search(it) } so only the latest query produces results.

questions.q: How do you collect a Flow safely in the UI?
questions.a: In Views: lifecycleScope.launch { repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) { flow.collect { } } }. In Compose: collectAsStateWithLifecycle(). Both stop collecting when the UI is in the background.

questions.q: How do Retrofit and OkHttp divide the work?
questions.a: Retrofit turns an annotated interface into HTTP calls and converts bodies with a converter such as kotlinx.serialization or Moshi. OkHttp is the HTTP client underneath: connections, pooling, TLS, caching, interceptors and timeouts.

questions.q: Application interceptor versus network interceptor?
questions.a: An application interceptor runs once per call, before caching and redirects: use it for auth headers and logging intent. A network interceptor runs for every network request including redirects and retries and sees the real wire data.

questions.q: How do you refresh an expired token?
questions.a: Use an OkHttp Authenticator, which is invoked on a 401. Refresh the token under a lock so parallel requests do not all refresh, then retry the original request with the new token. Stop after one failed attempt to avoid a loop.

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: Check whether another request already refreshed while you waited for the lock, by comparing the token on the failed request with the stored one.

questions.q: How does Room work, and why is it main-safe?
questions.a: Room generates DAO implementations from annotated interfaces at compile time and verifies SQL against the schema. suspend DAO functions and Flow queries run on a Room-managed executor. Flow queries re-emit whenever a table they read is invalidated.

questions.q: What does offline-first mean in practice?
questions.a: The local database is the single source of truth. The UI observes the database. Network responses are written to the database, never shown directly. Writes go to the database first and are synchronised later, usually with WorkManager, with a strategy for conflicts.

questions.q: What commonly leaks memory on Android?
questions.a: A long-lived object holding a short-lived one: static or singleton references to an Activity, View or Context; listeners never unregistered; inner classes and lambdas held by background work; coroutines in GlobalScope; Fragment view bindings not cleared in onDestroyView.

points.title: Follow-up
items: How does LeakCanary detect a leak?

points.title: What a senior answer adds
items: LeakCanary watches destroyed Activities, Fragments, views and ViewModels with weak references. If one is still reachable after a garbage collection it dumps the heap and reports the shortest strong reference path from a GC root.

questions.q: How do you improve app startup time?
questions.a: Measure first with Macrobenchmark and the reportFullyDrawn marker. Then: remove work from Application.onCreate, initialise libraries lazily, avoid disk and network on the main thread, keep the first screen layout light, and ship a Baseline Profile so ART compiles the startup path ahead of time.

questions.q: What causes jank?
questions.a: A frame taking longer than its budget (about 16.6 ms at 60 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz). Causes: main-thread work, heavy or nested layouts, overdraw, large bitmaps, garbage collection from allocation in hot paths, and in Compose unnecessary recomposition.

questions.q: What is a Baseline Profile?
questions.a: A list of classes and methods on critical user journeys shipped inside the app. ART uses it to compile those paths ahead of time at install, so the first runs are not spent interpreting and JIT compiling.

questions.q: How do you test a ViewModel that uses coroutines?
questions.a: Run tests with runTest. Replace Dispatchers.Main with a test dispatcher using Dispatchers.setMain in a rule. Inject dispatchers into classes that switch context so tests can supply the test dispatcher. Assert on the StateFlow value or collect emissions with a library such as Turbine.

questions.q: Local unit tests versus instrumented tests?
questions.a: Local tests run on the JVM of your machine: fast, no Android framework unless Robolectric simulates it. Instrumented tests run on a device or emulator with the real framework: slower, required for UI and integration behaviour.

questions.q: Mock, fake or stub?
questions.a: A stub returns fixed answers. A mock records calls so you can verify interactions. A fake is a light working implementation, such as an in-memory repository. Prefer fakes for your own interfaces: tests then check behaviour instead of call sequences.

questions.q: Where do you store an auth token?
questions.a: In app-private storage, encrypted with a key held in the Android Keystore, so the key material never leaves secure hardware where available. Never in plain SharedPreferences, external storage or logs. Prefer short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens.

questions.q: What is certificate pinning and what is the risk?
questions.a: The app accepts only server certificates whose public key matches a known hash, which defeats interception through a rogue or user-installed certificate authority. The risk is self-inflicted outage when the server certificate changes: always ship a backup pin and a way to update.

questions.q: What does R8 do?
questions.a: Shrinks (removes unused code), optimises (inlines, merges) and obfuscates (renames) the app, and converts to DEX. Code reached by reflection, such as JSON models and JNI entry points, needs keep rules or it will be removed or renamed.

questions.q: Build type versus product flavor versus build variant?
questions.a: A build type is how to build: debug or release, with settings such as minification and signing. A flavor is what to build: free or paid, staging or production. A variant is one combination of the two, such as stagingDebug.

questions.q: APK versus AAB?
questions.a: An APK is the installable file. An Android App Bundle is a publishing format: Google Play generates optimised split APKs per device from it, for density, ABI and language. Play requires bundles for new apps.

questions.q: implementation versus api in Gradle?
questions.a: implementation keeps the dependency private to the module, so changing it recompiles only that module. api exposes it to consumers, so a change recompiles everything downstream. Default to implementation.

questions.q: How do you roll out a risky release?
questions.a: Internal testing, then closed and open tracks, then a staged production rollout starting at a small percentage while watching crash-free rate and ANR rate. Halt the rollout if they regress. A released version cannot be un-released, so the fix is a new version; feature flags let you switch the risky code off without one.

questions.q: How do you approach a mobile system design question?
questions.a: Clarify requirements and constraints (offline, real time, scale, devices). Sketch the screens and main flows. Define the client architecture: layers, modules, state. Define the API and data model. Then go deep on the hard parts: caching and sync, pagination, real-time updates, background work, failure handling, security, testing and release. State trade-offs as you choose.

questions.q: Design the basket of an e-commerce app.
questions.a: Server owns price and stock truth; the client keeps a local copy in Room for instant UI. Quantity changes update the local row optimistically, are sent to the server debounced, and are reconciled with the response. Handle conflicts such as out-of-stock by showing the server result. A sealed UiState drives the screen, and the badge count is a Flow from the database.

points.title: Follow-up
items: What happens if the user changes quantity offline?

questions.q: How would you deliver real-time order tracking?
questions.a: A WebSocket or server-sent events while the screen is visible, with polling as fallback and push notifications when the app is in the background. Collect only while STARTED, reconnect with backoff, and treat every message as a full state or include a sequence number so missed messages are detectable.
